chunks.heading: Products
chunks.text:
Each product enforces the same policies you write in the [Platform](/platform), at a different point in your agent's path.

<Cards>
  <Card label="Product" icon="Waypoints" title="Intent Gateway" href="/products/intent-gateway">
    Policy on every tool call your agent's model returns. Change one base URL, no SDK.
  </Card>

  <Card label="Product" icon="Container" title="Intent Container" href="/products/intent-container">
    Holds each agent task to its objective on files, processes and network calls, down to the kernel.
  </Card>
</Cards>

chunks.heading: Connect an agent in one line
chunks.text:
Point your agent's SDK at the gateway. Your provider key, prompts and tools stay as they are.

```bash
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://gw.armoriq.ai/v1/t/<gateway-key>/a/<agent-id>
```

chunks.heading: Intent Gateway capabilities
chunks.text:
<Cards>
  <Card icon="Rocket" title="Quickstart" href="/products/intent-gateway/quickstart">
    Create a gateway key and send your first governed request.
  </Card>

  <Card icon="ShieldCheck" title="How enforcement works" href="/products/intent-gateway/enforcement">
    What the gateway does with each tool call, and what happens when ArmorIQ can't decide.
  </Card>

  <Card icon="Eye" title="Monitor mode" href="/products/intent-gateway/monitor-mode">

  </Card>
</Cards>

chunks.heading: Which one to start with
chunks.text:
* Your agent calls a model API through an OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini SDK: start with [Intent Gateway](/products/intent-gateway/quickstart). It takes a base URL change.
* Your agent runs in a sandbox and acts on files, shells and local sockets that never pass through an API: look at [Intent Container](/products/intent-container).
* You want enforcement inside your own code, per step: use the [SDK](/sdk).

chunks.heading: Getting started on OpenShell
chunks.text:
NVIDIA OpenShell is the surface available today. The ArmorIQ OpenShell middleware registers as supervisor middleware and is called before each sandbox request leaves, so an agent in an OpenShell sandbox is held to the plan its model issued. Nothing in OpenShell is modified, nothing is installed inside the sandbox, and the agent never learns it exists.

<Callout>
  This surface enforces at the tool-call connection OpenShell already owns. The kernel checks on files, processes and local sockets arrive on the [Linux and Docker surfaces](/products/intent-container#where-it-runs), both in preview.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
OpenShell calls the service at `PRE_CREDENTIALS`, before credentials are injected, for every outbound request a sandbox makes. It answers allow or deny, and OpenShell enforces the answer.

| Check          | Comes from                                                    | Refuses                                    |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Declared scope | `declared_tools`, written once by whoever creates the sandbox | A tool the sandbox was never set up to use |
| Captured plan  | The model's latest reply, with `-capture-plan`                | A tool the model did not ask for           |
| Policy         | The ArmorIQ control plane                                     | A tool the agent is not permitted to call  |

A call the model did not ask for is refused with `intent_drift_from_plan` before any policy is consulted. The reply is read before the sandbox receives it, so the plan is in place before the agent can act on it.

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
* OpenShell v0.1.2. Request-side checks work on earlier gateways with config `version = 1`; holding a sandbox to its model's plan needs v0.1.0 or later.
* An ArmorIQ organization and an API key, from [platform.armoriq.ai](https://platform.armoriq.ai). Policies are authored in the same organization, so the key and the policies that govern your agents live together.
* At least one policy. A new organization has no policies and the default is to block, so add one before your first run or every call is denied.

<Callout title="See it on one host first">
  The [examples/intent-demo](https://github.com/armoriq/armoriq-openshell-middleware/tree/main/examples/intent-demo) in the repo runs the whole thing on one Linux host, with a stand-in model and a scripted agent: the same call refused when the model did not ask for it, and allowed when it did.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: 1. Get the middleware
chunks.text:
A prebuilt `linux-amd64` binary ships in the [repo](https://github.com/armoriq/armoriq-openshell-middleware). To build it yourself:

```bash
go build -o openshell-middleware ./cmd/openshell-middleware
```

A single static binary, no runtime dependencies.

chunks.heading: 2. Create an API key and a starter policy
chunks.text:
Issue an API key in the dashboard. Then add a policy, since the default is to block. A minimal policy that exercises both decision paths, using two tool names as an example. Substitute tools your own agents actually call:

```yaml
name: OpenShell trial
scope:
  target_type: org
default_action: block
rules:
  - tool: your_read_tool     # allowed, and declared by the sandbox below
    action: allow
  - tool: your_write_tool    # declared by the sandbox, but policy refuses it
    action: block
```

A third tool that the sandbox never declares at all shows the in-process refusal, without a policy being consulted.

chunks.heading: 3. Run the middleware
chunks.text:
```bash
ARMORIQ_API_KEY=<key> ./openshell-middleware \
  -listen 0.0.0.0:50071 \
  -iap-url https://api.armoriq.ai \
  -timeout 2500ms
```

Add `-capture-plan` to hold each sandbox to its model's plan, on OpenShell v0.1.0 or later.

<Callout type="warn">
  Start the middleware before the gateway. OpenShell refuses to start when a registered middleware is unavailable. The key is read from the environment, not a flag, because a flag is visible in `ps` to every user on the host.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: 4. Register it with the gateway
chunks.text:
In your gateway config, normally `~/.config/openshell/gateway.toml`:

```toml
[openshell]
version = 2

[[openshell.supervisor.middleware]]
name = "armoriq-intent"
grpc_endpoint = "http://172.17.0.1:50071"
allow_insecure_transport = true   # same host only; use TLS otherwise
max_payload_bytes = 262144
timeout = "3s"
```

OpenShell v0.1.0 and later require `version = 2` and reject `version = 1`.

<Callout type="warn">
  `grpc_endpoint` must be reachable from the gateway and from every sandbox supervisor. Supervisors run inside the container, so `127.0.0.1` there is the container's own loopback, not your host. On a single box the Docker bridge address works. This is the most common setup mistake: the deployment looks healthy while every request is denied with `binding_not_described` because the supervisor could not reach the service. Raise the timeout above the 500ms default; a policy decision takes roughly half a second, and the failure mode is closed.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: 5. Attach it to a sandbox
chunks.text:
In the sandbox policy:

```yaml
network_middlewares:
  armoriq:
    name: ArmorIQ intent enforcement
    middleware: armoriq-intent
    order: 10
    on_error: fail_closed
    config:
      agent_id: "<the agent this sandbox runs>"
      declared_tools: ["your_read_tool", "your_write_tool"]
      # model_hosts: ["api.openai.com"]  # with -capture-plan
      # require_captured_plan: true      # only with -capture-plan
    endpoints:
      include: ["mcp.example.internal"]
```

`config` is delivered to the middleware on every request, so identity and the declared tool set travel with the sandbox. Apply it with `sandbox create --policy`. Keep `on_error: fail_closed`.

chunks.heading: What the workload sees
chunks.text:
Only a short reason code reaches the requester. Everything else stays in the logs.

| Code                         | Meaning                                                          |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `intent_blocked_by_policy`   | A policy refused it.                                             |
| `tool_not_in_plan`           | Not among the tools the sandbox declared.                        |
| `intent_drift_from_plan`     | Not asked for by the model's latest reply, with `-capture-plan`. |
| `intent_awaiting_approval`   | The decision needs a human; the call does not proceed.           |
| `intent_action_not_named`    | No tool could be identified in the request.                      |
| `intent_verification_failed` | No decision could be obtained, so the request is denied.         |

chunks.heading: Where to go next
chunks.text:
* The [Linux and Docker surfaces](/products/intent-container#where-it-runs) add kernel checks on files, processes and local sockets through KAP, both in preview.
* Request preview access, or ask about a platform not listed, on the [Intent Container product page](https://armoriq.ai/products/intent-container).
* The [Intent Containers series](https://armoriq.substack.com/p/containers-isolated-processes-ai) explains the design in five parts.

chunks.heading: Intent Container
chunks.text:
Agents work for hours across shells, files, APIs and other agents. Their access is granted once, at the start, and stays in place long after the task has moved on. File writes, process launches and local sockets never pass through an API gateway, so a gateway alone cannot hold them to the plan.

Intent Container holds every task to its objective.

chunks.heading: What it enforces
chunks.text:
* **Inherited authority.** Every process the task starts inherits the objective's authority, including child processes and threads.
* **Checks below the API.** Checks run on file access, program launch, network connections and IPC, not only on API calls.
* **Live changes.** Change an objective's authority while the task runs. Anything outside it fails closed from the next check.
* **Attributed decisions.** Each allow and deny is tied to the objective and the version of its authority that produced it.

chunks.heading: How it is built
chunks.text:
| Layer   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| intentd | Tracks each objective, its lineage and the authority it grants, and binds agent workloads to it before they start. Runs today on Google Agent Substrate.                         |
| KAP     | A Linux kernel subsystem for objective-scoped authority. Intent Lineage Groups are its core object, the kernel's security hooks enforce it, and securityfs is its control plane. |
| iVisor  | A userspace application kernel that applies the same checks where you can't change the kernel. Experimental.                                                                     |

chunks.heading: Where it runs
chunks.text:
| Platform               | Status    |                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| NVIDIA OpenShell       | Available | Intent enforcement through OpenShell middleware, with no change to the agent. [Get started](/products/intent-container/getting-started) and [View on GitHub](https://github.com/armoriq/armoriq-openshell-middleware) |
| Google Agent Substrate | Preview   | intentd runs on Substrate and binds each Actor to its objective.                                                                                                                                                      |
| Linux                  | Preview   | Run KAP in a supported kernel, or iVisor where you can't change the kernel.                                                                                                                                           |
| Docker Sandboxes       | Preview   | A coding agent in Docker's sandboxes, bound to its objective and enforced at the kernel by KAP.                                                                                                                       |
| Kubernetes             | Coming    | Intent Containers for agent sandboxes on Kubernetes.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| AWS Bedrock            | Coming    | Intent Containers for agents on Bedrock.                                                                                                                                                                              |

Start on the surface available today with [Getting started on OpenShell](/products/intent-container/getting-started). Request preview access, or ask about a platform not listed, on the [Intent Container product page](https://armoriq.ai/products/intent-container). The [Intent Containers series](https://armoriq.substack.com/p/containers-isolated-processes-ai) explains the design in five parts.

chunks.heading: How enforcement works
chunks.text: Enforcement applies when the base URL names an agent (`/v1/t/<gateway-key>/a/<agent-id>`). Without an agent, the gateway records the traffic and changes nothing.

chunks.heading: Each model turn
chunks.text:
1. Your agent sends a request. The gateway forwards it to the provider with your provider key untouched.
2. The model replies. If the reply contains tool calls, the gateway registers them with ArmorIQ as a plan and receives a signed intent token for it.
3. Each tool call is checked against the agent's active policy, using that token.
4. The gateway relays the reply. Allowed tool calls are unchanged. Blocked tool calls are removed, and a note naming the rule is added to the reply's text.

Streaming replies follow the same steps. Text streams to your agent as it arrives, and each tool call is released or withheld once its check returns.

chunks.heading: Verdicts
chunks.text:
| Verdict | What your agent receives                                                                                                                            |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Allow   | The tool call, exactly as the model wrote it.                                                                                                       |
| Block   | No tool call. The reply's text ends with a note such as `Tool call "record_payment" was blocked by policy: block:record_payment#0`.                 |
| Hold    | Treated as a block today. The gateway creates an approval request in the dashboard, but approving it does not release the agent's next attempt yet. |

An agent with no active policy has its tool calls allowed, and each one is recorded.

chunks.heading: When ArmorIQ can't decide
chunks.text:
If the check can't complete because ArmorIQ is unreachable, slow or rate limited, or the plan is refused, the gateway withholds the named agent's tool call and gives the reason in the note. Calls are never released just because a check failed.

| Situation                                                | Result                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| The agent in the URL doesn't exist in your organization  | Every tool call is withheld with `agent_unresolved` |
| The agent is disabled or still a draft                   | Every tool call is withheld                         |
| ArmorIQ is unreachable, times out or rate limits the key | The tool call is withheld                           |

chunks.heading: What is recorded
chunks.text:
* **A trace per request** in [Observability](/platform/observability): the model, token use, each tool call and its verdict, under the service `armoriq-llm-gateway`.
* **The plan** for each turn that asked for tools, with its signed intent token.
* **The agent's tools.** When a named agent's requests declare tools, the gateway sends that list to ArmorIQ, so [Policy Studio](/platform/policy-studio) can show them when you write rules.

Your provider key is forwarded to the provider unchanged. The gateway never stores or logs it.

chunks.heading: Intent Gateway
chunks.text:
Intent Gateway sits between your agent and its model provider. Your agent's SDK sends its requests to `gw.armoriq.ai` instead of the provider. The gateway forwards each request with your provider key untouched, then checks every tool call in the model's reply against your agent's policy before your code receives it.

Your framework, prompts, tools and provider key stay as they are. The only change is the base URL.

chunks.heading: What you get
chunks.text:
* **Every request on your dashboard.** Requests, tool calls and token use appear in [Observability](/platform/observability) under the agent that made them, whatever framework the agent runs on.
* **Policy on every tool call.** Name an agent in the URL and each tool call is checked against that agent's active policy. Allowed calls pass through unchanged. Blocked calls are removed from the reply, and the reply carries a note naming the rule that stopped them.
* **A signed plan for every turn.** Each model reply that asks for tools is recorded as a plan with a signed intent token, the same record the ArmorIQ SDK produces.
* **Closed when in doubt.** If ArmorIQ can't reach a decision for a named agent, that agent's tool call is withheld.

chunks.heading: Two ways to connect
chunks.text:
| Base URL                                                | What happens                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `https://gw.armoriq.ai/v1/t/<gateway-key>`              | Every request is recorded. Nothing is blocked.                                                |
| `https://gw.armoriq.ai/v1/t/<gateway-key>/a/<agent-id>` | Every request is recorded, and every tool call is checked against that agent's active policy. |

Start with the first to see your traffic, then add the agent to turn on enforcement.

chunks.heading: Supported clients
chunks.text:
| Client        | What works through the gateway                                      |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| OpenAI SDK    | Chat Completions, streaming and non-streaming, including tool calls |
| Anthropic SDK | Messages, streaming and non-streaming, including tool use           |
| Gemini        | Gemini models through the OpenAI SDK, with your Gemini key          |

chunks.heading: Limits today
chunks.text:
* **Approvals.** A hold rule works like a block. The gateway creates the approval request, but approving it does not release the agent's next attempt yet.
* **Claude through the OpenAI SDK.** Not supported. Use the Anthropic SDK for Claude models.
* **Rate.** A gateway key can make about 120 policy calls a minute. Each enforced model turn uses one plan, plus one check per tool call. Past that limit, a named agent's tool calls are withheld.
* **Long requests.** A request that runs longer than 5 minutes is cut off.
* **Agents.** Enforcement applies to an agent that already exists in ArmorIQ and is active. See [Add an agent](/platform/agents/add-agent).

chunks.heading: Next steps
chunks.text:
* **[Quickstart](/products/intent-gateway/quickstart)** - Connect an agent in a few minutes.
* **[How enforcement works](/products/intent-gateway/enforcement)** - What the gateway does with each tool call, and what happens when ArmorIQ can't decide.

chunks.heading: Monitor mode
chunks.text: Monitor mode checks every tool call against the agent's policy and records the verdict, but stops nothing. Run it for a week or two, read what policy would have done, adjust the rules, then switch it off to enforce.

chunks.heading: Turn it on
chunks.text:
1. Open **Gateway** in the dashboard sidebar.
2. Turn on **Monitor mode** under the page title. Org admins and IAM admins can change it.
3. Keep the agent named in your base URL (`/v1/t/<gateway-key>/a/<agent-id>`). Calls without an agent are recorded but not checked.

The change applies within about 90 seconds. It covers every agent in the organization that reaches ArmorIQ through Intent Gateway. Agents using the ArmorIQ SDK are not affected.

chunks.heading: What changes in Monitor mode
chunks.text:
|                                         | Monitor mode on                           | Monitor mode off                              |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Tool calls your agent receives          | Every call, exactly as the model wrote it | Allowed calls only; blocked calls are removed |
| Each call is checked against the policy | Yes                                       | Yes                                           |
| A held call creates an approval request | No, since the call already ran            | Yes                                           |
| A plan is marked failed or held         | No                                        | Yes                                           |
| Killing an agent stops its calls        | No                                        | Yes                                           |

Responses reach your agent with no added delay: the gateway relays the provider's reply first and checks the calls after.

chunks.heading: Read the report
chunks.text:
Below the switch, **What policy would have done** covers the last 7 days:

* Totals of calls that would be blocked, would be held, and were allowed.
* A row per tool and verdict, with the policy that decided it.
* The latest calls policy would have stopped, with the reason.

Use **Adjust policies** to change a rule, then watch the counts on new traffic. When the report only shows calls you want stopped, turn Monitor mode off.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
* ArmorIQ checks up to 120 calls per minute per gateway key, shared with plan creation. Past that, a call is recorded as not checked and still runs.
* A held call shows as "would hold", even if an approval for it already exists. After you switch Monitor mode off, held calls create approval requests, but approving one does not yet release the agent's next attempt. See [How enforcement works](/products/intent-gateway/enforcement).

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
* An ArmorIQ organization. See [Getting started](/platform/getting-started).
* To enforce policy, the agent registered in ArmorIQ with an active policy. See [Add an agent](/platform/agents/add-agent) and [Policies](/platform/policies).
* An agent that uses the OpenAI SDK or the Anthropic SDK.

chunks.heading: 1. Create a gateway key
chunks.text:
In the dashboard, open **Gateway** and click **Create gateway key**. Give the key a name you will recognise in audit logs and click **Create key**. The key is shown once, inside the base URL.

<Callout type="warn">
  The base URL contains the key. Anyone who has it can send traffic as your organization, so store it like any other API key and keep it out of source control.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: 2. Choose the agent
chunks.text:
Under **Agent policy**, pick the agent whose policy should apply. The base URL gains `/a/<agent-id>`.

Pick **No agent** to record traffic without blocking anything. You can add the agent later by changing the URL.

chunks.heading: 3. Point your SDK at the gateway
chunks.text:
Set the base URL your SDK already reads. Keep your provider key exactly as it is.

<Tabs items="['OpenAI, environment', 'OpenAI, TypeScript', 'OpenAI, Python', 'Anthropic, environment', 'Anthropic, TypeScript', 'Anthropic, Python']">
  <Tab value="OpenAI, environment">
    ```bash
    OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://gw.armoriq.ai/v1/t/<gateway-key>/a/<agent-id>
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="OpenAI, TypeScript">
    ```ts
    import OpenAI from "openai";

    const client = new OpenAI({
    ```

chunks.heading: 4. Send a request
chunks.text:
Run your agent as usual. The **Gateway** page shows **Gateway traffic seen** as soon as the first request arrives, and the trace appears in [Observability](/platform/observability).

To see enforcement, ask your agent to do something its policy blocks. The blocked tool call is missing from the reply, and the reply ends with a note such as:

```text
Tool call "record_payment" was blocked by policy: block:record_payment#0
```

chunks.heading: Optional: name the person using the agent
Glossary
chunks.text: Single source of truth for ArmorIQ-specific terminology. Every term here is also linked from the page where it's first used.

chunks.heading: Agent
chunks.text: An AI software entity that calls tools, typically an LLM-backed program (Claude, ChatGPT, a custom agent, a framework like Google ADK / CrewAI / LangChain), invoking external functionality. In ArmorIQ, every agent is registered with an `agent_id` and is bound by a [policy](/platform/policies).

chunks.heading: AIQraph
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's interactive topology visualization of agents, MCP servers, tools, and policies: how they connect and what's allowed to call what. See [AIQraph](/platform/aiqraph).

chunks.heading: API Key
chunks.text: The authentication credential the SDK and CLI use to talk to the ArmorIQ platform. Prefixed `ak_live_` (production), `ak_test_` (sandbox), or `ak_claw_` (legacy ArmorClaw standalone; no longer issued). See [API Keys](/platform/api-keys).

chunks.heading: ArmorClaude
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's integration product for Claude: installation and configuration to wire Claude agents through the ArmorIQ proxy. See [ArmorClaude](/armorclaude).

chunks.heading: ArmorClaw
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's security plugin for OpenClaw agents: intent verification, drift detection and policy enforcement. Uses standard `ak_live_` keys issued by the dashboard. See [ArmorClaw](/armorclaw).

chunks.heading: ArmorCodex
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's integration for code-generation agents and editors. See [ArmorCodex](/armorcodex).

chunks.heading: ArmorCopilot
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's integration for GitHub Copilot-style agents. See [ArmorCopilot](/armorcopilot).

chunks.heading: ArmorHealth
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's health-insurance-compliance product: coverage rules, claims processing, provider networks, and PHI access controls for AI agents. See [ArmorHealth](/armorhealth).

chunks.heading: ArmorPay
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's financial-compliance product for AI payment agents: amount thresholds, velocity limits, and transaction controls. See [ArmorPay](/armorpay).

chunks.heading: `armoriq.yaml`
chunks.text: The config-as-code manifest for an ArmorIQ-protected agent. Declares identity, MCP servers, policy, and intent settings. Has a published [JSON Schema](/schemas/armoriq.schema.json). Point your editor at it for IntelliSense. See [the YAML reference](/platform/sdk-cli/armoriq-yaml).

chunks.heading: CSRG (Canonical Structured Reasoning Graph)
chunks.text: Cryptographic proof that the tool an agent actually invoked matches the tool the LLM reasoned about. Enforced by default; can be disabled per-config via `intent.require_csrg: false` (not recommended in production). See [Intent Intelligence: How It Works](/platform/intent-intelligence/how-it-works).

chunks.heading: Delegation Request
chunks.text: A human-in-the-loop escalation raised when a tool call exceeds what an agent's policy allows on its own (typically a monetary or authority limit) instead of failing the call outright. The plan is held until a human with a higher-ranked role than the requester approves or rejects it (a requester can never approve their own request); approval records a `Delegate` [trust delta](#trust-delta). Separate from IAP's own agent-to-agent trust chain. See [Plans Governance](/platform/plans#delegation-and-approval).

chunks.heading: Drift
chunks.text: The condition where an agent's runtime tool invocation diverges from its signed Intent Assurance Plan. The proxy detects drift and refuses the call. See [Intent Intelligence](/platform/intent-intelligence).

chunks.heading: IAP (Intent Assurance Plan)
chunks.text: ArmorIQ's core security primitive. The proxy intercepts every tool call between an agent and an MCP server, derives a cryptographically signed *plan* of what the agent intends to do, and refuses to forward any call that doesn't match the plan. See [Intent Intelligence](/platform/intent-intelligence).

chunks.heading: Intent Token
chunks.text: A short-lived token (default `ttl_seconds: 300`) issued by the proxy after a plan is accepted. The SDK passes it on every `invoke()` call; the proxy refuses calls without a valid, matching token. Get one via `client.get_intent_token(plan)`.

chunks.heading: Kill Switch
chunks.text: A per-agent, enforcement-time block: while active, every tool call the agent makes is refused with `enforcementAction: block` before policy or OPA evaluation even runs, regardless of what any policy would otherwise allow. Set for a preset or custom duration, or indefinitely, from the agent's **Controls** tab, or via `POST /iap/agent/:id/kill` and lifted via `/iap/agent/:id/unkill`. Separate from [revoke](#revoke), which disables an agent in the registry instead. See [Agent Controls](/platform/agents/controls).

chunks.heading: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
chunks.text: The open JSON-RPC protocol AI agents use to call external tools (file systems, databases, APIs, etc.). ArmorIQ's proxy speaks MCP on both sides: agents talk to the proxy, the proxy talks to your MCP servers. See [MCP Servers](/platform/mcp-servers).

chunks.heading: MCP Server
chunks.text: A server that exposes tools to AI agents over MCP. ArmorIQ registers each MCP server under a short `id` (used in policy refs like `travel.book_flight`).

chunks.heading: Merkle Tree
chunks.text: A hash tree the CSRG uses to commit to an agent's reasoning steps; the proxy verifies a Merkle proof on every tool call.

chunks.heading: OPA (Open Policy Agent)
chunks.text: A third-party policy engine ([openpolicyagent.org](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/)) that ArmorIQ integrates for context-aware enforcement analytics. Runs alongside ArmorIQ's native policy engine. See [OPA Engine](/platform/opa-engine).

chunks.heading: Organization
chunks.text: The top-level tenancy unit in ArmorIQ. All agents, MCP servers, policies, API keys, and audit logs belong to exactly one org. See [Organizations](/platform/organizations).

chunks.heading: PAP
chunks.text: A pre-flight refinement step the SDK can call before a plan is finalized, returning a decision of `accepted`, `rejected`, or `escalated` plus any policy predicates that failed. ArmorIQ persists these decisions and exposes them read-only through the `/pap` decisions dashboard and its stats endpoints. The acronym isn't expanded anywhere in the codebase or its docs: treat "PAP" as this step's name rather than a confirmed expansion. See [Plans Governance](/platform/plans#pap-pre-flight).

chunks.heading: Personal Organization
chunks.text: The workspace organization automatically created for every account the first time it verifies its email, signs in via OAuth, or completes the CLI device-code flow (`ensurePersonalOrg`), named after the user, with them as `org_admin`. Lets a brand-new account register an MCP server, add an agent, or generate an API key immediately, with no manual setup step. See [Organizations](/platform/organizations).

chunks.heading: Policy
chunks.text: A set of allow / deny rules over `<mcp_id>.<tool_name>` pairs that determines which tools an agent can invoke. Deny always wins over allow. Authored either in `armoriq.yaml` or via [Policy Studio](/platform/policy-studio).

chunks.heading: Policy Studio
chunks.text: The form-based dashboard editor for authoring policies with a live YAML preview. See [Policy Studio](/platform/policy-studio).

chunks.heading: Proxy
chunks.text: The ArmorIQ service that sits between agents and MCP servers, enforces policy, validates intent tokens, and forwards approved calls. Hosted at `https://proxy.armoriq.ai` by default; self-hosting is possible by overriding `proxy.url` in `armoriq.yaml`.

chunks.heading: Quick Scan
chunks.text: Ad-hoc URL vulnerability scanning: paste a URL, get a security report. Useful for evaluating an MCP server before registering it. See [Quick Scan](/platform/quick-scan).

chunks.heading: Reasoning Graph
chunks.text: See [CSRG](#csrg-canonical-structured-reasoning-graph).

chunks.heading: Revoke
chunks.text: The action, on an agent's header, that sets the agent's registry status to `inactive` via `POST /agent/agents/:agentId/status`. Unlike a [kill switch](#kill-switch), revoke has no timer or expiry (it stays in effect until the agent is re-enabled) and shows a confirmation dialog before applying. Use revoke for indefinite lifecycle management; use kill to immediately stop tool calls at the enforcement layer. See [Agent Controls](/platform/agents/controls).

chunks.heading: Skill
chunks.text: A reusable, named capability an agent can be configured with. ArmorClaw scans skills for vulnerabilities. See [ArmorClaw](/armorclaw).

chunks.heading: Trust Delta
chunks.text: A signed, tamper-evident event-log entry in a plan's cryptographic chain of custody, not a reputation or trust *score*; there is no numeric trust rating for an agent or organization anywhere in the platform. Delta types include `ReAnchor` (the plan was modified after its initial commit), `Delegate` (a delegation request was approved), and `Revoke` (a token or delegation was revoked). See [Plan Detail Tabs: Trust Deltas](/platform/plans/tabs#trust-deltas).

This documentation covers every feature of the ArmorIQ platform console - from initial sign-up through advanced security configuration.

chunks.heading: AIQraph
chunks.text: AIQraph is an interactive node-and-edge visualization of your organization's estate - agents, MCP servers, tools, and policies, and how they connect. Navigate to **Graph** in the sidebar, at `/dashboard/graph`; the page itself is labeled **AIQ Graph**.

chunks.heading: Graph nodes
chunks.text:
The backend's estate endpoint emits these node types, and the graph renders most of them directly:

| Node Type                  | Description                                                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Org**                    | The organization container                                     |
| **MCPAgent**               | Registered AI agents in your organization                      |
| **MCPServer**              | MCP servers connected to your agents                           |
| **MCPTool**                | Individual tools exposed by MCP servers                        |
| **Policy** / **OpaPolicy** | Policies applied to agents or servers                          |
| **ApiKey**                 | Emitted by the backend but stripped from the rendered topology |
| **IntentPlan**             | Emitted by the backend but stripped from the rendered topology |
| **ToolInvocation**         | Only rendered in Live mode, as entries in the live feed        |

chunks.heading: Graph edges
chunks.text: Edge relationships come from the same estate endpoint: `owns`, `hosts`, `calls`, `invokes`, `executes`, `plans`, `authenticates`, `governs`, `secures`, and `compiles`.

chunks.heading: Layout options
chunks.text: The graph is rendered with React Flow, offering eight layouts: **Organic**, **Radial**, **Hub & Spoke**, **Structural**, **Tree**, **Sequential**, **Lens**, and **Grid**. Organic layout uses a custom physics simulation rather than d3-force.

chunks.heading: Stats bar
chunks.text: The top of the page shows a compact count: total **nodes**, total **edges**, and how many of those edges are **governed** by a policy.

chunks.heading: Node detail panel
chunks.text: Click any node to open a detail panel with its risk read, blast-radius stats, an **Attach policy** action where applicable, and an **Ask about this node** shortcut into AIQraph chat.

chunks.heading: Live mode
chunks.text: Switch to Live mode to see a real-time feed of tool invocations as `ToolInvocation` nodes, polled on a short interval, with a per-minute call-rate indicator.

chunks.heading: AIQraph chat
chunks.text:
The built-in chat panel sends questions about your topology to a backend endpoint that builds context from your live graph data and answers with a model. It runs in three modes:

| Chat Mode   | Description                                              |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Hybrid**  | Combines topology context with open-ended reasoning      |
| **Context** | Answers grounded strictly in the current graph selection |
| **Tools**   | Focuses on tool-level access and invocation questions    |

<Callout type="info">
  AIQraph reflects live data - registered agents, MCP servers, tools, policies, and (in Live mode) real tool invocations - rather than a static or planned topology.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Use cases
chunks.text: AIQraph helps you visualize which agents can reach which MCP servers and tools, spot connections that aren't covered by a policy, and follow real invocation activity as it happens.

chunks.heading: Registering a New Agent
chunks.text: Navigate to **Agents → Add Agent** or click the **+ Add Agent** button. The registration wizard guides you through:

chunks.heading: Step 1 - Setup Method
chunks.text:
Choose between:

* **Manual Configuration** - Enter all agent details manually
* **Auto-Detect** - ArmorIQ validates the URL and detects the framework

chunks.heading: Step 2 - Agent Details
chunks.text:
| Field           | Description                                      |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| **Agent Name**  | Unique identifier for the agent                  |
| **URL**         | The agent's base URL                             |
| **Environment** | Production, Staging, or Development              |
| **Description** | Description of the agent's purpose               |
| **Framework**   | Auto-detected (A2A or MCP) or manually specified |

ArmorIQ automatically validates the URL and performs **endpoint detection** to identify the agent's framework:

* **A2A** (Agent-to-Agent) - Google's agent interoperability protocol
* **MCP** (Model Context Protocol) - Anthropic's tool protocol

chunks.heading: Step 3 - Capabilities
chunks.text: Configure the agent's capabilities and supported features.

chunks.heading: Step 4 - Security Options
chunks.text: Enable vulnerability scanning and configure scan schedules, similar to MCP server setup.

chunks.heading: Agent Controls
chunks.text:
Every agent's detail page has a **Controls** tab with two independent ways to stop an agent: an immediate **kill switch** that blocks tool calls at enforcement time, and a **Revoke** action that disables the agent in the registry.

<Callout type="warn">
  Kill and revoke are separate mechanisms with different effects. Killing an agent blocks its tool calls without changing its registry status. Revoking an agent sets its registry status to inactive; it does not use the kill-switch table at all.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Kill switch
chunks.text:
The Controls tab shows a status card for the agent's current kill state:

* If the agent is **not killed**, you can kill it for a preset duration - **1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes**, or **Indefinite** - or enter a custom number of minutes. There is no confirmation dialog; clicking **Kill** takes effect immediately.
* If the agent **is killed**, the card shows a countdown to the expiry time (or "Active until manually lifted" for an indefinite kill) and a **Lift kill** button that clears it immediately, also without a confirmation dialog.

Killing an agent calls `POST /iap/agent/:agentId/kill` with an optional `durationSeconds` and `reason`; lifting it calls `POST /iap/agent/:agentId/unkill`. The dashboard currently sends a fixed reason string rather than a free-text reason you enter.

chunks.heading: What killing an agent actually does
chunks.text:
A kill is checked **before** policy and OPA evaluation on every tool call the agent makes through the IAP enforcement pipeline. While a kill is active:

* every tool call for that agent is blocked with `enforcementAction: block` and `reason: agent_killed`, regardless of what any policy would otherwise allow;
* the block is recorded as an IAP audit-log entry and an enforcement activity event.

A kill can be **timed** (it clears itself once `expiresAt` passes) or **indefinite** (`expiresAt` is null, and it stays active until an operator lifts it). Lifting a kill only records the timestamp it was cleared - it does not record who cleared it.

<Callout type="info">
  List every currently active kill for your organization with `GET /iap/agent-kills`.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Revoke
chunks.text:
**Revoke**, on the agent's header, is a different action: it sets the agent's registry status to `inactive` through `POST /agent/agents/:agentId/status`. A revoked agent stays in the registry and can be brought back with **Re-enable**, which sets status back to `active`. Unlike a kill, revoke has no timer or expiry - it stays in effect until you re-enable the agent, and it shows a confirmation dialog before applying.

Use revoke when you want an agent disabled indefinitely as part of normal lifecycle management. Use kill when you need to immediately and verifiably stop an agent's tool calls at the enforcement layer, optionally for a bounded window.

chunks.heading: Agents
chunks.text: The Agent Registry manages all your AI agents. Register agents, detect their framework type, run security scans, and monitor performance metrics.

chunks.heading: Topics
chunks.text:
* **[Agent Registry](/platform/agents/registry)**: Browse and manage registered AI agents.
* **[Add Agent](/platform/agents/add-agent)**: Register a new AI agent using the setup wizard.
* **[Agent Controls](/platform/agents/controls)**: Kill an agent's tool calls immediately, or revoke it from the registry.
* **[Scan Reports](/platform/agents/scan-reports)**: View security scan results and vulnerability details for agents.

chunks.heading: Agent Types
chunks.text:
Agents are categorized by type:

| Type           | Description                      |
| -------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **Assistant**  | General purpose AI assistants    |
| **Analyzer**   | Data analysis and insight agents |
| **Automation** | Workflow automation agents       |
| **Custom**     | Custom-built agents              |

chunks.heading: Agent Metrics
chunks.text:
Each agent card displays:

* **Capabilities** supported
* **API endpoints** exposed
* **Rate limit** configuration
* **Verification status** (verified/unverified)
* **Certificate** information
* **Uptime** percentage
* **Average response time**
* **Error rate**

chunks.heading: Agent Detail View
chunks.text: Click on any agent to open the detail panel. The detail view provides comprehensive information: * Connection URL and status * Security severity and vulnerability score * Owner and organization context * Certificate details * Performance metrics (uptime, response time, error rate) * Attached policies with member-level rules

chunks.heading: Available Actions
chunks.text:
| Action               | Description                        |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| **View Details**     | Open the full detail panel         |
| **Scan**             | Trigger a security scan            |
| **Delete**           | Remove the agent from the registry |
| **View Scan Report** | Navigate to the scan report page   |

<Callout type="info">
  Only users with **Organization Admin**, **Developer**, or **IAM Admin** roles can add or delete agents.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Scan Reports
chunks.text:
Agent scan reports include:

* Vulnerability breakdown by severity
* Individual vulnerability details with remediation recommendations
* Framework-specific checks (A2A or MCP protocol compliance)
* Option to trigger a rescan

chunks.heading: Agent Policies
chunks.text: Agents can have access policies attached that control which tools they can invoke, who can trigger them, and under what conditions. See [Policies](/platform/policies) for full details.

chunks.heading: Creating an API Key
chunks.text: Navigate to **API Keys → Create** or click the **+ Create Key** button.

chunks.heading: Step 1 - Name
chunks.text: Enter a descriptive **name** for the API key (e.g., "Production SDK", "Development Testing").

chunks.heading: Step 2 - Expiration
chunks.text:
Choose an expiration period:

| Option      | Duration            |
| ----------- | ------------------- |
| **1 Day**   | Expires in 24 hours |
| **7 Days**  | Expires in 1 week   |
| **30 Days** | Expires in 1 month  |
| **Never**   | No expiration       |

chunks.heading: Step 3 - Copy Your Key
chunks.text: After creation, the **full API key** is displayed **once**. Copy it immediately. The full API key is **only shown once** at creation time. If you lose it, you'll need to create a new key. Store it securely - never commit it to source control.

chunks.heading: Organization Limit
chunks.text: Each organization can have up to **10 API keys** active at a time. The create button is disabled when the limit is reached.

chunks.heading: Endpoint Logs
chunks.text: Navigate to **API Keys → Endpoint Logs** for detailed usage analytics. The endpoint logs show: * **Endpoint path** that was called * **HTTP method** (GET, POST, etc.) * **Request count** per endpoint * **Last access** timestamp * **API key names** that made the calls

chunks.heading: Filtering
chunks.text:
* **Search** by endpoint path
* **Filter by status** (success/error)
* **Filter by HTTP method**
* **Filter by date range**

chunks.heading: Using API Keys
chunks.text:
API keys are used to authenticate SDK requests. Include the key in the `X-API-Key` header:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.armoriq.ai/iap/sdk/token \
  -H "X-API-Key: ak_your_api_key_here" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"plan": {...}}'
```

For complete SDK integration instructions, see the [SDK & CLI Quickstart](/platform/sdk-cli/quickstart) - sixty seconds from this key to your first authorized tool call.

chunks.heading: API Dashboard
chunks.text: The API Keys dashboard provides usage analytics at a glance.

chunks.heading: KPI Cards
chunks.text:
| Metric               | Description                              |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| **Total Requests**   | Cumulative API calls made with your keys |
| **Total Keys**       | Number of active API keys                |
| **Error Rate**       | Percentage of failed requests            |
| **Servers & Agents** | Count of connected resources             |

chunks.heading: Request Trend Chart
chunks.text: A time-series chart showing API request volume over the selected timeframe.

chunks.heading: API Reference
chunks.text: This page is an organized map of the ArmorIQ backend's API surface - not an exhaustive endpoint list. Use it to find which area owns a capability, then follow the linked docs (or the in-app Swagger UI) for full request and response detail.

chunks.heading: Base URL
chunks.text: The backend has no global route prefix - every path below is served exactly as written, with no `/api` or `/v1` prefix. It listens on port `8080` by default (overridable with the `PORT` environment variable). Outside production, interactive Swagger docs are available at `/api-docs`.

chunks.heading: Authentication
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ has two authentication modes, and most controllers use exactly one:

| Mode           | Header                                                              | Used for                                                                                                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **JWT Bearer** | `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`                                       | Dashboard and user-facing calls - organization, user, dashboard, audit logs, notifications, and most policy and IAP dashboard routes |
| **API key**    | `x-api-key: <key>` (also accepted as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`) | SDK, agent, and plugin calls - delegation, observability ingest, token-usage ingest, and most IAP `sdk/*` routes                     |

A small number of routes accept **either** - for example, some policy-drafting endpoints the ArmorClaude plugin calls with its own API key instead of a full dashboard session. Plan and route activation endpoints stay JWT-only even where a sibling read endpoint accepts either. A separate `ProxyAuthGuard` covers proxy-only paths (obligation lookups, internal MCP routing) used by ArmorIQ's own enforcement proxy, not by SDKs or the dashboard directly.

chunks.heading: Rate limiting
chunks.text:
There is no global rate limit - most endpoints are unthrottled. Two named throttle buckets are configured and applied only where a route opts in:

| Bucket       | Limit                                   | Applied to                                      |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `auth`       | 5-10 requests/minute (varies by route)  | Login, OTP verification/resend, forgot-password |
| `delegation` | 30-60 requests/minute (varies by route) | Delegation create/approve/reject                |

chunks.heading: Controller areas
chunks.text:
| Area                                                        | Purpose                                                                                                | Representative endpoints                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **[/auth](/platform/authentication)**                       | Sign-up, sign-in, OAuth, sessions, password recovery                                                   | `POST /auth/register`, `POST /auth/login`, `GET /auth/google/callback`, `POST /auth/refresh`, `GET /auth/me`                                            |
| **[/organization](/platform/organizations)**                | Org CRUD, members, invites, roles, SSO/identity-provider setup                                         | `POST /organization`, `GET /organization/:orgId/members`, `POST /organization/:orgId/members/invite`, `PATCH /organization/:orgId/members/:userId/role` |
| **[/api-keys](/platform/api-keys)**                         | Create, list, revoke, and provision SDK API keys                                                       | `POST /api-keys`, `GET /api-keys`, `POST /api-keys/:apiKeyId/revoke`, `POST /api-keys/provision`                                                        |
| **[/policies](/platform/policies)**                         | Policy CRUD, activation, member and client rule bindings, AI-assisted drafting, YAML import/export     | `POST /policies`, `POST /policies/:policyId/activate`, `POST /policies/check-access`, `GET /policies/yaml/export/:policyId`                             |
| **[/iap](/platform/intent-intelligence)**                   | Intent plan enforcement, plans, audit, Merkle proofs, trust chain, agent kill switch                   | `POST /iap/sdk/enforce`, `GET /iap/plan/:planId`, `GET /iap/plan/:planId/merkle-tree`, `POST /iap/agent/:agentId/kill`, `POST /iap/trust/delegate`      |
| **[/delegation](/platform/plans#delegation-and-approval)**  | Human-in-the-loop approval for tool calls that exceed an agent's policy limit                          | `POST /delegation/request`, `GET /delegation/poll`, `POST /delegation/approve`, `POST /delegation/reject`                                               |
| **[/observability](/platform/observability/api-reference)** | Ingest OTLP traces, manage organization controls, and query traces, sessions, and token/cost analytics | `POST /v1/traces`, `GET /organization/:orgId/observability/sessions`, `GET /organization/:orgId/observability/analytics/summary`                        |
| **[/mcp](/platform/mcp-servers)**                           | MCP server registration, health, telemetry, vulnerabilities, certificates                              | `POST /mcp/register`, `GET /mcp/servers`, `POST /mcp/servers/:mcpId/scan`, `GET /mcp/certificates`                                                      |
| **[/agent](/platform/agents)**                              | Agent registration and status                                                                          | `POST /agent/register`, `GET /agent/agents`, `POST /agent/agents/:agentId/status`                                                                       |
| **[/pap](/platform/plans#pap-pre-flight)**                  | Read-only view of pre-flight plan-refinement decisions                                                 | `GET /pap/decisions`, `GET /pap/stats/overview`, `GET /pap/policy/snapshot`                                                                             |

chunks.heading: Other areas
chunks.text:
A few controllers exist outside the ten areas above and are documented alongside their feature rather than repeated here: **[/certificate](/platform/certificates)** (issue, check, revoke, rotate), **audit-log** (see [Audit Logs](/platform/audit-logs)), **dashboard** and **admin/dashboard** (product usage metrics), **user**, **notification**, **search**, **checkout/billing**, **referral**, **blog**, **proxy-enforcement** (the enforcement proxy's own token and OAuth flows), **access-requests** (waitlist capture), **aiqraph** (see [AIQraph](/platform/aiqraph)), and **armorclaw** (see [ArmorClaw](/platform/armorclaw)).

<Callout type="info">
  Endpoint lists here are representative, not exhaustive. Each linked page documents the routes relevant to that feature in more depth; for the complete route set, use the in-app Swagger UI at `/api-docs`.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Platform Architecture
chunks.text: ArmorIQ is composed of four core services that work together to provide end-to-end security for AI agent infrastructure:

chunks.heading: Topics
chunks.text:
* **[Service Breakdown](/platform/architecture/services)**: Frontend, backend, proxy, and CSRG-IAP service details.
* **[Request Flow](/platform/architecture/request-flow)**: End-to-end request flow and security layers.

chunks.heading: Authentication Architecture
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ uses a **JWT-based** authentication system:

```
User ──▶ Sign In ──▶ Backend issues JWT (15min access + refresh token)
                           │
                           ▼
              Frontend stores tokens in localStorage
                           │
                           ▼
              All API calls include:
              • Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
              • X-Organization-Id: <orgId>
                           │
                           ▼
              On 401 → auto-refresh via /auth/refresh → retry
              On refresh failure → redirect to /auth
```

**Three auth paths converge at the proxy:**

| Auth Method    | Used By        | Flow                                                            |
| -------------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **JWT Bearer** | Enterprise SDK | Frontend/SDK → `/iap/process` → receives proxy JWT              |
| **API Key**    | Customer SDK   | SDK sends `X-API-Key` header → proxy validates via backend      |
| **CSRG Proof** | Direct CSRG    | Sends `X-CSRG-Path` + `X-CSRG-Proof` headers with token in body |

chunks.heading: Organization Isolation
chunks.text:
Every resource is scoped to an organization:

* Frontend sends `X-Organization-Id` header with every authenticated request
* Backend verifies the user is a member of the specified organization
* All database queries are filtered by `orgId`
* Proxy extracts `orgId` from token claims
* CSRG embeds `orgId` in plan metadata for audit trails

chunks.heading: End-to-End Request Flow
chunks.text:
When an AI agent makes a tool call through ArmorIQ:

```
1. SDK/Agent requests an intent token
   POST /iap/process → Backend
   
2. Backend validates client + policies, builds plan document
   Backend → POST /intent → CSRG-IAP
   
3. CSRG builds reasoning graph, computes Merkle tree, signs token
   Returns: intent_reference, token, plan_hash, reasoning_graph
   
4. Backend wraps in proxy JWT with step proofs
   Returns proxy_token + plan_id + step_proofs[] to SDK
   
5. SDK makes tool call through proxy
   POST proxy.domain.com/tool
   Headers: Authorization: Bearer <proxy_token>
            X-CSRG-Path: /steps/[0]/tool
            X-CSRG-Proof: [merkle_siblings]
   
6. Proxy authenticates + validates:
   a. Verify JWT signature (HS256/RS256)
   b. Verify composite identity
   c. Backend /iap/verify-step (checks plan state)
   d. CSRG /verify/action (cryptographic Merkle proof)
   
7. If all checks pass → forward to target MCP server
   
8. Response returned to SDK + audit log created
```

chunks.heading: Security Layers
chunks.text:
| Layer                   | Mechanism                               | Purpose                          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **Authentication**      | JWT + OAuth + API Keys                  | Verify identity                  |
| **Authorization**       | Policy engine (PEP/PDP)                 | Enforce access rules             |
| **Intent Verification** | CSRG signed tokens                      | Prove plan authorization         |
| **Tamper Detection**    | Merkle tree proofs                      | Detect plan modifications        |
| **Trust Chain**         | Trust deltas (ReAnchor/Delegate/Revoke) | Track trust transitions          |
| **Audit**               | Merkle audit logs                       | Non-repudiable event trail       |
| **Domain Isolation**    | Domain mapping + DNS verification       | Ensure traffic routing integrity |

chunks.heading: 1. Frontend Console (React SPA)
chunks.text:
The web application that users interact with. Built with **React 18**, **TypeScript**, and **Tailwind CSS**.

**Responsibilities:**

* User authentication (email/password, Google OAuth, GitHub OAuth)
* Organization management
* MCP server and agent registration
* Policy creation with visual builder
* Dashboard with security metrics and analytics
* API key management
* Intent plan monitoring and visualization

**Connects to:** Backend API via HTTPS (`https://api.armoriq.ai`)

chunks.heading: 2. Backend API (NestJS)
chunks.text:
The central business logic layer built with **NestJS** and **Prisma ORM**.

**Key modules:**

| Module                          | Purpose                                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Auth**                        | JWT authentication, OAuth (Google/GitHub), OTP verification, password reset           |
| **Organization**                | Multi-tenant org management, memberships, quotas, invitations                         |
| **MCP**                         | MCP server registry, URL resolution, certificate management                           |
| **Agent Scanner**               | Agent registration, framework detection (A2A/MCP), security scanning                  |
| **Intent Assurance Plan (IAP)** | Intent plan processing, CSRG integration, Merkle tree construction, step verification |
| **Policies**                    | Policy CRUD, target-based rules, per-member and per-client access control             |
| **Domain Mapping**              | Custom domain → target URL mapping, DNS verification                                  |
| **Proxy Enforcement**           | Proxy token generation, OAuth2 authorization code, token exchange                     |
| **API Keys**                    | Key generation, validation, usage tracking                                            |
| **OAuth Client**                | OAuth 2.0 client registration and secret management                                   |
| **Dashboard**                   | Aggregated metrics, analytics, alerts                                                 |
| **Audit Log**                   | Timestamped, org-scoped audit trail                                                   |
| **Scan**                        | Vulnerability scanning engine for MCP servers                                         |

**Connects to:** CSRG-IAP for intent signing, Prisma DB for persistence

chunks.heading: 3. Proxy Server (NestJS)
chunks.text:
A **stateless** reverse proxy that intercepts all traffic between AI agents/SDKs and MCP servers.

**Responsibilities:**

* Authenticate incoming requests (JWT, API key, or CSRG proof headers)
* Resolve target URL from token claims or dynamic MCP lookup
* Enforce policies (tool access control, domain validation, audience checks)
* Verify each tool execution via backend Intent Assurance Plan (IAP) step verification
* Verify cryptographic Merkle proofs via CSRG
* Forward validated requests to the target MCP server
* Support SSE streaming and MCP session management
* Create audit logs for every proxied request

**Key design:** The proxy has **no database** - all validation is delegated to the backend and CSRG services.

chunks.heading: 4. CSRG-IAP (Python / FastAPI)
chunks.text:
The **Canonical Structured Reasoning Graph** engine provides cryptographic intent assurance.

**Responsibilities:**

* Build deterministic reasoning graphs from execution plans
* Compute Merkle trees over plan nodes for tamper detection
* Sign intent tokens with **Ed25519** (or ECDSA P-256 for GCP)
* Verify individual tool actions against the signed plan using Merkle proofs
* Track trust deltas (ReAnchor, Delegate, Revoke)
* Maintain append-only Merkle audit logs

chunks.heading: Log Sources
chunks.text:
Audit log entries are generated by multiple platform components:

| Source                                 | Events                                                             |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Backend API**                        | Resource CRUD operations, auth events, policy changes              |
| **Proxy Server**                       | Request interception, enforcement decisions, forwarding events     |
| **Intent Assurance Plan (IAP) Engine** | Intent plan processing, step verification, trust chain updates     |
| **CSRG**                               | Cryptographic operations, token signing, Merkle proof verification |
| **Scanner**                            | Vulnerability scan initiation, results, severity assessments       |

<Callout type="info">
  Audit logs are **organization-scoped** - you only see events relevant to your active organization. Switch organizations to view a different organization's logs.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Best Practices
chunks.text:
* **Monitor Critical logs daily** - These indicate security incidents requiring immediate attention
* **Set up regular review cadences** - Weekly review of Warning-level logs helps catch emerging patterns
* **Cross-reference with Intent Plans** - Combine audit logs with Intent Assurance Plan (IAP) details for a complete execution trace
* **Export for compliance** - Use audit logs to satisfy compliance reporting requirements

chunks.heading: Log Entry Format
chunks.text:
Each audit log entry contains:

| Field                 | Description                  |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| **Timestamp**         | When the event occurred      |
| **Severity**          | Critical, Warning, or Info   |
| **Source**            | Which agent(s) were involved |
| **Event Description** | What happened                |
| **IP Address**        | Origin IP of the action      |

chunks.heading: By Group
chunks.text:
Filter logs by the type of resource:

| Group      | Events Covered                                               |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Agents** | Agent registration, scans, deletions, tool invocations       |
| **MCPs**   | MCP server registration, scans, deletions, connection events |
| **Users**  | Login, registration, role changes, invitation events         |

chunks.heading: By Date Range
chunks.text:
Pre-configured time ranges:

| Range       | Period        |
| ----------- | ------------- |
| **7 Days**  | Last week     |
| **30 Days** | Last month    |
| **Quarter** | Last 3 months |
| **YTD**     | Year to date  |

chunks.heading: By Severity
chunks.text:
| Severity     | Description                                                         |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Critical** | Security incidents, policy violations, unauthorized access attempts |
| **Warning**  | Potential risks, unusual patterns, approaching limits               |
| **Info**     | Normal operations, routine events                                   |

chunks.heading: Log Detail View
chunks.text: Click on any log entry to open a detailed view with: * Full event description and context * Related entities (agents, servers, users) * Request metadata * Additional fields specific to the event type

chunks.heading: Pagination
chunks.text: Audit logs are paginated with **5 entries per page**. Navigate between pages using the pagination controls at the bottom.

chunks.heading: Audit Logs
chunks.text: Audit Logs provide a comprehensive, timestamped record of all significant actions across your organization. Every login, resource change, scan, policy update, and proxy enforcement event is logged.

chunks.heading: Topics
chunks.text:
* **[Filtering & Search](/platform/audit-logs/filtering)**: Filter audit logs by group, date range, and severity.
* **[Log Sources & Best Practices](/platform/audit-logs/best-practices)**: Understanding log sources and audit review best practices.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The Action Queue at `/armorclaw/action-queue` shows all in-progress and completed ArmorClaw actions.

chunks.heading: Running Actions
chunks.text:
Active actions appear at the top with a status indicator. Types include:

| Action Type         | Description                                   |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| **Discovery**       | Scanning for ArmorClaw installations          |
| **Scan**            | Running a vulnerability scan against an agent |
| **Policy Dispatch** | Pushing a policy to target agents             |

chunks.heading: Completed Actions
chunks.text:
Below the running actions, a history of completed actions is shown:

| Column        | Description                                                                        |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Action**    | What was performed (discovery, scan, dispatch)                                     |
| **Target**    | The installation, agent, or policy involved                                        |
| **Status**    | `completed` or `failed`                                                            |
| **Timestamp** | When the action finished                                                           |
| **Details**   | Summary of results (e.g., "3 vulnerabilities found", "Policy applied to 5 agents") |

chunks.heading: Status Indicators
chunks.text:
| Status        | Description                                          |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Running**   | Action is currently in progress (animated indicator) |
| **Completed** | Action finished successfully                         |
| **Failed**    | Action encountered an error                          |

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The Agents & Skills page at `/armorclaw/agents` shows all agents detected from your ArmorClaw installations, along with their loaded skills and risk assessments.

chunks.heading: Installation Filter
chunks.text: Use the installation filter at the top to narrow the agent list to a specific ArmorClaw installation.

chunks.heading: Agent List
chunks.text:
Each agent is displayed as an expandable row:

| Column                  | Description                                        |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Agent Name**          | The agent identifier                               |
| **Installation**        | Which ArmorClaw installation this agent belongs to |
| **Skills Count**        | Number of loaded skills                            |
| **Vulnerability Score** | Overall vulnerability score (0-100), color-coded   |

chunks.heading: Vulnerability Score Colors
chunks.text:
| Range  | Color  | Risk Level  |
| ------ | ------ | ----------- |
| 0-30   | Green  | Low risk    |
| 31-60  | Yellow | Medium risk |
| 61-100 | Red    | High risk   |

chunks.heading: Skill Details
chunks.text:
Click an agent row to expand and see its loaded skills:

| Field          | Description                                                     |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Skill Name** | The name of the loaded skill                                    |
| **Version**    | Skill version number                                            |
| **Source**     | Where the skill came from: `bundled`, `downloaded`, or `remote` |
| **Risk Level** | Risk assessment for this skill                                  |

chunks.heading: Actions
chunks.text:
| Action                  | Description                                                      |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Enumerate Skills**    | Re-scan an agent to discover newly loaded skills                 |
| **Run Scan**            | Trigger a vulnerability scan for a specific agent                |
| **Sync from ArmorClaw** | Pull latest agent and skill data from the ArmorClaw installation |

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: When ArmorClaw runs a discovery scan, it produces a **detection report** for each host. This page describes the structure and fields of these reports.

chunks.heading: Report Structure
chunks.text:
Each detection report contains:

| Field            | Description                                        |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Host**         | The hostname or IP address scanned                 |
| **Platform**     | Detected operating system and architecture         |
| **Install Path** | Where ArmorClaw was found (e.g., `/opt/armorclaw`) |
| **Distribution** | The ArmorClaw distribution type                    |
| **Version**      | Installed ArmorClaw version                        |
| **Check Result** | Whether ArmorClaw was found                        |

chunks.heading: Check Results
chunks.text:
| Result    | Description                                           |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| **Found** | ArmorClaw installation detected at the specified path |
| **Clean** | No ArmorClaw installation found on this host          |

chunks.heading: Platform Identification
chunks.text:
The report includes OS and platform details:

| Field              | Description                             |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| **OS**             | Operating system (e.g., Linux, macOS)   |
| **Architecture**   | CPU architecture (e.g., x86\_64, arm64) |
| **Kernel Version** | Kernel version string                   |

chunks.heading: Using Reports
chunks.text:
Detection reports feed into the [Installations](/platform/armorclaw/installations) table. Hosts where ArmorClaw is **found** are added as tracked installations. Hosts that are **clean** are not added but are recorded in the scan history.

<Callout type="info">
  Detection reports are generated by the ArmorClaw discovery script. Run `curl -fsSL https://armoriq.ai/install/armorclaw-discovery.sh | bash -s -- --inventory` on target hosts to produce reports.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: ArmorClaw
chunks.text:
ArmorClaw is ArmorIQ's **agent security scanning product** that detects ArmorClaw deployments, enumerates agent skills, runs vulnerability scans, and dispatches remediation policies.

ArmorClaw operates in its own dedicated dashboard at `/armorclaw/*`, separate from the main ArmorIQ dashboard.

chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text:
ArmorClaw is an optional product. To enable it:

1. Go to **Settings → [Product Preferences](/platform/settings/product-preferences)**.
2. Toggle **ArmorClaw** on.
3. The ArmorClaw section appears in your sidebar with the following navigation items.

chunks.heading: Navigation
chunks.text:
| Page                                                               | Description                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| **[Installations](/platform/armorclaw/installations)**             | Discover and manage ArmorClaw deployments     |
| **[Agents & Skills](/platform/armorclaw/agents-skills)**           | Enumerate agent skills and run scans          |
| **[Vulnerability Scans](/platform/armorclaw/vulnerability-scans)** | View scan results and findings                |
| **[Policy Workflow](/platform/armorclaw/policy-workflow)**         | Build and dispatch remediation policies       |
| **[Action Queue](/platform/armorclaw/action-queue)**               | Track running and completed actions           |
| **[Intent Dashboard](/platform/armorclaw/intent-dashboard)**       | Monitor intent plans within ArmorClaw context |

chunks.heading: Workflow
chunks.text:
A typical ArmorClaw workflow:

1. **Discover** - Run the discovery script to find ArmorClaw installations on your infrastructure.
2. **Enumerate** - List agents and their loaded skills from discovered installations.
3. **Scan** - Run vulnerability scans against agents to identify security issues.
4. **Remediate** - Create policies and dispatch them to affected agents.
5. **Monitor** - Track remediation actions in the action queue.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The Installations page at `/armorclaw/installations` lets you discover ArmorClaw deployments across your infrastructure and track their status.

chunks.heading: Discovery Script
chunks.text:
To discover ArmorClaw installations, run the provided shell script on your target hosts:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://armoriq.ai/install/armorclaw-discovery.sh | bash -s -- --inventory
```

chunks.heading: Customization
chunks.text:
Before running, you can configure:

| Setting          | Default          | Description                       |
| ---------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------- |
| **Host Pattern** | `*`              | Pattern to match target hostnames |
| **Install Path** | `/opt/armorclaw` | Path where ArmorClaw is installed |

Click **Copy** to copy the configured command to your clipboard.

chunks.heading: Installation Table
chunks.text:
Discovered installations appear in a table:

| Column           | Description                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| **Label**        | A name for this installation                   |
| **Host**         | The hostname where ArmorClaw is installed      |
| **Path**         | The installation directory                     |
| **Distribution** | ArmorClaw distribution type                    |
| **Version**      | Installed version                              |
| **Status**       | Current status badge                           |
| **Agent Count**  | Number of agents detected on this installation |

chunks.heading: Status Badges
chunks.text:
| Status      | Color  | Description                            |
| ----------- | ------ | -------------------------------------- |
| **Active**  | Green  | Installation is running and reporting  |
| **Stale**   | Yellow | Installation has not reported recently |
| **Offline** | Red    | Installation is unreachable or errored |

When you authenticate via the ArmorIQ CLI or SDK, a **device approval flow** opens in your browser. This lets you verify and authorize the device connection securely.

Navigate to `/auth/device` or follow the link provided by the CLI after running `armoriq login`.

chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text:
1. **Start CLI Login** - Run `armoriq login` in your terminal. The CLI generates a user code and opens your browser.
2. **Verify Code** - The Device Approval page displays the user code. Confirm it matches what the CLI shows.
3. **Select API Key** - If you have multiple API keys, choose which one to authorize for this device session.
4. **Approve** - Click **Approve** to complete the authorization.
5. **Auto-Close** - After approval, the page shows a success message and automatically closes after 3 seconds.
