chunks.heading: Password Recovery
chunks.text: If you signed up with an email and password, you can reset a forgotten password from the sign-in page.

chunks.heading: Request a reset
chunks.text:
1. Click **Forgot password?** on the sign-in page and enter your email.
2. ArmorIQ emails a reset link if an account exists for that address.

<Callout type="info">
  The response is identical whether or not the email matches an account, so the flow can't be used to discover which emails are registered.
</Callout>

The reset token is valid for **one hour**. Requesting a reset does not invalidate your current password until you complete the reset with a new one.

chunks.heading: Reset your password
chunks.text:
Follow the emailed link and set a new password. The link only works once - the token is cleared as soon as it's used - and it stops working after the one-hour window even if unused.

<Callout type="warn">
  Password reset is only available for accounts that signed up with email and password. If your account uses Google or GitHub sign-in, reset your password through that provider instead - ArmorIQ has no local password to reset.
</Callout>

Both the request and reset steps are rate-limited to guard against abuse.

chunks.heading: Session Management
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ uses **JWT tokens** for session management:

| Token             | Lifetime   | Purpose                    |
| ----------------- | ---------- | -------------------------- |
| **Access Token**  | 15 minutes | Authenticates API requests |
| **Refresh Token** | Long-lived | Obtains new access tokens  |

chunks.heading: Automatic Token Refresh
chunks.text: When your access token expires, the platform **automatically refreshes** it using the refresh token. This happens transparently - you won't be interrupted.

chunks.heading: Session Expiry
chunks.text:
If the refresh token is also expired or invalid, you'll be redirected to the sign-in page. This can happen if:

* You've been inactive for an extended period
* Your account has been modified by an admin
* You signed out from another device

chunks.heading: Certificates
chunks.text: ArmorIQ issues and tracks X.509 certificates that establish trusted TLS identity for the MCP servers and agents in your registry. Certificates back the connections the proxy verifies before it will route a tool call, and the dashboard surfaces their status, expiry, and rotation history alongside the resource they belong to.

chunks.heading: What a certificate provides
chunks.text:
A certificate binds a domain name and common name to a key pair and an issuer chain. ArmorIQ uses this to confirm that an MCP server or agent endpoint is who it claims to be before the proxy trusts traffic to it. Certificates are organization-scoped and can be attached to an MCP server or an agent record.

<Callout type="info">
  The Certificates screen aggregates three sources into one view: certificates issued through ArmorIQ's own certificate service, plus certificate metadata already stored on MCP server and agent records. Only the first kind can be rotated through Google Certificate Authority Service: see [Lifecycle](/platform/certificates/lifecycle) for the distinction.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Issuance
chunks.text: New certificates are issued against **Google Certificate Authority Service (CAS)**. ArmorIQ generates an RSA-2048 key pair and a certificate signing request, then calls CAS using the CA pool configured for the organization's identity provider (project, location, and pool ID) to obtain a signed certificate with a one-year lifetime. If an active, unexpired certificate already exists for the same domain, issuance reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.

chunks.heading: Encryption at rest
chunks.text:
The issued private key is encrypted with **Google Cloud KMS** before it is stored, using a KMS key resource configured through the `CERT_KMS_KEY_NAME` environment variable. If that variable is not set, the backend logs a warning and stores the private key in plaintext instead. Operators running their own instance should set `CERT_KMS_KEY_NAME` to keep private keys encrypted at rest.

<Callout type="warn">
  `CERT_KMS_KEY_NAME` is not included in the shipping `.env.example`. Set it explicitly in your deployment configuration; otherwise certificate private keys are persisted unencrypted.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: The Certificates screen
chunks.text:
Open a server or agent's **Certificates** view from the MCP dashboard to see every certificate in the organization in one table.

Each row shows:

| Column                | Description                                                              |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **MCP / fingerprint** | The owning resource plus the certificate's fingerprint and serial number |
| **Issuer**            | Issuing CA and issue date                                                |
| **Profile**           | Certificate profile badge                                                |
| **Days**              | Days remaining until expiry, color-coded as it approaches the deadline   |
| **Status**            | `valid`, `expiring`, or `expired`                                        |
| **Auto**              | Whether auto-rotation is on or off for that certificate                  |

A 12-month expiry timeline highlights the 30-day danger window, and a stat strip summarizes active, expiring, expired, auto-rotate, and BYO certificate counts along with average certificate lifetime.

chunks.heading: Actions
chunks.text:
* **Rotate now**: available on any certificate that is not `valid`, and as a bulk **Rotate expiring** action that rotates every expiring certificate in one click.
* **Download cert** and **Export (CSV/JSON)**: client-side export of certificate metadata.
* **Import BYO cert**: present in the UI but disabled today; the dashboard shows "Requires backend support" because there is no bring-your-own-certificate import endpoint yet.

<Callout type="info">
  The **Auto** column is display-only in the current dashboard. The backend does expose a toggle for auto-rotation (see [Lifecycle](/platform/certificates/lifecycle)), but the UI does not yet call it, so today auto-rotation is set at issuance time rather than toggled from this screen.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Next
chunks.text: * [Lifecycle: expiry monitoring, rotation, and revocation](/platform/certificates/lifecycle)

chunks.heading: Expiry monitoring
chunks.text: A daily job checks every active certificate at **06:00 UTC** and flags any certificate expiring within 30 days. The job crosses four thresholds: **30, 14, 7, and 1 day(s)** remaining, and records an expiry event the first time a certificate passes each one, so operators see escalating warnings as an expiry date approaches rather than a single alert.

chunks.heading: Auto-renewal
chunks.text:
Each certificate has an **auto-rotation** flag. When a certificate crosses an expiry threshold and auto-rotation is enabled for it, the backend automatically rotates that certificate (revoking the old one and issuing a replacement) without operator action. If auto-rotation is off, the expiry job only logs a warning; nothing is rotated automatically.

<Callout type="info">
  Auto-rotation is set when a certificate is created. The dashboard's Certificates table shows the current **Auto** state as On or Off, but does not yet expose a control to change it from the UI: set it through the underlying update endpoint if you need to change it for an existing certificate.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Manual rotation
chunks.text:
Rotating a certificate revokes the current certificate and issues a new one for the same domain and subject fields, keeping certificate history linked through a `previousCertId` reference. From the dashboard, rotate a single certificate with **Rotate now**, or rotate every currently-expiring certificate in one action with the bulk **Rotate expiring** control.

<Callout type="warn">
  Only certificates issued through ArmorIQ's own certificate service can be rotated through Google CAS. Certificate metadata sourced from an MCP server or agent record's own configuration is shown in the same table for visibility, but rotating it does not call CAS: you need to re-issue that server or agent's certificate directly instead.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Revocation
chunks.text: Revoking a certificate calls Google CAS to revoke the underlying CA-issued certificate, then marks the certificate `revoked` in ArmorIQ regardless of whether CAS accepts the revocation. A handful of CAS error conditions (the certificate isn't found in the CA pool, or the request is otherwise not fulfillable at the CA) are treated as a local-only revocation rather than a hard failure, since the certificate is no longer usable in ArmorIQ either way. Any other CAS error is surfaced rather than silently ignored.

chunks.heading: Status values
chunks.text:
A certificate's status is one of:

| Status    | Meaning                                                                    |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `active`  | Currently valid and trusted                                                |
| `expired` | Past its validity window                                                   |
| `revoked` | Explicitly revoked, through the dashboard or automatically during rotation |

chunks.text: See [Certificates](/platform/certificates) for how private keys are encrypted at rest with Cloud KMS and the `CERT_KMS_KEY_NAME` configuration it depends on.

chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text:
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of how the Intent Assurance Plan processes and enforces execution plans:

```
1. SDK/Agent submits an execution plan
       │
2. Backend validates policies and builds canonical plan
       │
3. CSRG builds deterministic reasoning graph
       │
4. Merkle tree computed over graph nodes
       │
5. Ed25519 token signed with plan_hash
       │
6. Token + step proofs returned to SDK
       │
7. Each tool call verified:
   a. JWT signature check
   b. Backend step verification
   c. CSRG Merkle proof verification
       │
8. If verified → request forwarded to MCP server
   If not → request blocked + audit logged
```

<Callout type="info">
  The CSRG (Canonical Structured Reasoning Graph) ensures **cryptographic non-repudiation** - once a plan is committed, neither the agent nor any intermediary can execute unauthorized tool calls without detection.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Intent token signing
chunks.text:
Intent tokens are signed with **Ed25519 (EdDSA)** when the backend has signing keys configured via `IAP_TOKEN_ED25519_PRIVATE_KEY` and `IAP_TOKEN_ED25519_PUBLIC_KEY`. The signed payload includes the plan, user, agent, and context identifiers; the `plan_hash` and `merkle_root`; the CSRG token and step proofs; and the resolved policy validation result (allowed and denied tools, matched policies, and the default enforcement action).

Verify a token's signature yourself with the current public signing key, published unauthenticated at:

```http
GET /iap/public-key
```

This returns the algorithm, whether Ed25519 signing is currently enabled, and the public key in both PEM and JWK form.

<Callout type="warn">
  `GET /iap/public-key/:kid` is a different, unrelated endpoint that looks up CSRG/KMS-backed keys by key ID for a separate RS256 verification path. Use the plain `GET /iap/public-key` (no `kid`) for the Ed25519 intent-token key described here.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Legacy HS256 fallback
chunks.text: If `IAP_TOKEN_ED25519_PRIVATE_KEY` isn't configured, the backend signs intent tokens with the legacy shared-secret **HS256** algorithm instead. On verification, the backend inspects the token's `alg` header: an `EdDSA` token is verified against the Ed25519 public key, and any other token is verified as HS256. This keeps older HS256 tokens valid during a migration window - there's no separate feature flag, the fallback is controlled purely by whether an Ed25519 signing key is present.

| **Avg Plan Size**     | Average number of steps per execution plan            |

chunks.heading: Timeline Chart
chunks.text:
View intent plan activity over configurable time ranges:

* **24 hours** - Hourly breakdown of today's activity
* **7 days** - Daily trend for the past week
* **30 days** - Monthly overview

chunks.heading: Active Plans
chunks.text: A live list of currently executing plans with their status, agent, and progress.

chunks.heading: Agent Activity
chunks.text: Breakdown of which agents are generating the most intent plans.

chunks.heading: Endpoint Usage
chunks.text: Chart showing which MCP server endpoints are being called most frequently.

chunks.heading: Policy Violations
chunks.text: Summary of recent policy violations with severity and affected resources.

chunks.heading: Intent Intelligence
chunks.text: Intent Intelligence is powered by the Intent Assurance Plan (IAP) - ArmorIQ's core security innovation. The IAP intercepts every tool call between AI agents and MCP servers, creates cryptographically signed execution plans, and validates each action against the authorized plan.

chunks.heading: Video Walkthrough
Topics
chunks.text:
* **[IAP Dashboard](/platform/intent-intelligence/iap-dashboard)**: KPI metrics, timeline charts, and active plan monitoring for the Intent Assurance Plan (IAP).
* **[Plans List](/platform/intent-intelligence/plans)**: Browse all intent plans with status, risk levels, and pagination.
* **[Plan Detail](/platform/intent-intelligence/plan-detail)**: CSRG reasoning graph, Merkle tree, trust deltas, and audit trail.
* **[How It Works](/platform/intent-intelligence/how-it-works)**: End-to-end flow of intent plan creation, verification, and enforcement.

See [Plans Governance](/platform/plans) for the delegation and approval lifecycle behind plan status, and for how the Merkle audit chain and trust deltas are verified.

chunks.heading: Plan Detail
chunks.text: Click on any plan to view its full details.

chunks.heading: Plan Overview
chunks.text:
* **Status** and **risk level**
* **Description** of what the plan does
* **Owner** and **agent** information
* **Endpoint** being targeted
* **Node count** and timing breakdown

chunks.heading: Cryptographic Identity
chunks.text:
| Field                  | Description                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Trust Domain**       | The security domain this plan operates in                                    |
| **Merkle Root Hash**   | Root hash of the plan's Merkle tree                                          |
| **Composite Identity** | `SHA256(userId\|agentId\|contextId\|planHash)` - binds user, agent, and plan |
| **CSRG Plan Hash**     | Hash of the canonical reasoning graph                                        |

chunks.heading: Execution Timeline
chunks.text:
A step-by-step breakdown showing each node's:

* **Name** and **endpoint**
* **Status** (executing / completed / planned / failed / blocked)
* **Risk level** and **severity**
* **Duration** of execution

chunks.heading: CSRG Reasoning Graph
chunks.text: A visual tree showing the plan's reasoning and execution path. The graph is built deterministically from the plan document: * Each node has a **path-based identifier** (e.g., `/steps/[0]/tool`) * Nodes are connected by their hierarchical relationships * The graph provides a visual audit of how the plan was structured

chunks.heading: Merkle Tree Snapshot
chunks.text:
The persisted Merkle tree showing:

* **Leaf nodes** - Individual plan step hashes
* **Internal nodes** - Combined hashes building up to the root
* **Merkle proofs** - Inclusion proofs for verifying individual steps
* **Root hash** - The plan\_hash that's embedded in the signed token

chunks.heading: Trust Deltas
chunks.text:
Trust deltas track changes to the trust chain:

| Delta Type   | Description                                                    |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **ReAnchor** | Plan was modified - shows the modified fraction and new hash   |
| **Delegate** | Trust was delegated to a downstream agent with a subset policy |
| **Revoke**   | A token or delegation was revoked                              |

chunks.heading: Audit Logs
chunks.text:
A step-by-step execution audit trail for the plan. Each entry records:

* Timestamp
* Action performed
* Result (success/failure)
* Related metadata

chunks.heading: Plans List
chunks.text: Navigate to **Intent Plans → All Plans** for a paginated list of all intent plans. Each plan shows: | Column | Description | | -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | **Plan ID** | Unique identifier | | **Owner** | User who initiated the plan | | **Agent** | AI agent executing the plan | | **Status** | Current execution state | | **Created** | Timestamp of plan creation | | **Nodes** | Number of steps in the plan | | **Risk Level** | Assessed risk (Critical/High/Medium/Low) |

chunks.heading: Status Types
chunks.text:
A plan's status is computed at read time rather than only stored, so a held delegation or a passed expiry can change what status you see even if nothing else about the plan changed:

| Status                   | Meaning                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **killed**               | An operator killed the agent while this plan was active; killed always takes priority over any other status                          |
| **completed**            | All steps finished executing                                                                                                         |
| **approved**             | A held plan was approved and can proceed                                                                                             |
| **held**                 | Waiting on a pending delegation approval, or on backend hold logic                                                                   |
| **blocked** / **failed** | Policy or execution failure prevented the plan from completing                                                                       |
| **rejected**             | A pending delegation for this plan was rejected                                                                                      |
| **expired**              | The plan's `expiresAt` passed while it was still active; a background job also periodically reaps stale active plans into this state |
| **active**               | Default - the plan is in progress and none of the above apply                                                                        |

See [Plans Governance](/platform/plans) for the full lifecycle, including how delegation approvals and rejections feed into this status.

chunks.heading: Risk Levels
chunks.text:
| Level        | Description                                               |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Critical** | Involves privileged operations or sensitive data access   |
| **High**     | Contains multiple tool invocations with broad permissions |
| **Medium**   | Standard operations with moderate scope                   |
| **Low**      | Read-only or well-constrained operations                  |

chunks.heading: Registering a New MCP Server
chunks.text: Navigate to **MCP Servers → Add Server** or click the **+ Add Server** button. The registration is a **multi-step wizard**:

chunks.heading: Step 1 - Selection
chunks.text:
Choose your setup method:

* **Manual Configuration** - Enter all details manually
* **Auto-Detect** - ArmorIQ scans the URL and detects configuration automatically

chunks.heading: Step 2 - Server Details
chunks.text: | Field | Description | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | **Server Name** | A unique identifier for the server | | **Environment** | Production, Staging, or Development | | **URL** | The server's base URL (e.g., `https://mcp.example.com`) | | **Port** | Server port number | | **Protocol Version** | MCP protocol version (e.g., `2024-11-05`) | | **Auth Method** | Authentication method (e.g., API Key) | | **Version** | Server software version | | **Repository URL** | Source code repository (optional) | | **Description** | Brief description of the server's purpose |

chunks.heading: Step 3 - Capabilities
chunks.text:
Toggle the MCP capabilities this server supports:

* **Resources** - The server provides resources to agents
* **Tools** - The server exposes callable tools
* **Prompts** - The server provides prompt templates
* **Sampling** - The server supports LLM sampling

chunks.heading: Step 4 - Security
chunks.text: * **Vulnerability Scanning** - Enable automatic scanning * **Auto-Fix** - Automatically apply recommended fixes * **Scan Schedule** - Set recurring scan frequency After completing the wizard, ArmorIQ registers the server and automatically triggers the first security scan.

chunks.heading: MCP Servers
chunks.text: The MCP Server Registry is where you manage all your Model Context Protocol servers. Register servers, run security scans, monitor vulnerabilities, and ensure compliance.

chunks.heading: Topics
chunks.text:

* **[Add MCP Server](/platform/mcp-servers/add-server)**: Register a new MCP server using the multi-step wizard.
* **[Scan Reports](/platform/mcp-servers/scan-reports)**: View vulnerability assessments and security findings for MCP servers.

chunks.heading: Registry Dashboard
chunks.text: The registry page displays metric cards and a categorized view of all your MCP servers.

chunks.heading: Metric Cards

chunks.heading: Categorized View

Servers are organized by category:

chunks.heading: Server Detail View

The detail view shows: * **URL** and connection status * **Severity level** and **vulnerability score** * **Owner** and **organization** * **Certificate information** (issuer, validity, expiration) * **Last scan date** and results * **Policies** attached to this server with member-level rules

chunks.heading: Scan Reports
chunks.text:
Navigate to a server's scan report via **MCP Servers → \[Server Name] → Scan Report** or from the detail panel.

The scan report includes:

Each server can have policies attached that define fine-grained access rules. View attached policies from the server detail panel.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The OPA Configuration page is accessible at **Settings → OPA Policy Settings** (`/dashboard/settings/opa`). Here you configure how the OPA engine operates and upload custom Rego policies.

chunks.heading: Enforcement Mode
chunks.text:
Toggle between enforcement modes:

| Mode        | Description                                                                     |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Enforce** | OPA decisions are applied to all tool call requests                             |
| **Shadow**  | OPA evaluates requests but does not enforce - decisions are logged for analysis |

chunks.heading: External OPA URL
chunks.text: If you run your own OPA instance, enter its URL here. Leave empty to use ArmorIQ's built-in OPA engine.

chunks.heading: Custom Rego Policies
chunks.text:
Upload your own Rego policy files to extend OPA's decision logic:

1. Click **Upload Rego Policy**.
2. Select a `.rego` file from your system.
3. The file uploads and appears in the list of custom policies.

chunks.heading: Managing Uploaded Policies
chunks.text:
| Action     | Description                                     |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| **View**   | See the uploaded Rego file name and upload date |
| **Delete** | Remove a custom Rego policy                     |

chunks.heading: Saving
chunks.text:
Click **Save Configuration** to apply your changes. The OPA engine picks up the new settings and policies immediately.

<Callout type="info">
  Custom Rego policies are evaluated alongside ArmorIQ's built-in policies. Write your Rego rules in the `armoriq.authz` package to integrate with the existing decision pipeline.
</Callout>

chunks.text: The OPA Dashboard at `/dashboard/opa-dashboard` provides real-time analytics on how the OPA engine is evaluating and enforcing policy decisions.

chunks.heading: OPA Engine
chunks.text: The OPA Engine integrates **Open Policy Agent** into ArmorIQ for fine-grained, context-aware policy enforcement. It runs alongside the native policy engine and provides detailed analytics on enforcement decisions.

chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text:
OPA Engine is an optional product. To enable it:

1. Go to **Settings → [Product Preferences](/platform/settings/product-preferences)**.
2. Toggle **OPA Engine** on.
3. The OPA Engine section appears in your sidebar.

chunks.heading: Enforcement Modes
chunks.text:
| Mode         | Description                                                                                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Enforce**  | OPA decisions are applied - tool calls are allowed or blocked based on OPA evaluation                         |
| **Shadow**   | OPA evaluates decisions but does not enforce them - results are logged for comparison with native enforcement |
| **Disabled** | OPA is not active                                                                                             |

chunks.heading: Backend API Reference
chunks.text: This page is for developers and operators who call the ArmorIQ backend directly. Use the OTLP route to send traces, and the organization routes to read telemetry and manage controls. SDKs and Collectors normally send traces for you.

chunks.heading: Authentication and organization scope
chunks.text:
| API                                                 | Authentication                                      | Organization selection                         |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `POST /v1/traces`                                   | API key in `x-api-key` (or `Authorization: Bearer`) | Resolved from the API key                      |
| `GET /observability/policy/lease`                   | API key in `x-api-key`                              | Resolved from the API key                      |
| `POST /observability/spans` (legacy)                | API key in `x-api-key`                              | Resolved from the API key                      |
| All `/organization/:orgId/observability/...` routes | Bearer JWT                                          | `orgId` path parameter plus a membership check |

The organization and product always come from the API key. A request body or a span attribute cannot choose another organization, product, or user. A key with no organization gets `400`. A key with no product gets `403` with `relogin_required`.

Each organization route needs a permission. The table below names it. See [Organization controls](/platform/observability/organization-controls#permissions) for what each permission allows.

chunks.heading: Endpoints
chunks.text:
| Method            | Path                                                                   | Permission                     | Purpose                                 |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `POST`            | `/v1/traces`                                                           | API key                        | Ingest OTLP traces                      |
| `GET`             | `/observability/policy/lease`                                          | API key                        | Get the SDK policy lease                |
| `POST`            | `/observability/spans`                                                 | API key                        | Legacy JSON ingest, for older SDKs only |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy`                            | Metadata read                  | Get the organization policy             |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy/effective`                  | Metadata read                  | Get the effective policy                |
| `PATCH`           | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy`                            | Settings manage                | Replace the organization policy         |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy/scopes`                     | Metadata read                  | List scope overrides                    |
| `PATCH`           | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy/scopes/:scopeType/:scopeId` | Settings manage                | Save a scope override                   |
| `DELETE`          | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policy/scopes/:scopeType/:scopeId` | Settings manage                | Remove a scope override                 |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/usage`                             | Metadata read                  | Get quota use                           |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/pipeline-health`                   | Metadata read                  | Get ingest counters                     |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/alerts`                            | Alert read                     | List quota warnings                     |
| `GET`, `POST`     | `/organization/:orgId/observability/alert-rules`                       | Alert read, Alert manage       | List and create alert rules             |
| `PATCH`, `DELETE` | `/organization/:orgId/observability/alert-rules/:ruleId`               | Alert manage                   | Change or disable a rule                |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/alert-rules/:ruleId/firings`       | Alert read                     | List firings of a rule                  |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/audit`                             | Settings manage (view)         | List change history                     |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/execution-story`                   | Content read                   | Get one normalized execution story      |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/sessions`                          | Metadata read                  | List sessions                           |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/sessions/:id`                      | Content read                   | Get one session with traces             |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/traces`                            | Metadata read                  | List traces                             |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/traces/:id`                        | Content read                   | Get one trace with spans                |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/policies/:policyId`                | Metadata read                  | Aggregate one policy                    |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/analytics/summary`                 | Metadata read                  | Get overview metrics                    |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/tokens`                            | Metadata read                  | Group token and cost usage              |
| `POST`            | `/organization/:orgId/observability/export`                            | Export create and content read | Start an encrypted export               |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/export/:jobId`                     | Export create and content read | Get export status                       |
| `GET`             | `/organization/:orgId/observability/export/:jobId/download`            | Export create and content read | Download the export                     |
| `DELETE`          | `/organization/:orgId/observability/data`                              | Delete execute                 | Delete traces                           |

chunks.heading: Ingest traces (OTLP)
chunks.text:
```http
POST /v1/traces
x-api-key: YOUR_ARMORIQ_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/x-protobuf
Content-Encoding: gzip
```

The body is a standard OTLP `ExportTraceServiceRequest` in protobuf. You can send it uncompressed or with `gzip`. SDKs and Collectors do this for you. See [Deploy an OpenTelemetry Collector](/platform/observability/collector) for a working configuration.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
| Rule                         | Value                                                                       |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Content type                 | `application/x-protobuf` only. Others, including OTLP/JSON, get `415`.      |
| Content encoding             | None, or `gzip`. Others get `415`.                                          |
| Body as sent                 | At most 1,000,000 bytes. More gets `413`.                                   |
| Body after decompression     | At most 4,000,000 bytes. More gets `413`.                                   |
| Resource blocks in a request | At most 64                                                                  |
| Scope blocks in a resource   | At most 64                                                                  |
| Spans in a scope             | At most 500                                                                 |
| Spans in a request           | At most 2,000                                                               |
| Traces in a request          | At most 500                                                                 |
| Attributes                   | At most 64 on a resource and on a span, 32 on a scope, an event, and a link |
| Events and links in a span   | At most 32 each                                                             |
| One string                   | At most 4,096 bytes. A longer content value is cut.                         |
| Rate                         | 120 requests each minute for each API key                                   |

The body size, content type, and `gzip` checks run before the API key check. If a request has more than 64 resource blocks, more than 64 scope blocks in a resource, or more than 500 spans in one scope, ArmorIQ rejects the whole request with `400`. For the other bounds, ArmorIQ rejects only the spans that they affect and counts them as rejected.

chunks.heading: Responses
chunks.text:
| Status             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`              | The request is accepted. The body is an OTLP response. If ArmorIQ rejected some spans for a reason that a retry cannot fix, the body has `partial_success` with `rejected_spans` and a short `error_message`. |
| `200` (empty body) | Capture is Off for the organization or product, or ingest is switched off. Nothing was stored.                                                                                                                |
| `400`              | The payload is malformed, empty, or over a structure bound                                                                                                                                                    |
| `401`              | The API key is missing, not valid, or expired                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `403`              | `relogin_required`: the key has no product, or it is a tool-product key outside a personal workspace                                                                                                          |
| `413`              | The body is too large                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `415`              | Wrong content type or encoding                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `429`              | A rate limit, or the monthly quota. For quota, the response has `Retry-After: 60` and a `partial_success` body.                                                                                               |
| `503`              | Storage or the policy store is not available for a short time. Retry.                                                                                                                                         |

chunks.heading: Duplicate behavior
chunks.text: ArmorIQ stores each span one time. It matches on organization, product, trace ID, and span ID. If a batch arrives again, ArmorIQ counts the repeats as duplicates and does not apply them twice. A request that was retried after a `429`, a `503`, or a network error is safe. A quota reservation for a retry is also recognized and not charged twice.

chunks.heading: Get the SDK policy lease
chunks.text:
```http
GET /observability/policy/lease
x-api-key: YOUR_ARMORIQ_API_KEY
```

The SDK calls this route to learn what it may capture. The response has `revision`, `captureMode`, `debugExpiresAt`, `contentCaptureAllowed`, `externalContentCaptureAllowed`, `externalContentAllowed`, `contentReasonCode`, `expiresAt`, and sometimes `generation`. A lease lasts at most 5 minutes, or until the debug window ends if that is sooner. If ArmorIQ cannot read the policy, it returns a short `metadata` lease with all content flags off and `contentReasonCode` set to `policy_unavailable`.

The lease is only a hint for the SDK. ArmorIQ does not trust the SDK for policy. It reads the organization policy again, with a row lock, in the same database transaction as each write, and it redacts the data again.

chunks.heading: Organization policy and scopes
chunks.text:
`PATCH /organization/:orgId/observability/policy` replaces the whole policy. Send every field:

| Field                                          | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `expectedRevision`                             | The revision that you loaded, at least 1. A different current revision gives `409`.                                                         |
| `captureMode`                                  | `off`, `metadata`, `enhanced`, or `debug`                                                                                                   |
| `debugExpiresAt`                               | Required for `debug`: a future time, at most 24 hours ahead. It must be `null` for any other mode. You cannot make an active window longer. |
| `contentCaptureAllowed`                        | Allow content in `enhanced` and `debug`                                                                                                     |
| `externalContentCaptureAllowed`                | Allow content to go to an external destination. It needs the external export permission.                                                    |
| `monthlySpanQuota`, `monthlyStorageBytesQuota` | Monthly limits. Safe whole numbers, sent as numbers and returned as strings.                                                                |
| `samplingRate`                                 | A whole number from 0 to 100, or `null`                                                                                                     |
| `retentionDays`, `legalHold`                   | Retention settings. A legal hold change needs the legal hold permission.                                                                    |

A change to the debug window needs the debug permission, as well as the settings permission.

`PATCH .../policy/scopes/:scopeType/:scopeId` saves an override. `scopeType` is `product`, `environment`, or `agent`. Send `captureMode` and, after the first save, `expectedRevision`. A scope can only lower the mode. Only the `product` scope is enforced at ingest. ArmorIQ applies the `product` scope that matches the product of the API key.

`GET .../policy/effective` returns what applies now:

* `organization`: `captureMode`, `effectiveCaptureMode`, and `revision`;
* `scopes`: for each, `scopeType`, `scopeId`, `captureMode`, `effectiveCaptureMode`, `revision`, and `enforced`;
* `switches`: `otlpIngest`, `enhancedContent`, `debugCapture`, and `leaseDelivery`, the operator switches.

chunks.heading: Usage, pipeline health, and alerts
chunks.text:
* `GET .../usage` accepts an optional `product`. It returns the period start and, for the organization (and for the product if you ask), the committed and reserved counts and the limit for spans and storage, as strings, plus `warnings`. A warning is `span_quota_80_percent` or `storage_quota_80_percent`.
* `GET .../pipeline-health` needs `from` and `to` and accepts `product`. The range is at most 31 days. It returns `requestCount`, `failedRequestCount`, `acceptedSpans`, `rejectedSpans`, `duplicateSpans`, `mappingFailureSpans`, `avgExportLatencyMs`, `maxExportLatencyMs`, `effectiveFrom`, and `effectiveTo`. `effectiveFrom` and `effectiveTo` can be wider than your range for older data.
* `POST .../alert-rules` takes `conditionType`, `threshold`, `windowMinutes` (1 to 1,440), and optionally `severity` (`info`, `warning`, `critical`) and `enabled`. The condition types are `policy_denial_rate`, `tool_error_rate`, `model_error_rate`, `p95_latency`, `token_cost_budget`, `token_count_budget`, `retry_rate`, `timeout_rate`, `exporter_ingest_rejection_rate`, and `missing_telemetry`. `DELETE` disables the rule. It does not remove it.
* A firing has `id`, `ruleId`, `openedAt`, `lastSeenAt`, `resolvedAt`, `value`, `lastValue`, and sample IDs of the source traces.
* `GET .../audit` accepts `limit` (at most 200) and `includeLeases`. Each entry has `auditEventId`, `actorType`, `actorId`, `product`, `action`, `beforeSummary`, `afterSummary`, and `createdAt`.

chunks.heading: Execution story, export, and delete
chunks.text:
* `GET .../execution-story` finds one normalized execution story. Give one of `traceId`, `otelTraceId` (32 lower-case hexadecimal characters), `sessionId`, `conversationId`, `workflowRunId`, `agentId`, `product`, or `risTicketId`.
* `POST .../export` starts an encrypted export. Send `limit` (1 to 100 traces). It answers `202` with a `jobId`. At most 2 exports can be open for an organization. Poll `GET .../export/:jobId`, then call the download route.
* `DELETE .../data` takes `traceIds`, 1 to 100 UUID version 4 values. It answers with `requested`, `deleted`, `status`, and `invalidatedExports`. It answers `409` while a legal hold is active.

chunks.heading: Legacy ingest
chunks.text:
`POST /observability/spans` takes the older JSON record that older SDKs send. ArmorIQ keeps the route open for a limited time so that clients that you have not upgraded still deliver data. It uses the same policy, redaction, quota, and storage rules as OTLP. The current SDKs (`armoriq-sdk` 0.8.17, `@armoriq/sdk` 0.8.23) never call it, and no SDK falls back to it. Do not start new work on it. See [Migrate from the legacy recorder](/platform/observability/migration).

A request has `product` and up to 500 `batches`. Each batch has one `trace` and its `spans`. The response is `202` with `accepted`, `duplicate`, `rejected`, and `traceIds`. If capture is Off, the response also has `captureDisabled: true`. The fields are in the [data model](/platform/observability/data-model#legacy-json-records).

chunks.heading: List sessions
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/sessions?days=7&limit=50&status=active
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

Query parameters:

| Parameter | Type    | Default | Constraints                                  |
| --------- | ------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `days`    | integer | `7`     | 1–90                                         |
| `limit`   | integer | `50`    | 1–200                                        |
| `cursor`  | string  | none    | Opaque cursor from the previous page         |
| `status`  | string  | none    | `active`, `completed`, `expired`, or `error` |
| `userId`  | UUID    | none    | Exact match                                  |
| `agentId` | string  | none    | Exact match                                  |

```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
      "orgId": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444",
      "userId": null,
      "agentId": "support-agent",
      "product": "armoriq-sdk",
      "startedAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.000Z",
      "lastActivityAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.240Z",
      "traceCount": 1,
      "totalInputTokens": 420,
      "totalOutputTokens": 96,
      "totalCacheReadTokens": 0,
      "totalCacheWriteTokens": 0,
      "totalCostUsd": 0.00201,
      "status": "active"
    }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "OPAQUE_CURSOR",
  "hasMore": true
}
```

`nextCursor` is omitted on the final page.

chunks.heading: Get a session
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/sessions/SESSION_ID
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

The response contains every session field plus a chronological `traces` array. Each trace includes the base trace record and list metrics:

```json
{
  "id": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
  "orgId": "44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444",
  "userId": null,
  "agentId": "support-agent",
  "product": "armoriq-sdk",
  "startedAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.000Z",
  "lastActivityAt": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.240Z",
  "traceCount": 1,
  "totalInputTokens": 420,
  "totalOutputTokens": 96,
  "totalCacheReadTokens": 0,
  "totalCacheWriteTokens": 0,
  "totalCostUsd": 0.00201,
  "status": "active",
  "traces": [
    {
      "id": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
      "sessionId": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
      "name": "iap.plan",
      "startTime": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.000Z",
      "endTime": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.240Z",
      "durationMs": 240,
      "status": "ok",
      "userId": null,
      "agentId": "support-agent",
      "attributes": { "input": "Find the account owner" },
      "tags": ["armoriq-sdk", "allowed"],
      "totalInputTokens": 420,
      "totalOutputTokens": 96,
      "totalCostUsd": 0.00201,
      "spanCount": 1,
      "errorCount": 0,
      "inputPreview": "Find the account owner",
      "outputPreview": null
    }
  ]
}
```

The session-detail trace array is capped at 50,000 rows. If a session exceeds the cap, the response keeps the most recent traces and the backend logs a warning.

If the session ID does not exist in the organization, the current endpoint returns HTTP `200` with JSON `null`, not `404`.

chunks.heading: List traces
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/traces?days=7&limit=100&status=error&minDurationMs=500
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

| Parameter       | Type    | Default | Constraints                                   |
| --------------- | ------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `days`          | integer | `7`     | 1–90                                          |
| `limit`         | integer | `50`    | 1–200                                         |
| `cursor`        | string  | none    | Opaque cursor from the previous page          |
| `sessionId`     | UUID    | none    | Exact match                                   |
| `name`          | string  | none    | Exact trace-name match                        |
| `status`        | string  | none    | `ok`, `error`, or `denied`                    |
| `userId`        | UUID    | none    | Exact match                                   |
| `agentId`       | string  | none    | Exact match                                   |
| `minDurationMs` | integer | none    | Minimum duration, inclusive                   |
| `hasError`      | boolean | none    | `true` selects non-`ok`; `false` selects `ok` |

`hasError` overrides `status` when both are supplied.

The response uses the same cursor envelope as sessions. Trace items contain the base trace fields plus `totalInputTokens`, `totalOutputTokens`, `totalCostUsd`, `spanCount`, `errorCount`, `inputPreview`, and `outputPreview`.

chunks.heading: Get a trace
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/traces/TRACE_ID
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

```json
{

  "sessionId": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
  "name": "iap.plan",

  "endTime": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.240Z",
  "durationMs": 240,
  "status": "ok",
  "userId": null,
  "agentId": "support-agent",
  "attributes": { "input": "Find the account owner" },
  "tags": ["armoriq-sdk", "allowed"],
  "product": "armoriq-sdk",
  "source": "sdk",
  "spans": [
    {
      "id": "33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333",
      "parentSpanId": null,
      "sessionId": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
      "kind": "generation",
      "name": "llm.generate",
      "startTime": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.050Z",
      "endTime": "2026-07-17T09:00:00.200Z",
      "durationMs": 150,
      "status": "ok",

        "kind": "generation",
        "model": "gpt-4o",

        "finishReason": "stop"
```

If the trace ID does not exist in the organization, the current endpoint returns HTTP `200` with JSON `null`, not `404`.

chunks.heading: Get policy aggregates
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/policies/contacts-read?days=7
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

```json
{
  "policyId": "contacts-read",
  "policyName": "Contacts read policy",
  "calls": 120,
  "allowed": 115,
  "denied": 5,
  "avgDurationMs": 18,
  "p50DurationMs": 14,
  "p95DurationMs": 42,
  "topMatchedRules": [
    { "ruleId": "allow-support", "count": 115 },
    { "ruleId": "deny-untrusted", "count": 5 }
  ]
}
```

`days` defaults to 7 and accepts 1–90. `calls` includes `allow`, `deny`, `hold`, and `ask`. The `allowed` subtotal counts only `allow`, while `denied` counts only literal `deny`; `hold` and `ask` appear in neither subtotal. Summary `topFailingPolicies` likewise counts literal `deny` decisions only.

chunks.heading: Get the analytics summary
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/analytics/summary?days=7
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

```json
{
  "period": 7,
  "totalTraces": 980,
  "totalSessions": 82,
  "totalErrors": 12,
  "totalTokens": {
    "input": 250000,
    "output": 64000,
    "cacheRead": 18000,
    "cacheWrite": 4000
  },
  "totalCostUsd": 4.812345,
  "p50DurationMs": 120,
  "p95DurationMs": 920,
  "topFailingPolicies": [
    { "policyId": "contacts-read", "count": 5 }
  ],
  "tracesPerMinute": 1.7
}
```

`tracesPerMinute` uses a trailing 60-minute window, clamped to the requested period. The other metrics use the requested `days` period.

chunks.heading: Get token aggregates
chunks.text:
```http
GET /organization/ORG_ID/observability/tokens?days=7&groupBy=model
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT
```

`groupBy` accepts `model`, `tool`, or `session` and defaults to `model`.

```json
{
  "groupBy": "model",
  "items": [
    {
      "key": "gpt-4o",
      "inputTokens": 250000,
      "outputTokens": 64000,
      "cacheReadTokens": 18000,
      "cacheWriteTokens": 4000,
      "costUsd": 4.812345
    }
  ]
}
```

Model and session groups aggregate `generation` spans. Tool groups read generic `span` records and use `attributes.toolName`; tools without generation attributes can therefore have zero token totals.

chunks.heading: Pagination
chunks.text: Session and trace lists use cursor pagination ordered by timestamp and ID. Treat `nextCursor` as opaque and send it unchanged in the next request. A malformed cursor returns `400 Invalid cursor`.

chunks.heading: Retention and aggregation limits
chunks.text:
* Default retention is 30 days.
* `OBSERVABILITY_RETENTION_DAYS` changes retention on the backend.
* A UTC retention job runs daily at 03:00 and deletes old traces; their spans are cascade-deleted. Old sessions are deleted by `lastActivityAt`.
* In-memory analytics queries scan at most 50,000 rows. A result that reaches this cap is approximate and logs a backend warning.

Next: [use the dashboard](/platform/observability/dashboard) or [troubleshoot API and shipping failures](/platform/observability/troubleshooting).

chunks.heading: ArmorCodex and ArmorClaude Observability
chunks.text:
ArmorCodex and ArmorClaude both map one agent turn to one `iap.plan` trace, but they cannot use the same delivery design. ArmorCodex receives each hook in a new process; ArmorClaude normally keeps a daemon alive across hooks.

<Callout type="warn">
  This page describes the plugin builds that bundle an **older SDK**. Those builds use the older recorder and send each turn to `POST /observability/spans`. Builds that bundle the current SDK send each turn over OpenTelemetry (OTLP) to `POST /v1/traces`, with the capture modes and limits in [What data is captured](/platform/observability/data-capture). Their per-turn delivery design is not described on this page. Check the SDK version that your plugin build uses. The backend keeps the old route open for a limited time for those builds. See [Migrate from the legacy recorder](/platform/observability/migration).
</Callout>

| Behavior           | ArmorCodex                                 | ArmorClaude                                              |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Runtime            | New short-lived process for every hook     | Long-lived daemon, with an in-process fallback           |
| Turn state         | Append-only NDJSON on disk                 | Per-session recorder registry in memory                  |
| Trace completion   | Assemble and ship during `Stop`            | End the trace during `Stop`; background shipper sends it |
| Session cleanup    | Stale-file sweep on a later `SessionStart` | Flush and remove the recorder on `SessionEnd`            |
| Typical visibility | After the `Stop` hook finishes shipping    | After `Stop` and the next background flush               |

Both integrations are additive and fail-open. A telemetry exception does not modify the hook's policy result. Boundary work is still real work: ArmorCodex awaits shipping in `Stop`, and ArmorClaude awaits final shipping in `SessionEnd`, so an unavailable endpoint can add latency at those boundaries.

chunks.heading: ArmorCodex
chunks.text: ArmorCodex has no persistent observability daemon. A recorder created by one hook process cannot be resumed by the next process, so the bridge accumulates a turn on disk and constructs a fresh recorder only when it is ready to ship.

chunks.heading: Turn lifecycle
chunks.text:
```text
UserPromptSubmit ── append trace metadata + plan-start span
PreToolUse / PermissionRequest ── append check + policy spans
PostToolUse ── append tool-report span
Stop ── rename, assemble, add token usage, ship, delete
```

1. `UserPromptSubmit` creates the turn metadata and an `iap.plan.start` span. If a later hook arrives without metadata, `Stop` can synthesize a minimal trace record.
2. `PreToolUse` and `PermissionRequest` append an `iap.check` span and a nested `policy_call` span. Allow and deny decisions are preserved.
3. `PostToolUse` appends a `tool.report` span with `ok` or `error` status inferred from the hook payload.
4. `Stop` claims the turn file, reconstructs the trace, adds per-turn generation usage from the transcript, and posts the complete trace once.

The bridge uses a file named for a SHA-256 hash of the hook session ID rather than placing the raw session ID in a path. The backend receives the session ID only when it is a valid UUID.

chunks.heading: Append-only NDJSON
chunks.text:
Each hook appends one self-contained JSON line to a per-turn NDJSON file. The file is opened with `O_APPEND | O_CREAT | O_WRONLY`, and each record is written in a single operation. This avoids the lost-update race of reading a JSON document, modifying it, and renaming a replacement while another hook process is doing the same.

Attribute objects are capped before serialization and every NDJSON line is limited to 3,800 bytes. If the process is killed during a write, assembly skips only the malformed final line and keeps other complete records.

chunks.heading: Assembly and shipping at `Stop`
Stale cleanup
chunks.text:
A turn that never reaches `Stop` leaves an unshipped file. On a later `SessionStart`, ArmorCodex removes live or claimed observability files older than six hours. Partial stale traces are deleted rather than sent long after their original turn.

There is a narrow late-hook edge case: a hook that appends after `Stop` has renamed and shipped the prior file creates a new file at the original path. That record can be associated with a later turn or eventually removed by stale cleanup. The normal hook order completes tool hooks before `Stop`.

chunks.heading: Enable or opt out
chunks.text:
Observability is enabled when an API key is available. It uses the configured ArmorIQ backend base URL and sends product `armorcodex`.

The configuration bridge honors a forwarded `disable_observability` plugin option, but the current packaged plugin metadata may not expose it in a configuration UI. The environment variable below is the reliable customer-facing opt-out.

Set the opt-out environment variable before starting Codex:

```bash
export ARMORCODEX_OBSERVABILITY_DISABLED=true
```

Accepted true values include `true`, `1`, `yes`, `y`, and `on`. If no API key is configured, ArmorCodex does not create observability records or make ingest requests.

chunks.heading: ArmorClaude
chunks.text:
ArmorClaude normally routes hooks through one long-lived daemon. The observability bridge keeps a module-level registry keyed by the hook session ID, so a recorder and active trace persist across the turn's hook events.

The non-daemon fallback is best-effort and process-local. It cannot provide the same cross-hook in-memory nesting as the daemon path.

chunks.heading: Per-request effective configuration
chunks.text:
Each hook forwards the current authentication and observability configuration to the daemon. The daemon creates an immutable effective snapshot for that request by overlaying those values onto its startup configuration. This prevents an old, environment-poor daemon configuration from silently disabling telemetry for new hook requests and avoids mutating shared configuration while sessions run concurrently.

The first event for a session creates its recorder from the effective request configuration. The registry correlates later events under the same hook session ID. Only UUID session and user IDs are sent in UUID-typed backend fields; the free-form agent ID is preserved.

chunks.heading: Turn and session lifecycle
chunks.text:
```text
UserPromptSubmit ── start iap.plan trace
PreToolUse ── add check + policy spans
PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure ── add tool-report span
Stop ── end trace for background shipping
SessionEnd ── end any active trace, flush, remove recorder
Daemon shutdown ── flush already-ended traces
```

* `UserPromptSubmit` closes any prior active trace, starts the next `iap.plan` trace, and records a bounded prompt preview.
* `PreToolUse` records `allow`, `deny`, or `ask` as a nested policy call.
* `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure` record tool output with `ok` or `error` status.
* `Stop` closes the current trace. Ended traces become eligible for the SDK background shipper, which flushes every five seconds by default.
* `SessionEnd` closes any remaining trace, explicitly flushes the recorder, stops its per-session timer, and removes it from the registry.
* Daemon shutdown and idle-timeout cleanup flush already-ended traces from every live recorder.

ArmorClaude also reports cumulative transcript token usage through the separate dashboard token-usage path at `Stop`. The current observability bridge itself records policy and tool spans; it does not add transcript-derived generation spans to the `iap.plan` trace.

chunks.heading: Enable or opt out
chunks.text:
Observability is enabled by default when an API key is available. It uses the configured ArmorIQ backend base URL and sends product `armorclaude`.

Disable it with the `disable_observability` plugin option or with:

```bash
export ARMORIQ_OBSERVABILITY_DISABLED=true
```

The plugin option takes precedence over the legacy environment value. Accepted true values include `true`, `1`, `yes`, `y`, and `on`.

chunks.heading: Data visibility
chunks.text:
Neither integration streams spans to the dashboard while a turn is active.

* ArmorCodex sends the assembled trace during `Stop`.
* ArmorClaude ends the trace during `Stop` and normally sends it on the next shipper flush.
* The dashboard polls every 30 seconds.

It is normal for the turn to finish before its trace appears. See the [dashboard guide](/platform/observability/dashboard) for refresh behavior and [troubleshooting](/platform/observability/troubleshooting) for missing or delayed data.

chunks.heading: Failure and privacy boundaries
chunks.text:
All bridge operations catch telemetry failures so they do not change enforcement. Failed batches can still be dropped, and awaited boundary shipping can still delay hook completion.

Telemetry can include prompts, policy inputs, tool inputs, and tool outputs. The bridges apply bounded sanitization such as depth, item-count, string-length, attribute-size, and known secret-pattern limits. ArmorCodex also redacts a bounded set of sensitive field names before writing observability records. These controls are not general-purpose data-loss prevention and do not guarantee that every secret or personal value is removed.

Avoid placing credentials in prompts or tool arguments, restrict access to the observability dashboard, and use safe placeholders when debugging. See the [shared data model](/platform/observability/data-model) for exact span fields and the [observability overview](/platform/observability) for the end-to-end architecture.

chunks.heading: Deploy an OpenTelemetry Collector
chunks.text:
This guide is for operators and platform engineers. You get working Collector configurations that receive traces from ArmorIQ SDKs and forward them with batching, retry, size limits, and TLS. The ArmorIQ API key comes from an environment variable. No file holds a secret.

An **OpenTelemetry Collector** is a program that you run. It receives trace data, changes it, and sends it on to one or more destinations. A **span** is one timed step in an agent run, and a **trace** is all the spans of one run.

chunks.heading: When to use a Collector
chunks.text:
Use a Collector when you need one of these:

* **Send traces to ArmorIQ and to another tool.** An SDK has one export choice. For a second destination, the SDK sends to the Collector and the Collector sends to both.
* **Use transport features the TypeScript SDK does not have.** The TypeScript SDK exporter does not support mTLS, custom CA files, HTTP proxy settings, gRPC, or compression. Set these on the Collector.
* **Keep credentials out of application processes.** The Collector holds the ArmorIQ API key and the keys for other tools.
* **Control memory and queues in one place.**

If you only need ArmorIQ dashboards, do not use a Collector. Keep the default `armoriq` export. See [Choose who exports your traces](/platform/observability/provider-ownership).

chunks.heading: How the data flows
chunks.text: 1. Set the SDK to `exporter=external` with the Collector as the endpoint. 2. The Collector receives spans on its OTLP HTTP port. 3. The Collector limits memory, groups spans into batches, and sends each batch to every destination. The SDK does **not** send your ArmorIQ API key to the Collector. The Collector holds the key and adds it when it forwards to ArmorIQ. ArmorIQ takes your organization and product from that key only. It ignores any such value inside the spans. Use one key for each organization and product that you forward.

chunks.heading: What ArmorIQ accepts
chunks.text:
Set your Collector inside these limits. ArmorIQ rejects a request that is outside them.

| Rule                     | Value                                                                          |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Route                    | `POST /v1/traces`                                                              |
| Content type             | `application/x-protobuf` only. OTLP/JSON gets `415`.                           |
| Compression              | None, or `gzip`. Another value gets `415`.                                     |
| Authentication           | Header `x-api-key: <your key>`. `Authorization: Bearer <your key>` also works. |
| Size of the body as sent | At most 1,000,000 bytes. A larger body gets `413`.                             |
| Size after decompression | At most 4,000,000 bytes.                                                       |
| Spans in one scope       | At most 500                                                                    |
| Spans in one request     | At most 2,000                                                                  |
| Rate                     | 120 requests each minute for each API key. More gets `429`.                    |

ArmorIQ answers with these codes:

| Answer       | Meaning                                                                                                        | What the Collector does         |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `200`        | Accepted. A `partial_success` field can list spans that ArmorIQ rejected for a reason that a retry cannot fix. | Does not retry                  |
| `400`        | The request is malformed or over a limit.                                                                      | Does not retry                  |
| `401`        | The API key is missing or not valid.                                                                           | Does not retry. Fix the key.    |
| `413`, `415` | Body too large, or wrong content type or compression.                                                          | Does not retry. Fix the config. |
| `429`        | A rate limit or the monthly span quota. For quota, the answer includes `Retry-After: 60`.                      | Retries                         |
| `503`        | ArmorIQ storage or policy is not available for a short time.                                                   | Retries                         |

A retry is safe. ArmorIQ stores each span one time, even when a batch arrives twice.

chunks.heading: Configuration for ArmorIQ only
chunks.text:
Save this as `otelcol.yaml`. The file holds no secret. The Collector reads `ARMORIQ_API_KEY` from its environment.

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
        # Turn on TLS for traffic from your applications.
        tls:
          cert_file: /etc/otelcol/tls/server.crt
          key_file: /etc/otelcol/tls/server.key

processors:
  # Put memory_limiter first. It refuses data before the Collector runs out of memory.
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512
    spike_limit_mib: 128
  # Keep every batch inside the ArmorIQ limits.
  batch:
    send_batch_size: 256
    send_batch_max_size: 500
    timeout: 5s

exporters:
  otlphttp/armoriq:
    endpoint: https://api.armoriq.ai # the exporter adds /v1/traces
    headers:
      x-api-key: ${env:ARMORIQ_API_KEY}
    compression: gzip
    timeout: 15s
    tls:
      insecure: false
      min_version: "1.2"
    retry_on_failure:
      enabled: true
      initial_interval: 1s
      max_interval: 30s
      max_elapsed_time: 300s
    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      num_consumers: 4
      queue_size: 1000

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/armoriq]
```

What each part does:

* **Batching.** `batch` sends a group of spans after 256 spans or 5 seconds, whichever comes first. `send_batch_max_size: 500` splits a larger group. This keeps each request under the ArmorIQ limit of 500 spans for each scope. The batch processor default is 8,192 spans, which is too large for ArmorIQ.
* **Retry.** `retry_on_failure` retries a failed send with a growing wait, from 1 second up to 30 seconds. It stops after 5 minutes. Then the Collector drops that batch.
* **Bounds.** `memory_limiter` caps memory use. `sending_queue.queue_size` caps how many batches wait for a destination that is slow or down. When the queue is full, the Collector drops new data. It does not use unlimited memory.
* **TLS.** The `https://` endpoint uses TLS, and `insecure: false` keeps certificate checks on. The receiver `tls` block protects the link from your applications.
* **API key.** `${env:ARMORIQ_API_KEY}` reads the key from the environment when the Collector starts. If the variable is not set, the key is empty and ArmorIQ answers `401`.
* **Protocol.** The exporter default is protobuf with gzip. Do not set `encoding: json`. ArmorIQ rejects JSON.

<Callout type="info">
  Newer Collector releases rename the `otlphttp` exporter to `otlp_http`. The old name still works as an alias. Use the name that your Collector version documents.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Configuration for ArmorIQ and a second tool
chunks.text:
Use one pipeline for each destination. If one destination is slow, the other does not wait.

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
        tls:
          cert_file: /etc/otelcol/tls/server.crt
          key_file: /etc/otelcol/tls/server.key

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512
    spike_limit_mib: 128
  batch/armoriq:
    send_batch_size: 256
    send_batch_max_size: 500
    timeout: 5s
  batch/vendor:
    send_batch_size: 512
    send_batch_max_size: 1024
    timeout: 5s

exporters:
  otlphttp/armoriq:
    endpoint: https://api.armoriq.ai
    headers:
      x-api-key: ${env:ARMORIQ_API_KEY}
    timeout: 15s
    tls:
      insecure: false
    retry_on_failure:
      enabled: true
      initial_interval: 1s
      max_interval: 30s
      max_elapsed_time: 300s
    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      queue_size: 1000

  otlphttp/vendor:
    # The full traces URL from the vendor's OTLP documentation.
    traces_endpoint: ${env:VENDOR_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT}
    headers:
      authorization: ${env:VENDOR_OTLP_AUTHORIZATION}
    timeout: 15s
    tls:
      insecure: false
    retry_on_failure:
      enabled: true
      max_elapsed_time: 300s
    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      queue_size: 1000

service:
  pipelines:
    traces/armoriq:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch/armoriq]
      exporters: [otlphttp/armoriq]
    traces/vendor:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch/vendor]
      exporters: [otlphttp/vendor]
```

The second tool has its own limits. Check its OTLP documentation for the maximum batch size.

chunks.heading: Keep content away from the second tool
chunks.text:
The SDK sends prompt and tool content to a Collector only when your organization allows external content. See [What data is captured](/platform/observability/data-capture#what-leaves-armoriq-when-you-export). You can also remove content in the Collector before it reaches a tool. The `attributes` processor is in the Collector contrib distribution:

```yaml
processors:
  attributes/no-content:
    actions:
      - key: gen_ai.input.messages
        action: delete
      - key: gen_ai.output.messages
        action: delete
      - key: gen_ai.tool.call.arguments
        action: delete
      - key: gen_ai.tool.call.result
        action: delete
```

Add `attributes/no-content` to the `traces/vendor` pipeline, after `memory_limiter` and before the batch processor.

chunks.heading: Run the Collector
chunks.text:
Pass the key from your secret store into the environment. Do not write it in a file or a command history.

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -e ARMORIQ_API_KEY \
  -v "$PWD/otelcol.yaml:/etc/otelcol/config.yaml:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/tls:/etc/otelcol/tls:ro" \
  -p 4318:4318 \
  otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:<version> \
  --config /etc/otelcol/config.yaml
```

Replace `<version>` with a release tag that you have tested. In Kubernetes, put the key in a Secret and map it to the environment variable with `secretKeyRef`.

chunks.heading: Point the SDK at the Collector
chunks.text:
Set the SDK to `external` and give it the Collector address.

```bash
export ARMORIQ_OTEL_EXPORTER=external
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=https://collector.example.com:4318/v1/traces
```

* The SDK accepts `http:` only for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, and `::1`. For any other host, use `https:`.
* A good pattern is a Collector next to each application, for example as a sidecar. The SDK sends to `http://localhost:4318/v1/traces` on the same machine. The Collector then sends over TLS to ArmorIQ. This also works for the TypeScript SDK, which has no setting for a custom certificate authority.
* If the Collector needs a header, set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS`. See [Choose who exports your traces](/platform/observability/provider-ownership#settings-reference).

<Callout type="warn">
  Spans that reach ArmorIQ through `external` export carry the attributes of an external export, not every ArmorIQ-only attribute. For example, the TypeScript SDK writes the session ID as the standard `session.id` instead of `armoriq.session_id`, and ArmorIQ does not store `session.id`. A trace that arrives this way can lack its session link and other ArmorIQ-only fields. Open the first trace in the dashboard and check it before you rely on the Collector path for ArmorIQ.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Check that it works
chunks.text:
1. Run one agent request.
2. Look at the Collector logs. There must be no export errors for `otlphttp/armoriq`.
3. In ArmorIQ, open **Settings > Observability** and read **Usage and pipeline health**. The count of accepted spans must rise. See [Organization controls](/platform/observability/organization-controls#usage-and-pipeline-health).

chunks.text:
