chunks.heading: Identity Provider
chunks.text:
<Callout type="info">
  This page is about certificates for your AI agents. To let your team sign in through Google Workspace, Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, see [Single Sign-On (SSO)](/platform/authentication/sso).
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The Identity Provider settings allow you to configure **Google Certificate Authority Service (CAS)** for your organization. This enables cryptographic identity for your AI agents through certificate issuance.

Navigate to **Settings → Identity Provider** or go to `/dashboard/settings/identity-provider`.

chunks.heading: Configuration Fields
chunks.text:
| Field                    | Description                                                                                    | Example                            |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| **Service Account JSON** | Google Cloud service account credentials in JSON format. Paste the full JSON key file content. | `{"type": "service_account", ...}` |
| **GCP Project ID**       | Your Google Cloud project ID. Auto-filled when you paste the service account JSON.             | `my-project-123`                   |
| **CA Pool Location**     | The region where your CA pool is hosted.                                                       | `us-central1`                      |
| **CA Pool ID**           | The ID of your Certificate Authority pool.                                                     | `prod-agent-ca`                    |

chunks.heading: Setup Steps
chunks.text:
1. **Create a CA Pool** in Google Cloud Certificate Authority Service.
2. **Create a Service Account** with permissions to issue certificates from that pool.
3. **Download the JSON key file** for the service account.
4. **Paste the JSON** into the Service Account JSON field - the GCP Project ID auto-fills.
5. **Enter the CA Pool Location** and **CA Pool ID**.
6. Click **Complete Setup**.

chunks.heading: Status Messages
chunks.text:
* **Success** - Configuration saved. A green checkmark confirms the setup.
* **Error** - Invalid credentials or missing fields. An error message with details appears.

Status messages auto-clear after 5 seconds.

<Callout type="info">
  The service account needs the `roles/privateca.certificateRequester` role on the target CA pool to issue certificates.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.text: The Settings section provides organization administration tools, primarily focused on user and team management.

chunks.heading: Topics
chunks.text:
* **[Team Members](/platform/settings/team-members)** - View, search, and manage organization members.
* **[Invitations & Requests](/platform/settings/invitations)** - Invite members and manage join requests.
* **[Identity Provider](/platform/settings/identity-provider)** - Configure Google CAS certificate authority for agent identity.
* **[Single Sign-On](/platform/authentication/sso)** - Let your team sign in through your company's identity provider.
* **[Product Preferences](/platform/settings/product-preferences)** - Enable or disable optional products (OPA Engine, ArmorClaw, ArmorHealth, ArmorPay) in your sidebar.

chunks.heading: Invitations
chunks.text: Send email invitations to new team members: 1. Click **Invite Member** 2. Enter the email address 3. Select a role to assign 4. Click **Send Invitation** The invitee receives an email with a link to accept the invitation. Invited users who don't have an ArmorIQ account will be prompted to create one first. The invitation link is preserved and applied after account creation.

chunks.heading: Join Requests
chunks.text: Manage incoming join requests from users who found your organization via search: * **View** the requester's name, email, and request date * **Approve** - Grant them access to the organization * **Reject** - Deny the request

chunks.heading: Team Quota
chunks.text:
The default team size limit is **5 members**. The invite button is disabled when the limit is reached.

<Callout type="info">
  Contact ArmorIQ support to request an increase in team size or other resource quotas.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Product Preferences lets you control which optional products appear in your sidebar navigation. Navigate to **Settings → Product Preferences** or go to `/dashboard/settings/products`.

chunks.heading: Available Products
chunks.text:
| Product         | Icon       | Description                                                                            |
| --------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **OPA Engine**  | Activity   | Enforce fine-grained, context-aware access policies with Open Policy Agent integration |
| **ArmorClaw**   | Puzzle     | Detect and remediate vulnerabilities in ArmorClaw installations and agent skills       |
| **ArmorHealth** | HeartPulse | Author and enforce health-domain compliance policies for insurance AI agents           |
| **ArmorPay**    | FileCheck  | Define and automate payment compliance policies for financial AI agents                |

chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text:
Each product is displayed as a card with a toggle:

* **Enabled** - The card border turns orange, the icon badge is highlighted, and status shows **"In sidebar"**. The product's navigation items appear in the sidebar.
* **Disabled** - The card is gray, status shows **"Hidden"**. The product's navigation items are hidden from the sidebar.

Click the circular toggle on any product card to enable or disable it. Changes take effect immediately - the sidebar updates in real time.

chunks.heading: Header
chunks.text:
The page header shows the count of currently active products (e.g., "2 of 4 active").

<Callout type="info">
  Product preferences are saved per-user. Enabling a product only adds it to your own sidebar - it does not affect other team members.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Users
chunks.text: View and manage all organization members: | Column | Description | | ---------- | --------------------------------- | | **Name** | Member's full name | | **Email** | Email address | | **Role** | Assigned organization role | | **Status** | Active / Pending | | **Joined** | When they joined the organization | **Actions available:** * **Search** by name or email * **Filter** by role or status * **Edit role** - Change a member's role * **Remove** - Remove from the organization * **Download** - Export member data as JSON

chunks.heading: Roles
chunks.text: View all available organization roles: | Role | Key Capabilities | | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Organization Admin** | Full management - members, resources, policies, settings | | **IAM Admin** | Identity management - members, roles, OAuth clients | | **Developer** | Resource management - MCP servers, agents, proxy, monitoring | | **Analyst** | Security operations - scans, vulnerabilities, reports | | **Viewer** | Read-only - dashboards and reports |

chunks.heading: Permissions
chunks.text: A detailed access matrix showing exactly which permissions each role grants. This helps administrators understand the scope of each role before assigning it.

chunks.heading: Google Workspace
chunks.text:
Google Workspace sign-in uses an OAuth client that you create in Google Cloud. Only accounts on your verified domains can sign in through it.

<Callout type="info">
  You need permission to create OAuth clients in a Google Cloud project that belongs to your Google Workspace organization. You do not need Google Workspace super admin access.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Create the OAuth client in Google Cloud
chunks.text:
1. Open the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com) and select a project in your Workspace organization.
2. Go to **APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen** (shown as **Google Auth Platform** in newer consoles). If it asks you to set one up:
   * App name: for example `ArmorIQ`.
   * User support email: an address you manage.
   * Audience: **Internal**, so only your Workspace accounts can use it.
3. Go to **Clients** (or **Credentials**) and click **Create client** (or **Create credentials → OAuth client ID**).
4. Application type: **Web application**. Name: for example `ArmorIQ SSO`.
5. Leave **Authorized JavaScript origins** empty. Under **Authorized redirect URIs**, click **Add URI** and paste the **Redirect URI** shown on the ArmorIQ setup page:

```text
https://sso.armoriq.ai/callback
```

6. Click **Create**, then copy the **Client ID** and **Client secret**. Store the secret safely; Google may not show it again.

chunks.heading: Connect it in ArmorIQ
chunks.text:
1. In **Settings → Single sign-on**, under **Identity provider**, choose **Google Workspace**.
2. **Client ID**: paste the client ID. It ends in `.apps.googleusercontent.com`.
3. **Client secret**: paste the secret. Use the eye icon to check what you pasted.
4. **Name on the sign-in page** (optional): for example `Acme Google`.
5. Click **Save connection**.

<Callout type="warn">
  Verify a domain first. Google sign-in is limited to your verified domains, so the connection cannot be saved without one.
</Callout>

Next: [test the connection and turn SSO on](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable).

chunks.heading: Single Sign-On (SSO)
chunks.text: Single sign-on lets people on your company's email domain sign in to ArmorIQ through your identity provider (IdP) instead of a separate ArmorIQ password. You set it up yourself in **Settings → Single sign-on**.

chunks.heading: Supported identity providers
chunks.text:
| Provider                                            | Protocol              |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| **Google Workspace**                                | OpenID Connect (OIDC) |
| **Okta**, and any other provider that supports OIDC | OpenID Connect (OIDC) |
| **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD)          | OpenID Connect (OIDC) |

<Callout type="info">
  ArmorIQ supports OIDC only. Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace and most other identity providers support it, so SAML is not needed.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
* You need the **Org Admin** or **IAM Admin** role in the organization.
* You need access to your company domain's **DNS settings**, to prove you own the domain.
* You need admin access to your **identity provider**, to create an app for ArmorIQ.

chunks.heading: How setup works
chunks.text:
The setup page walks you through four steps:

1. **[Verify a domain](/platform/authentication/sso/verify-domain)**: add a DNS TXT record that proves your company owns the domain.
2. **Connect provider**: create an app in your identity provider and enter its details. See the guide for [Google Workspace](/platform/authentication/sso/google-workspace), [Okta](/platform/authentication/sso/okta) or [Microsoft Entra ID](/platform/authentication/sso/microsoft-entra-id).
3. **[Test sign-in](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable)**: sign in once through your identity provider to prove the connection works.
4. **[Turn on](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable#turn-sso-on)**: people on your verified domains can now sign in with SSO.

chunks.heading: What changes for your team
chunks.text:
* **Signing in.** On the sign-in page, people choose **Continue with SSO** and enter their work email. ArmorIQ sends them to your identity provider and back.
* **SSO is optional.** People can still sign in with email and password, Google or GitHub.
* **Existing accounts are kept.** Someone who already has an ArmorIQ account with the same email signs in to that account, with all their organizations.
* **New people get their own workspace.** Someone signing in for the first time gets a personal workspace. SSO does not add them to your organization; [invite them](/platform/settings/invitations) to give them access.

chunks.heading: Who can see and change SSO
chunks.text:
| Role                 | Single sign-on page                                          |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Org Admin, IAM Admin | Full setup: domains, provider, test, turn on and off, remove |
| Developer, Viewer    | Read-only: whether SSO is on, and for which domains          |
| Analyst              | No access                                                    |

Every change is recorded in the [audit log](/platform/audit-logs) with who made it.

<Callout type="warn">
  Changing the provider settings turns SSO off until a new test sign-in passes. This keeps a mistyped value from locking your team out.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Microsoft Entra ID
chunks.text: Microsoft Entra ID sign-in uses an app registration in your tenant. Only people in that tenant can sign in through it.

chunks.heading: Register the app in Entra
chunks.text:
1. In the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com), go to **App registrations** and click **New registration**.
2. Name: for example `ArmorIQ`.
3. Supported account types: **Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single tenant)**.
4. Redirect URI: platform **Web**, with the **Redirect URI** shown on the ArmorIQ setup page:

```text
https://sso.armoriq.ai/callback
```

5. Click **Register**. On the app's **Overview**, copy the **Application (client) ID** and the **Directory (tenant) ID**.
6. Go to **Certificates & secrets → Client secrets** and click **New client secret**. Choose an expiry and click **Add**.
7. Copy the secret's **Value** right away. Entra only shows it once. Do not copy the **Secret ID**.

<Callout type="warn">
  Client secrets in Entra expire. Note the expiry date and [update the secret in ArmorIQ](#rotate-the-client-secret) before it expires, or SSO sign-in stops working.
</Callout>

The app needs Microsoft Graph's **User.Read** permission, which new registrations include by default. If your tenant requires admin consent for apps, grant it under **API permissions**.

chunks.heading: Connect it in ArmorIQ
chunks.text:
1. In **Settings → Single sign-on**, under **Identity provider**, choose **Microsoft Entra ID**.
2. **Directory (tenant) ID**: paste the tenant ID. It looks like `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`.
3. **Client ID**: paste the Application (client) ID.
4. **Client secret**: paste the secret's value.
5. **Name on the sign-in page** (optional): for example `Acme Microsoft`.
6. Click **Save connection**.

<Callout type="info">
  ArmorIQ signs people in by their Entra sign-in name (user principal name). It must be on one of your verified domains: `jane@acme.com` works when `acme.com` is verified, but `jane@acme.onmicrosoft.com` does not.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Rotate the client secret
chunks.text:
Create a new client secret in Entra, then in ArmorIQ paste it into **Client secret** and click **Save connection**. Saving turns SSO off until a new [test sign-in](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable) passes, so run the test and turn SSO back on straight away.

Next: [test the connection and turn SSO on](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable).

chunks.heading: Okta and Other OIDC Providers
chunks.text: Use **Okta or other OIDC** for Okta and for any identity provider that supports OpenID Connect (for example OneLogin, JumpCloud, Ping Identity or Auth0).

chunks.heading: Create the app in Okta
chunks.text:
1. In the Okta Admin Console, go to **Applications → Applications** and click **Create App Integration**.
2. Sign-in method: **OIDC - OpenID Connect**. Application type: **Web Application**. Click **Next**.
3. App integration name: for example `ArmorIQ`.
4. Grant type: keep **Authorization Code**.
5. **Sign-in redirect URIs**: replace the example with the **Redirect URI** shown on the ArmorIQ setup page:

```text
https://sso.armoriq.ai/callback
```

6. **Sign-out redirect URIs**: remove the example; ArmorIQ does not need one.
7. **Assignments**: choose who may use ArmorIQ, either everyone in your organization or specific groups.
8. Click **Save**. On the app's **General** tab, copy the **Client ID** and **Client secret**.

chunks.heading: Find your issuer URL
chunks.text:
The issuer URL identifies your Okta authorization server:

| Okta setup                    | Issuer URL                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Most organizations            | `https://<your-okta-domain>`, for example `https://acme.okta.com`                                   |
| A custom authorization server | `https://<your-okta-domain>/oauth2/<server-id>`, for example `https://acme.okta.com/oauth2/default` |

For other providers, the issuer is the `issuer` value in the provider's OpenID configuration at `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.

chunks.heading: Connect it in ArmorIQ
chunks.text:
1. In **Settings → Single sign-on**, under **Identity provider**, choose **Okta or other OIDC**.
2. **Issuer URL**: paste the issuer, starting with `https://`.
3. **Client ID** and **Client secret**: paste the values from Okta.
4. **Name on the sign-in page** (optional): for example `Acme Okta`.
5. Click **Save connection**.

ArmorIQ checks the issuer when you save. It must be reachable over the public internet and publish an OpenID configuration that names the same issuer.

<Callout type="info">
  Your identity provider must mark users' email addresses as verified (the `email_verified` claim). Okta does this for activated users. A user whose email is not verified cannot sign in with SSO.
</Callout>

Next: [test the connection and turn SSO on](/platform/authentication/sso/test-and-enable).

chunks.heading: Test and Turn On
chunks.text: After you save a connection, the **Test and turn on** card appears on the setup page. SSO stays off until a test sign-in passes for the current settings.

chunks.heading: Run a test sign-in
chunks.text:
1. Click **Run test sign-in**.
2. Your identity provider opens. Sign in with a company account on one of your verified domains.
3. You come back to the setup page with the result.

A test never creates an account or signs anyone in to ArmorIQ. It only checks that the connection works.

If the test fails, the page explains why. See [Troubleshooting](/platform/authentication/sso/troubleshooting#test-sign-in-results) for each message.

chunks.heading: Turn SSO on
chunks.text:
When the test passes, click **Turn on SSO**. A banner confirms which domains now sign in through your identity provider.

To check it, open a private browser window, go to the ArmorIQ sign-in page, choose **Continue with SSO** and enter your work email.

chunks.heading: Change the settings
chunks.text:
You can edit the provider settings at any time:

* The client secret is never shown again. Leave **Client secret** blank to keep the saved one, or paste a new one to replace it.
* **Saving turns SSO off** until a new test sign-in passes. Run the test and turn SSO back on after every change.

chunks.heading: Turn SSO off
chunks.text: Click **Turn off SSO** and confirm. People stop signing in through your identity provider right away and use email, Google or GitHub instead. You can turn SSO back on without testing again, as long as the settings have not changed.

chunks.heading: Remove the connection
chunks.text: Under **Remove SSO connection**, click **Remove connection** and confirm. This deletes the connection and its client secret. Your verified domains stay. To use SSO again, connect a provider and test it from the start.

chunks.heading: Domain verification
chunks.text:
| Problem                                      | What to check                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Verify** says the TXT record was not found | Wait a few minutes and try again. Check the record with `dig +short TXT acme.com`.                                                                      |
| The record exists but still is not found     | The name may be wrong. Many DNS providers add the domain for you, so a name of `acme.com` creates `acme.com.acme.com`. Use `@` or leave the name empty. |
| The domain is refused when you add it        | Shared email providers (`gmail.com`, `outlook.com` and similar) cannot be used, and a domain verified by another organization cannot be added.          |

chunks.heading: Saving the connection
chunks.text:
| Message                                                       | What to check                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The issuer URL must point to a public identity provider       | The issuer must be reachable from the internet over `https://`. Internal or private addresses are refused.            |
| Could not read the OpenID configuration from that issuer URL  | The issuer is wrong or unreachable. Open `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` in a browser to check it.        |
| That URL publishes a different issuer                         | Use the exact `issuer` value from the provider's OpenID configuration, for example with or without `/oauth2/default`. |
| Enter your Microsoft Entra tenant ID                          | Use the **Directory (tenant) ID** GUID, not a domain name or `common`.                                                |
| Verify at least one domain before connecting Google Workspace | Verify a domain first.                                                                                                |

chunks.heading: Test sign-in results
chunks.text:
| Message                                                                  | Cause and fix                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The account you signed in with isn't on one of your verified domains     | Sign in with a company account, or verify that account's domain. For Entra, the user's sign-in name must be on a verified domain. |
| Your identity provider didn't confirm that the email address is verified | The user's email is not marked verified in your identity provider. Verify it there and test again.                                |
| Your identity provider didn't send a usable email address                | The user has no email address in your identity provider. Add one and test again.                                                  |
| Your identity provider refused the sign-in                               | Check the client ID, the client secret and the redirect URI registered in your identity provider.                                 |
| The connection changed while the test was running                        | Someone saved the settings during the test. Run it again.                                                                         |
| The test was started in another tab or browser / The test expired        | Run the test again from the setup page and finish it within 10 minutes.                                                           |

chunks.heading: Errors at your identity provider
chunks.text:
| Error                                                                  | Fix                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `redirect_uri_mismatch` (Google) or a redirect URI error (Okta, Entra) | The redirect URI in your identity provider must be exactly `https://sso.armoriq.ai/callback`, with `https` and no trailing slash.                                                       |
| Google: **Access blocked** or **admin has restricted this app**        | Your Google Workspace admin restricts third-party apps. Ask them to allow the OAuth client, or create it in a project inside your Workspace organization with an **Internal** audience. |
| Okta: user is not assigned to the client application                   | Assign the user, or one of their groups, to the ArmorIQ app in Okta.                                                                                                                    |
| Entra: the user needs admin approval                                   | Grant admin consent under **API permissions** in the app registration.                                                                                                                  |

chunks.heading: Signing in
chunks.text:
| Problem                                                   | What to check                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Continue with SSO** says SSO isn't set up for the email | SSO is off, or the email's domain is not verified in your organization.                                   |
| A new person lands in their own workspace                 | Expected. SSO does not add people to your organization; [invite them](/platform/settings/invitations).    |
| Sign-in stopped working for everyone                      | The client secret may have expired (common with Entra). Paste a new one, save, test and turn SSO back on. |

chunks.heading: Verify a Domain
chunks.text: SSO only applies to email domains your organization has verified. Verification proves you control the domain, so no other organization can route your employees' sign-ins.

chunks.heading: Add the domain
chunks.text:
1. Go to **Settings → Single sign-on**.
2. Under **Company domains**, enter your email domain (for example `acme.com`) in **Add a domain** and click **Add**.
3. The domain shows **Waiting for DNS record**, with the record to publish:

| Type  | Name | Value                                      |
| ----- | ---- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `TXT` | `@`  | `armoriq-domain-verification=<your-token>` |

Use the copy buttons on the page. The value is unique to your organization and domain.

<Callout type="info">
  `@` means the domain itself (`acme.com`). If your DNS provider does not accept `@`, leave the name empty or enter the full domain.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Publish the record
chunks.text:
Add one TXT record at the company that hosts your domain's DNS. It sits alongside your existing records and changes nothing else.

<Tabs items="["GoDaddy", "Cloudflare", "Amazon Route 53", "Other providers"]">
  <Tab value="GoDaddy">
    1. Open **My Products → Domains**, select the domain, then **DNS**.
    2. Click **Add New Record**.
    3. Type: **TXT**. Name: `@`. Value: the value from ArmorIQ. TTL: leave the default.
    4. Click **Save**.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Cloudflare">
    1. Select the domain, then **DNS → Records**.
    2. Click **Add record**.
    3. Type: **TXT**. Name: `@`. Content: the value from ArmorIQ.
    4. Click **Save**.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Amazon Route 53">
    1. Open **Hosted zones** and select the domain.
    2. Click **Create record**.
    3. Leave **Record name** empty. Record type: **TXT**. Value: the value from ArmorIQ, in double quotes.
    4. Click **Create records**.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Other providers">
    Create a **TXT** record on the root of the domain (often written `@`) with the value from ArmorIQ. If you are unsure where your DNS is hosted, look up the domain's name servers or ask whoever manages your domain.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

chunks.heading: Verify
chunks.text:
New records can take a few minutes to appear, and occasionally longer. Back on the setup page, click **Verify**. When the record is found, the domain shows **Verified**.

To check the record yourself before verifying:

```bash
dig +short TXT acme.com
# or
nslookup -type=TXT acme.com
```

The output should include `armoriq-domain-verification=...`. You can delete the TXT record after the domain is verified, but keeping it does no harm.

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
* **Company domains only.** Shared email providers such as `gmail.com` or `outlook.com` cannot be used.
* **One organization per domain.** Once a domain is verified, no other organization can verify it. If another organization already uses your domain, contact support.
* **Up to 20 domains** per organization. Add every email domain your team uses, for example `acme.com` and `acme.io`.

chunks.heading: Removing a domain
chunks.text: Click **Remove** next to the domain. If SSO is on, people on that domain stop signing in with SSO right away, and removing your last verified domain turns SSO off. ArmorIQ asks you to confirm before removing a verified domain.

chunks.heading: Custom frameworks
chunks.text: Any framework that lets you intercept tool calls can be wrapped with ArmorIQ in about ten lines. This page shows the universal pattern, then concrete recipes for four popular frameworks. If yours isn't listed, the pattern at the top works for anything.

chunks.heading: The universal pattern
chunks.text:
Every tool call in any framework boils down to "run this action with these params." The ArmorIQ three-step flow sits between intent and execution:

```python
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

client = ArmorIQClient()  # one per process


def guarded_tool_call(
    mcp: str,
    action: str,
    params: dict,
    user_email: str,
    llm: str = "gpt-4o",
):
    """Drop-in replacement for any direct tool call."""
    plan = client.capture_plan(
        llm=llm,
        prompt=f"Call {mcp}.{action}",
        plan={
            "goal": action,
            "steps": [{"action": action, "mcp": mcp, "params": params}],
        },
    )
    token = client.get_intent_token(plan, validity_seconds=300)
    return client.invoke(
        mcp=mcp,
        action=action,
        intent_token=token,
        params=params,
        user_email=user_email,
    )
```

That function is all you need. Call it from inside your framework's tool-call path and every invocation goes through ArmorIQ's plan → token → invoke loop - signed, policy-checked, audited.

<Callout type="info">
  The examples below all use the pattern above. The only thing that changes is **where** you call it - that's the framework-specific part.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: CrewAI
chunks.text:
CrewAI tools subclass `BaseTool`. Override `_run()` to route the call through `guarded_tool_call`:

```python
from crewai.tools import BaseTool
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

client = ArmorIQClient()


class BookFlightTool(BaseTool):
    name: str = "book_flight"
    description: str = "Book a flight with given origin, destination, and date."

    def _run(self, origin: str, destination: str, date: str, user_email: str):
        plan = client.capture_plan(
            llm="gpt-4o",
            prompt=f"Book flight from {origin} to {destination}",
            plan={
                "goal": "book_flight",
                "steps": [
                    {
                        "action": "book_flight",
                        "mcp": "travel-mcp",
                        "params": {"from": origin, "to": destination, "date": date},
                    },
                ],
            },
        )
        token = client.get_intent_token(plan)
        result = client.invoke(
            mcp="travel-mcp",
            action="book_flight",
            intent_token=token,
            params={"from": origin, "to": destination, "date": date},
            user_email=user_email,
        )
        return result.data


# Use as a regular CrewAI tool
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew

researcher = Agent(
    role="Travel booker",
    goal="Book flights for users",
    tools=[BookFlightTool()],
)
task = Task(description="Book SFO→JFK on 2026-05-10", agent=researcher)
crew = Crew(agents=[researcher], tasks=[task])
result = crew.kickoff(inputs={"user_email": "alice@acme.com"})
```

chunks.heading: Generic CrewAI adapter
chunks.text:
If you want a single adapter that wraps every CrewAI tool:

```python
class ArmorIQTool(BaseTool):
    """CrewAI tool that routes every call through ArmorIQ."""

    name: str
    description: str
    mcp: str          # which MCP hosts this tool
    action: str       # tool name on the MCP
    user_email: str   # the end user scope

    def _run(self, **params):
        return guarded_tool_call(
            mcp=self.mcp,
            action=self.action,
            params=params,
            user_email=self.user_email,
        ).data
```

One class, many instances - one per tool you want to expose.

chunks.heading: LangChain
chunks.text:
LangChain's `BaseTool` has the same shape. Override `_run()`:

```python
from langchain.tools import BaseTool
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

client = ArmorIQClient()


class BookFlightTool(BaseTool):
    name = "book_flight"
    description = "Book a flight"

    def _run(self, origin: str, destination: str, date: str, user_email: str = None):
        plan = client.capture_plan(
            llm="gpt-4o",
            prompt=f"Book flight from {origin} to {destination}",
            plan={
                "goal": "book_flight",
                "steps": [
                    {
                        "action": "book_flight",
                        "mcp": "travel-mcp",
                        "params": {"from": origin, "to": destination, "date": date},
                    },
                ],
            },
        )
        token = client.get_intent_token(plan)
        return client.invoke(
            mcp="travel-mcp",
            action="book_flight",
            intent_token=token,
            params={"from": origin, "to": destination, "date": date},
            user_email=user_email,
        ).data
```

Pass `user_email` via the agent executor's inputs:

```python
from langchain.agents import AgentExecutor

agent_executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=[BookFlightTool()])
agent_executor.invoke({"input": "Book SFO→JFK", "user_email": "alice@acme.com"})
```

chunks.heading: Async variant
chunks.text: For `_arun`, same idea - `ArmorIQClient` is sync, so either call it in a thread executor or use an async HTTP client wrapper.

chunks.heading: OpenAI Assistants
chunks.text:
The OpenAI Assistants API runs tools in a structured loop with `run.required_action.submit_tool_outputs.tool_calls`. Intercept each `tool_call` before submitting outputs:

```python
from openai import OpenAI
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

openai_client = OpenAI()
armoriq_client = ArmorIQClient()


def run_with_armoriq(assistant_id: str, thread_id: str, user_email: str):
    run = openai_client.beta.threads.runs.create(
        thread_id=thread_id,
        assistant_id=assistant_id,
    )

    while True:
        run = openai_client.beta.threads.runs.retrieve(
            thread_id=thread_id, run_id=run.id
        )

        if run.status == "completed":
            return

        if run.status == "requires_action":
            tool_outputs = []
            for call in run.required_action.submit_tool_outputs.tool_calls:
                # Each tool_call has: id, function.name, function.arguments
                import json

                args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
                mcp, action = call.function.name.split(".", 1)  # e.g. "travel-mcp.book_flight"

                plan = armoriq_client.capture_plan(
                    llm="gpt-4o",
                    prompt=f"Call {call.function.name}",
                    plan={
                        "goal": action,
                        "steps": [{"action": action, "mcp": mcp, "params": args}],
                    },
                )
                token = armoriq_client.get_intent_token(plan)
                result = armoriq_client.invoke(
                    mcp=mcp,
                    action=action,
                    intent_token=token,
                    params=args,
                    user_email=user_email,
                )

                tool_outputs.append({
                    "tool_call_id": call.id,
                    "output": json.dumps(result.data),
                })

            openai_client.beta.threads.runs.submit_tool_outputs(
                thread_id=thread_id,
                run_id=run.id,
                tool_outputs=tool_outputs,
            )

        elif run.status in ("failed", "cancelled", "expired"):
            raise RuntimeError(f"Run ended: {run.status}")
```

Name your tools with a dotted prefix (`travel-mcp.book_flight`) so you can parse `(mcp, action)` out of `call.function.name`. Alternatively, maintain a tool registry mapping tool name → MCP.

chunks.heading: Anthropic tool-use
chunks.text:
Anthropic's Messages API returns `tool_use` blocks in the response. Intercept each block before executing:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

claude = Anthropic()
armoriq_client = ArmorIQClient()

# Your tool registry - maps Claude tool name → (mcp, action)
TOOL_REGISTRY = {
    "book_flight": ("travel-mcp", "book_flight"),
    "search_hotels": ("travel-mcp", "search_hotels"),
}


def chat_with_armoriq(messages, tools, user_email: str):
    while True:
        response = claude.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
            max_tokens=1024,
            tools=tools,
            messages=messages,
        )

        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return response

        tool_results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue

            mcp, action = TOOL_REGISTRY[block.name]
            plan = armoriq_client.capture_plan(
                llm="claude-sonnet-4-5",
                prompt=f"Call {block.name}",
                plan={
                    "goal": action,
                    "steps": [{"action": action, "mcp": mcp, "params": block.input}],
                },
            )
            token = armoriq_client.get_intent_token(plan)
            result = armoriq_client.invoke(
                mcp=mcp,
                action=action,
                intent_token=token,
                params=block.input,
                user_email=user_email,
            )

            tool_results.append({
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": str(result.data),
            })

        # Feed results back for the next turn
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})
```

chunks.heading: Your own framework
chunks.text:
Any framework with a "here's the tool about to run" hook works. The pattern:

1. **Intercept** - find the hook where your framework calls a tool.
2. **Plan** - call `client.capture_plan(llm=..., prompt=..., plan={...})` with a `steps` entry for the tool call.
3. **Token** - `client.get_intent_token(plan)`.
4. **Invoke** - `client.invoke(mcp, action, token, params, user_email=...)`.
5. **Return** - pass `result.data` back to your framework as the tool output.

If your framework has no tool-call hook at all (raw LLM with no structured tools), you can still use the SDK directly - build the plan manually from the LLM's output, get a token, invoke through ArmorIQ's proxy.

chunks.heading: Error handling across frameworks
Performance tips
chunks.text:
* **One `ArmorIQClient` per process.** It's thread-safe and reuses HTTP connections.
* **`capture_plan` is local.** It computes hashes; no network.
* **`get_intent_token` is network.** Cache tokens per-plan if you'll invoke the same plan multiple times within `validity_seconds`.
* **`invoke` is network.** One round-trip per tool call.
* **`client.resolve_user(email)`** caches for 5 minutes - safe to call at the start of every request.

chunks.heading: Google ADK
chunks.text:
The ArmorIQ SDK ships a first-class integration for [Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)](https://github.com/google/adk). One factory lives for the life of your process; per-request, you build a scoped bundle tied to one end-user email and install it on your agent. ArmorIQ hooks into ADK's native `before_tool_callback` / `after_tool_callback` / `after_model_callback` lifecycle, so every tool call goes through plan → token → invoke automatically.

```bash
pip install armoriq-sdk google-adk
```

chunks.heading: Setup in three lines
chunks.text:
Create one factory at process start, then per request build a user-scoped bundle, install it, and uninstall after the run.

```python
import os
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from armoriq_sdk.integrations.google_adk import ArmorIQADK

# 1. One factory per process - caches bootstrap (org, MCPs, toolMap).
armoriq = ArmorIQADK(api_key=os.environ["ARMORIQ_API_KEY"])

# Your regular ADK agent - nothing ArmorIQ-specific here.
root_agent = Agent(
    name="assistant",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    tools=[...],
)

async def handle_request(user_email: str, message: str):
    # 2. Per-request bundle scoped to this end user.
    scope = armoriq.for_user(user_email, goal=message)

    # 3. Install ArmorIQ callbacks on the agent for this run.
    scope.install(root_agent)
    try:
        async for event in runner.run_async(user_id=user_email, new_message=message):
            yield event
    finally:
        # Always uninstall so the next request starts clean.
        scope.uninstall(root_agent)
```

What `install()` wires up, as ADK callbacks on the agent:

| ADK hook               | ArmorIQ work                                                 |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `after_model_callback` | Capture the LLM's tool calls as a plan, mint an intent token |
| `before_tool_callback` | Check the policy for this user + tool; block, allow, or hold |
| `after_tool_callback`  | Write the audit log for this invocation                      |

chunks.heading: Factory options
chunks.text:
```python
armoriq = ArmorIQADK(
    api_key=os.environ["ARMORIQ_API_KEY"],  # required
    default_mcp_name="travel",              # if a tool name has no mcp prefix
    tool_name_parser=None,                  # custom `(tool_name) → (mcp, action)` parser
    validity_seconds=300,                   # intent token lifetime
    mode="sdk",                             # session mode
    llm="agent",                            # label used in plan capture
)
```

Most integrations only need `api_key`.

chunks.heading: How tool names map to MCPs
chunks.text:
ADK tools have flat names (`book_flight`); ArmorIQ needs to know which MCP that tool lives on (`travel-mcp.book_flight`). The factory resolves this in order:

1. **Platform mapping** - ArmorIQ bootstraps your `toolMap` from the registered MCPs and finds the right MCP for each tool name.
2. **Double-underscore convention** - if your tool is named `travel__book_flight`, the factory splits on `__` → (`travel`, `book_flight`).
3. **`default_mcp_name`** - fallback when the name has no other signal.
4. **Custom `tool_name_parser`** - pass a function `(str) → (mcp, action)` to override entirely.

chunks.heading: Per-user scoping with `for_user()`
chunks.text:
Every ADK run is tied to one end-user. Build the scope once per request and the bundle automatically tags every downstream plan, token, invocation, and audit log with that email.

```python
scope = armoriq.for_user("alice@customer.com", goal="Plan a trip to Paris")
```

Per-user context (membership, policies, approver chain) is cached 5 minutes - calling `for_user` in a tight loop is cheap.

To invalidate the cache after a policy change:

```python
armoriq.invalidate_user("alice@customer.com")
```

chunks.heading: Multi-user SaaS pattern
chunks.text:
A typical request handler looks like this. One factory, many user scopes:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()
armoriq = ArmorIQADK(api_key=os.environ["ARMORIQ_API_KEY"])

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    scope = armoriq.for_user(req.user_email, goal=req.message)
    scope.install(root_agent)
    try:
        events = []
        async for event in runner.run_async(
            user_id=req.user_email,
            new_message=req.message,
        ):
            events.append(event)
        return {"events": events}
    finally:
        scope.uninstall(root_agent)
```

Every user's audit log is cleanly separated. Every policy that targets `alice@customer.com` (by email, by membership, or by role) is evaluated correctly.

chunks.heading: Multi-agent hierarchies
chunks.text:
ADK supports nested agents (agent-of-agents). The ArmorIQ bundle only installs callbacks on the agent you pass to `install()`. For nested agents, install on each one you want protected:

```python
scope = armoriq.for_user(user_email)
scope.install(root_agent)
scope.install(child_agent_1)
scope.install(child_agent_2)
try:
    # ... run ...
finally:
    scope.uninstall(root_agent)
    scope.uninstall(child_agent_1)
    scope.uninstall(child_agent_2)
```

chunks.heading: Policy holds and delegation
chunks.text:
When a tool call requires human approval, ArmorIQ's `before_tool_callback` returns a **hold** - ADK blocks the tool call and surfaces the delegation info. Your run handler can wait for approval and resume.

The ADK bundle handles the hold/retry loop automatically when the policy is configured for auto-polling. Configure the hold-approval timeout on the factory:

```python
armoriq = ArmorIQADK(
    api_key=os.environ["ARMORIQ_API_KEY"],
    validity_seconds=600,  # longer window for approval-gated flows
)
```

For the full delegation workflow (creating approvers, approving from a manager account, auditing decisions), see [Policies](/platform/policies) and [Delegation](/platform/policies/enforcement).

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text:
| What you see                                     | Why                                                              | Fix                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `before_tool_callback failed` in logs            | ArmorIQ couldn't reach the backend/proxy                         | Check network + `ARMORIQ_API_KEY`; calls fall through without enforcement on failure                                |
| Every tool blocked with `PolicyBlockedException` | Policy doesn't allow this user for these tools                   | Update the policy in the [dashboard](/platform/policies)                                                            |
| Tool name resolves to `unknown.book_flight`      | The factory can't map your tool name to an MCP                   | Set `default_mcp_name=...` or pass a custom `tool_name_parser`                                                      |
| `IntentMismatchException` after tool fires       | ADK passed params that differ from what was captured in the plan | Usually means the tool's args aren't deterministic; make sure the tool's `params` match what the LLM reasoned about |

chunks.heading: Full worked example
chunks.text:
```python
import os
import asyncio
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.genai import types
from armoriq_sdk.integrations.google_adk import ArmorIQADK

# Your tools - same as vanilla ADK
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """Get current weather for a city."""
    return {"city": city, "temp": 22, "units": "celsius"}

# ArmorIQ factory - once per process
armoriq = ArmorIQADK(
    api_key=os.environ["ARMORIQ_API_KEY"],
    default_mcp_name="weather-mcp",
)

# ADK agent - nothing ArmorIQ-specific
root_agent = Agent(
    name="weather_bot",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="A weather assistant",
    tools=[get_weather],
)

session_service = InMemorySessionService()
runner = Runner(agent=root_agent, app_name="weather-app", session_service=session_service)

async def ask(user_email: str, question: str):
    # Ensure a session exists for this user
    session = await session_service.create_session(
        app_name="weather-app",
        user_id=user_email,
        session_id="default",
    )

    # Wrap the run with ArmorIQ per-user scope
    scope = armoriq.for_user(user_email, goal=question)
    scope.install(root_agent)
    try:
        async for event in runner.run_async(
            user_id=user_email,
            session_id=session.id,
            new_message=types.Content(
                role="user",
                parts=[types.Part(text=question)],
            ),
        ):
            if event.content and event.content.parts:
                print(event.content.parts[0].text)
    finally:
        scope.uninstall(root_agent)

asyncio.run(ask("alice@customer.com", "What's the weather in Paris?"))
```

The call to `get_weather` goes through ArmorIQ's policy check - `weather-mcp.get_weather` for `alice@customer.com` - and the audit log shows the full chain.

chunks.heading: Frameworks
chunks.text: ArmorIQ ships first-class adapters for several frameworks - the adapter wraps the tool-calling lifecycle and every tool call routes through the ArmorIQ loop. For anything without an adapter, use the **raw-client pattern**: call `ArmorIQClient` directly from inside your tool wrapper. Ten lines of glue code, works with anything.

chunks.heading: Which frameworks have an adapter
chunks.text:
| Framework      | Adapter                                  | Guide                                                       |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Google ADK** | `ArmorIQADK` (Python + TypeScript)       | [Google ADK guide](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/google-adk) |
| **LangChain**  | `ArmorIQLangChain` (Python + TypeScript) | [LangChain integration](/sdk/integrations/langchain)        |
| **Strands**    | `ArmorIQStrands` (Python + TypeScript)   | [Strands integration](/sdk/integrations/strands)            |
| **Langflow**   | bundled component (Python)               | [Langflow integration](/sdk/integrations/langflow)          |
| **CrewAI**     | `ArmorIQCrew` (Python, token-only)       | [CrewAI integration](/sdk/integrations/crewai)              |

Everything else uses the raw-client pattern, which works with any framework that lets you intercept a tool call before it runs. That includes the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs directly, and any proprietary scaffold. [Custom frameworks](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom) has worked examples for the [OpenAI Assistants run loop](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom#openai-assistants), [Anthropic `tool_use` blocks](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom#anthropic-tool-use), [CrewAI `BaseTool`](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom#crewai) and [LangChain](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom#langchain).

<Callout type="info">
  [Integrations](/sdk/integrations) is the source of truth for adapter status,
  including the capability differences between the full adapters and CrewAI's
  narrower token-only path. Check there rather than this table if the two ever
  disagree.
</Callout>

*Raw client* means the SDK doesn't ship a framework-specific wrapper - you write a tiny adapter (about 10 lines) that calls `client.invoke()` from inside your existing tool. The approach is the same across every framework; examples for the common ones are on the [Custom frameworks](/platform/sdk-cli/frameworks/custom) page.

chunks.heading: How integration works at a high level
chunks.text:
Every framework has somewhere to intercept tool calls before they hit the network:

* **Google ADK** - `after_model_callback` / `before_tool_callback` / `after_tool_callback` on the `Agent`.
* **Strands** - `AfterModelCallEvent` / `BeforeToolCallEvent` / `AfterToolCallEvent` lifecycle hooks.
* **LangChain** - a callback handler passed via `config={"callbacks": [...]}`.
* **CrewAI** - subclass `BaseTool`, override `_run()`.
* **OpenAI Assistants** - the `function_call` step in your run loop.
* **Anthropic** - `tool_use` blocks in the response stream.

In each case you insert the ArmorIQ three-step flow:

```
capture_plan → get_intent_token → invoke
```

The ADK, Strands and LangChain adapters wire those hooks for you. The raw-client pattern asks you to wire them yourself - more verbose, but works everywhere.
