chunks.heading: Roadmap
chunks.text:
Planned improvements to the shipped adapters:

* **CrewAI** - per-user scoping and per-call policy enforcement. The adapter today mints one token per `kickoff()` and routes tool calls through the proxy, but does not evaluate policy per call.
* **CrewAI on TypeScript** - the adapter is currently Python-only.

Current status always lives on [Integrations](/sdk/integrations).

chunks.heading: API keys
chunks.text: Find them in **Settings → API Keys**. There are two kinds, and most people never create one by hand.

chunks.heading: Device keys
chunks.text:
Created for you when you approve a machine during [install](/tools/quickstart). They carry a device
name and device id, and they are what lets your terminal report runs.

You do not create these here. They appear here, and you can revoke them here.

chunks.heading: Keys you create
chunks.text:
For the SDK or CLI, or for a second tool you are wiring up yourself. **Create key** opens a dialog
asking for three things:

* **Name.** Required, so you can tell keys apart later.
* **Product.** All products, ArmorClaude, ArmorCodex, or ArmorCopilot. Scoping a key to one
  product limits the blast radius if it leaks.
* **Expiration.** Never, 30 days, 7 days, or 1 day.

<Callout type="warn">
  The secret is shown exactly once, when the key is created. Copy it then. If you lose it, revoke
  the key and make a new one. There is no way to see it again.
</Callout>

If the dialog reports that the server did not return the secret, revoke that key and try again
rather than assuming it works.

chunks.heading: Revoking
chunks.text:
Each row shows the key name, its type, its product, its status, the device if it has one, the key
prefix, when it was created, and when it was last used, or that it has never been used.

Revoking takes two clicks, **Revoke** then **Confirm revoke**. Revoke a key when a laptop is lost,
when you are done with an integration, or when a key has never been used and you cannot say why it
exists.

chunks.heading: What a key does not tell you
chunks.text:
An active key means a key exists and has not been revoked. It does not mean a machine is currently
connected or currently reporting. The **Tools** screen makes that distinction explicitly, pairing
key status with whether a real evaluated session was actually seen. Scopes exist in the data model
but there is no scope picker in the console today, so keys are not scope-restricted from this
screen.

chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.text: You do not need this page to use the product. It is here for the person who has to approve it.

chunks.heading: The shape of it
chunks.text: **The guardrail decides and records. The console never decides.** That split is what lets the console promise it is showing real evidence: it has no way to compute a decision, so it can only render one that was already made and stored. The console does write, but only the inputs and the account around them, such as policy drafts, published versions, API keys and billing. No evidence it displays is ever produced by it.

chunks.heading: The parts
chunks.text:
**The plugin on your machine.** ArmorClaude for Claude Code, ArmorCodex for Codex. It sees the
tool calls your assistant attempts, applies the published policy profile, and reports what happened.
Installed with one command; see [Quickstart](/tools/quickstart).

**The SDK.** TypeScript and Python. Carries device identity and the enforcement and telemetry
calls. The plugins depend on it, so a plugin cannot quietly fail to report.

**The backend.** Receives policy checks and telemetry, stores sessions and tool evidence, and
serves the console. Policy evaluation runs through a dedicated engine and fails closed: when
evaluation fails, the call is denied rather than allowed.

**The console.** A static single-page app at `tools.armoriq.ai`, served over HTTPS with
framing disabled and a no-referrer policy. It runs no server of its own and reads the backend over
authenticated requests. It does keep state in your browser: your session tokens, the selected
workspace, your theme, and your prompt library all live in browser storage.

chunks.heading: What this means for a review
chunks.text:
* **Source code is not transmitted.** The plugin reports tool names, timings, decisions, token
  counts, and session and device identifiers.
* **Machine credentials are scoped and local.** The install writes one ingestion-scoped key to
  `~/.armoriq/credentials.json` with owner-only permissions, and only after you approve a short
  code shown in the browser.
* **Enforcement fails closed.** A failed policy evaluation denies.
* **The reporting path is auditable.** Ingest health is exposed in the product, so a silent
  reporting failure is visible rather than indistinguishable from low activity.
* **Revocation is self-serve.** Revoking a device key in the console is a two-click action and
  cuts off that machine's access.

For what is not yet built, including the absence of team roles and approval workflows, see
[Limits](/tools/limits).

chunks.heading: You, in the console
chunks.text:
Three ways in at [tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai):

* **Google**, with "Continue with Google".
* **GitHub**, with "Continue with GitHub".
* **Email and password.** Signing up this way sends a six-digit code to your address. The code
  lasts five minutes, and you can ask for a new one after a minute.

Forgotten passwords are handled by a reset link sent to your email.

Your name, email and photo come from whichever provider you signed in with. **Settings → Profile**
shows your display name and email as read-only.

chunks.heading: Your workspace
chunks.text:
A workspace is created automatically the first time you sign in, named after you. You do not set one
up.

One account has one workspace today. There is no workspace switcher, and there is no way to invite
anyone into yours. See [Limits](/tools/limits).

Only workspace admins can rename a workspace, in **Settings → General**.

chunks.heading: Your machine
chunks.text:
Your terminal does not sign in with your password. During [install](/tools/quickstart), the command
prints a short code and opens a browser tab. You approve the machine there, and only then is a key
created for it.

That key is written to `~/.armoriq/credentials.json` with owner-only permissions. It is scoped to
run ingestion, which is why approving a machine does not hand it your account.

<Callout>
  Always check that the code shown in the browser matches the one printed in your terminal before
  approving. A code is valid for 15 minutes.
</Callout>

Approved machines appear in **Settings → API Keys** with a device name attached, and on the
**Tools** screen under connection evidence. Revoking the key disconnects that machine.

chunks.heading: Staying signed in
chunks.text:
The console keeps you signed in and renews the session quietly in the background. When renewal
fails, you are returned to the sign-in page rather than shown stale data. After signing in you land
back on the page you were trying to reach, as long as it is a page within the console.

chunks.heading: Tour of the console
chunks.text:
The console at [tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai) is where you read everything your
assistants did. It does not make decisions itself. It shows what was recorded.

The sidebar carries six screens: **Home**, **Analytics**, **AI Chat**, **Sessions**, **Intent
Plans**, and **Policies**. Several more screens exist and are reached by links from those pages, or
by typing the address. Press <kbd>⌘K</kbd> anywhere to search policies, agents, and pages.

chunks.heading: Home
chunks.text:
The first screen after sign-in, and the one to check daily. Until your first run arrives it shows
the setup timeline instead. After that it becomes **Workspace overview**, with five counters: intent
plans and tokens over the last 24 hours, estimated spend and actions prevented over 30 days, and how
many things are **awaiting you**.

Below that, **Today's briefing** lists actions held for a human decision, and **Recent runs** shows
the latest activity with a verdict on each.

<Callout>
  The counters describe recorded activity. They do not measure how much went unreported, and the
  page says so rather than implying full coverage.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Sessions
chunks.text:
A session is one stretch of work with your assistant. This screen lists them with totals for the
workspace you are in, sorted by token spend by default. Use the sort toggle for most recent instead.
Filter by harness (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini), search the loaded rows, and sort by tokens or by
recency. Each row expands to show cache reads and writes, how many model rows the session has, and
when it was first seen. The per-model breakdown itself is on the session detail. **View activity**
on any row opens the session detail.

chunks.heading: Session detail
chunks.text:
The screen that answers "what did it actually do?". It has two halves, deliberately kept apart.

**Recorded session usage** is imported transcript usage: processed tokens, input including
cache, output, cache reads, and a row per model.

**Runtime evidence** is the tool and policy record. It holds the **MCP call ledger**, oldest
call first, filterable to failed calls, retried calls, or calls with a policy link. Select any call
to open an evidence drawer with its execution outcome, timing, policy result, and plan link.

Above the ledger, a three-step evidence chain summarises the session: call evidence, retry and
timing, then policy result. Underneath are four tables: **Tools** with call counts, errors and
average duration, **MCP servers**, **Policies** with allow, deny, hold and ask counts, and
**Models** with tokens in and out.

Policy links are reported honestly as one of three states: linked on this span, linked by call id,
or no policy link. A missing link means evidence was not reported. It is not proof the agent was
unprotected.

chunks.heading: Analytics
chunks.text:
Tokens, estimated cost, and latency, sliced the ways you actually ask for.

Pick a range (24 hours, 7, 30, 90 days, or all time), then filter by harness, by repository, and by
whether **Armor was on**, meaning a policy or tool was evaluated in that session. The daily chart
toggles between cost and tokens.

The tiles cover processed tokens, cached input, uncached input, output, and cache savings. A latency
card gives p50 and p95 turn wall time per harness, including any time the machine was asleep
mid-turn, which is why occasional outliers look large. Below that are breakdowns by model, by
session, and an **Agent session activity** table you can filter to one agent or one session UUID.

<Callout type="warn">
  Costs are estimates from configured model rates, not bills. Usage with no configured rate is
  excluded from cost and the page tells you how many tokens that affected.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: Policies and Policy Studio
chunks.text:
Two different things, kept on separate screens because they enforce in different places.

**Policies** lists server-side policies that apply to agents and MCP servers, with status tabs,
a decision filter, priority sorting, and card, list or timeline views.

**[Policy Studio](/tools/policy-studio)** is where you author the rules your local plugin
enforces: per-tool allow, block or hold, a folder lock, and the default for anything unmatched. This
is the screen most people want.

chunks.heading: Tools
chunks.text:
Which tools are configured, which were actually observed, and which were evaluated by ArmorIQ.
Filter by product, or by evidence: observed in 24 hours, guarded in 24 hours, errors in 24 hours, or
unused for 30 days. A **Connection evidence** card at the top reports whether an active device key
exists and whether a correlated evaluated session was found. The wording is careful on purpose: an
active key is not proof of a live connection, and configuration is inventory evidence, not live
reachability.

chunks.heading: Runs
chunks.text:
Executed agent actions across products, newest first, with a verdict on each: Running, OK, Blocked,
Held, Failed, or Unknown. Filter by product, agent, or verdict, search across action, tool, agent
and session, toggle extra columns, and **Export** copies the table to your clipboard as CSV.

chunks.heading: Intent Plans
chunks.text:
Every agent turn becomes a signed intent plan. This screen tracks how closely each run followed its
plan and where it drifted, with tiles for plan count, on-plan rate, held, and blocked. Each row
expands to show steps executed, risk level, model, tokens, cost, and the stated intent.

chunks.heading: Inbox
chunks.text:
Workspace notifications and actions held for a human decision, split into today and earlier.

<Callout type="warn">
  You cannot approve or dismiss a held action here yet. The console tells you what is waiting;
  resolving it happens in the agent workflow that raised it.
</Callout>

chunks.heading: AI Chat
chunks.text:
Ask about your recorded usage and policy activity in plain language, such as "how many tokens have I
used in 4 days?" or "which policies were most blocked in 30 days?". Answers stream back with
evidence cards that name their source, the window, and when the data was retrieved. Chat history is
not saved. Each conversation lives in the browser tab until you leave it.

chunks.heading: Other screens
chunks.text:
* **Machines** at `/users`: which machines are spending tokens, ranked, with cost estimates.
* **Graph** at `/graph`: a map from workspace to product to session to tools, MCP servers, and
  policy decisions.
* **Agents** at `/agents`: agents registered in the workspace, with a register dialog.
* **MCP Servers** at `/mcp-servers`: register, scan, and monitor MCP servers and their tools.
* **Prompts** at `/prompts`: reusable prompt templates with `{{variable}}` substitution. These
  are saved only in your browser, are not synced to your team, and are instructions rather than
  enforced policy.

chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.text:
Opens as a dialog over whatever you were looking at. **Profile** and **Appearance** cover your
account: name and email come from the provider you signed in with, and theme and density apply
instantly on this device. **General** renames the workspace, which admins only can do. **[API
Keys](/tools/api-keys)** manages keys for the SDK and CLI. **Billing** holds your plan, the monthly
or yearly choice, Stripe checkout, the customer portal and your invoices, with the invoice list
limited to admins. **Install** repeats the install commands so you can add another machine without
leaving the console.

chunks.heading: Enforcement
chunks.text:
Every action your assistant attempts resolves to exactly one outcome.

| Outcome   | What happened                        | Where you see it        |
| --------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| **Allow** | The call ran.                        | Allowed, on the session |
| **Hold**  | The call paused for a human.         | Held, and in your Inbox |
| **Deny**  | The call was stopped.                | Blocked, on the session |
| **Error** | The check itself could not complete. | Failed, on the session  |

Policy Studio labels these **Allow**, **Hold**, and **Block** on its buttons. Session evidence
labels them **Allowed**, **Held**, **Blocked**, and **Failed**.

The Policies table on a session detail carries a fifth count, **Ask**, tracked separately from Hold
so that the per-policy counts reconcile against the call total.

chunks.heading: How one is reached
chunks.text:
A tool call is checked against your workspace policy before it runs. The most specific thing wins: a
rule naming that tool takes precedence over the default for unmatched tools.

Policy evaluation is blocking, and it fails closed. If the check cannot complete, the call does not
quietly proceed as an allow. It is recorded as an error, which is why **Error** is a real outcome
you will occasionally see rather than a category that silently disappears.

chunks.heading: Two enforcement points
chunks.text:
**The plugin on your machine** enforces the profile you publish from
[Policy Studio](/tools/policy-studio). This is what stops a tool call before it runs.

**The server** holds policies that apply to agents and MCP servers, listed on the Policies
screen with their own actions: block, hold, allow and log, alert, and quarantine.

They are separate. Publishing a profile in Policy Studio does not change a server-side policy, and
the console does not pretend otherwise.

chunks.heading: How a decision is tied to a call
chunks.text:
On the session detail screen, each recorded call reports how confidently its policy decision could
be matched to it:

* **Linked on this span.** The decision and the call are the same record. Strongest evidence.
* **Linked by call id.** Matched by identifier across records.
* **No policy link.** No decision evidence arrived for this call.

The third case means evidence is missing, not that the call was unguarded. The console reports the
gap rather than filling it in, which is the same principle described in
[Telemetry](/tools/telemetry).

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
You do not have to read any of this to use ArmorIQ. Install it and it works. This page is for when
you want to know what it is actually doing.

chunks.heading: 1. Every action gets checked before it runs
chunks.text:
An AI coding assistant does not just write text. It reads your files, edits them, runs shell
commands, and calls out to the internet. Each of those is a **tool call**, and each one is a moment
where something can go wrong.

ArmorIQ sits between the assistant and your machine. Before a tool call runs, it is checked against
your rules, and it comes back with one of four answers.

<DecisionFlow />

**Allow** and the action runs, as normal. **Hold** and it pauses for you to approve, which is
the setting most people want on the things they care about. **Deny** and it never runs at all.

You control how strict this is. Everything your rules do not name falls through to a single setting,
which you can leave permissive while you watch what your assistant actually does, then tighten once
you know. [Writing rules](/tools/policy-studio) covers that choice.

chunks.heading: 2. Every call is recorded, in order
chunks.text:
A **session** is one stretch of work with your assistant. ArmorIQ records each call in that session,
what was decided, and how long it took.

<SessionTape />

This is the part people find most useful early on, and it has nothing to do with blocking. It
answers the question you cannot otherwise answer: *what did it actually touch?* When a test starts
failing or a file changed and you are not sure why, the session is the receipt.

chunks.heading: 3. The week tells you where to put a rule
chunks.text:
One session tells you what happened. A few weeks tell you what keeps happening, and that is what you
write rules against.

<DecisionTrend />

The useful signal is the thin band on top. Hundreds of allowed calls are noise. The handful that
needed you, or that got stopped, are where your attention belongs.

chunks.heading: What ArmorIQ never does
chunks.text:
The numbers above are the ones that were recorded, and nothing else. If telemetry did not arrive,
you see "unavailable" rather than a confident zero, and a session with no recorded calls says so
instead of showing an empty dashboard that looks like a quiet day. That matters more than it sounds.
A security tool that shows you a reassuring blank screen when it is actually broken is worse than no
tool, because you stop looking.

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ Tools
chunks.text:
AI coding assistants do not just suggest code. They read your files, edit them, run shell commands,
and call out to the internet, often faster than you can follow. ArmorIQ Tools gives you two things:

* **A record.** Every action your assistant took, in order, with what it touched.
* **A say.** Rules that stop or pause the actions you do not want it taking on its own.

Install it with one command. You choose what gets stopped, and you can start by just watching.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://armoriq.ai/install_armorclaude.sh | bash
```

That is for Claude Code. For Codex, use `install_armorcodex.sh`. Then open
[tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai) to watch runs arrive.

chunks.heading: Start here
chunks.text:
<Cards>
  <Card title="Quickstart" href="/tools/quickstart" icon="Rocket">
    Install, approve your machine, and get your first recorded run. About five minutes.
  </Card>

  <Card title="How it works" href="/tools/how-it-works" icon="Activity">
    What actually happens to a tool call, what a session records, and what a week tells you.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Tour of the console" href="/tools/console" icon="LayoutDashboard">
    Every screen at tools.armoriq.ai and what each one answers.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Writing rules" href="/tools/policy-studio" icon="ShieldCheck">
    Policy Studio: allow, hold, or block a tool, and lock a folder.
  </Card>
</Cards>

chunks.heading: Is this for me?
chunks.text:
It fits if you use **Claude Code** or **OpenAI Codex** and any of these is true:

* You want to let the assistant work on its own, but not blindly.
* Something changed and you need to know what the assistant did and when.
* You have a folder, a credential file, or a production config you never want touched.
* You are paying for tokens and want to see where they went, by session and by machine.

It is built around a single workspace per account today. There is no team management and no invites,
though billing does exist in **Settings → Billing**. See [Limits](/tools/limits) for the full list
of what is not built, so you can decide with the real picture.

Everything else sits under **Reference** in the sidebar: signing in, API keys, enforcement,
telemetry, architecture, and limits.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
The product claims to show you only what was really recorded. That principle is worth very little if
the documentation oversells the product itself, so here is what is not built.

chunks.heading: Not built yet
chunks.text:
* **Approving held actions in the console.** The Inbox shows you what is waiting, but you
  resolve it in the agent workflow that raised it. There is no approve or dismiss button.
* **Teams.** No invites and no member list. One account, one workspace, one person. Roles do
  exist on the backend, and a workspace can mark you an admin or not, which is why a few
  actions can come back asking for an admin even though you cannot invite anyone.
* **Switching workspaces.** Your account has exactly one.
* **Chat history.** Conversations with AI Chat live in the browser tab and are gone when you
  leave.
* **Key scopes.** You can scope a key to a product, but not to a set of permissions.

chunks.heading: Built, in case you were told otherwise
chunks.text:
* **Billing.** **Settings → Billing** is real: Free and Pro, a monthly or yearly toggle, Stripe
  checkout, the customer portal, invoices and a promo box. Pro is **$9 a month or $90 a
  year**, flat, no per-call overage. Invoices are admin-only.

chunks.heading: Rough edges
chunks.text:
* **ArmorCodex is younger than ArmorClaude.** The install path is less mature, and Policy Studio
  cannot sync a profile to it, because its current policy format does not support it. Codex
  sessions are still recorded.
* **Prompts are browser-local.** They are saved per account and workspace in your own browser,
  not synced to anyone, and not installed into your agents. Export anything you care about
  before clearing browser data.
* **Some screens are reachable only by link or address.** Tools, Runs, Agents, MCP Servers,
  Graph, Machines, Inbox, and Prompts are not in the sidebar.

chunks.heading: Things that look like bugs and are not
chunks.text:
* **Costs are estimates.** They are computed from configured model rates, not from a bill. Usage
  with no configured rate is excluded, and the page tells you how many tokens that was.
* **A session with tokens but no tools.** Historical token imports cannot reconstruct policy
  decisions, errors, or retries. The session is labelled rather than padded out.
* **A missing policy link on a call.** It means that evidence was not reported for that call. It
  is not proof the agent was running unprotected, and the console will not claim either way.
* **P95 latency unavailable.** Shown when there are fewer than 20 comparable calls, because a
  p95 over a handful of samples is noise.
* **A large latency number.** Latency is turn wall time, which includes any period your machine
  was asleep in the middle of a turn.

chunks.heading: Reporting something
chunks.text:
If a screen shows you a number you think is wrong, the session detail view is the place to check it:
it separates imported token usage from runtime tool evidence, so you can see which of the two
disagrees.

chunks.heading: Writing rules
chunks.text:
Policy Studio is where you decide what your assistant may do on its own. It publishes a policy
profile that the ArmorClaude plugin enforces locally.

Open it at **tools.armoriq.ai/policy-studio**, or from the **Policies** screen with **Open
plugin Policy Studio**.

chunks.heading: Tool rules
chunks.text:
A tool rule is one line: a tool name, and what should happen when the assistant calls it.

| Button    | What happens                                         |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Allow** | The call runs.                                       |
| **Hold**  | The call pauses and waits for a human to approve it. |
| **Block** | The call never runs.                                 |

Tool names autocomplete from the ones your assistant actually has: `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`,
`Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `Bash`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `Skill`, `Agent`, and `Task`. The
wildcard `*` matches every tool.

A good first rule for most people is `Bash` set to **Hold**. Reading and searching stay
instant, and anything that runs a shell command waits for you.

chunks.heading: Folder access rule
chunks.text:
Give it one absolute path and the assistant is blocked from file-path tool calls underneath it.
Use it for a credentials directory, a customer data folder, or anything you never want read.

<Callout type="warn">
  This is not an OS sandbox. It blocks direct file-path tool calls under that folder. Shell
  commands, relative paths, symlinks, and tools that take no file path need enforcement of their
  own. Do not rely on this alone to protect secrets.
</Callout>

The path has to be canonical and absolute, with no `.` or `..` segments.

chunks.heading: Default for unmatched tools
chunks.text:
Whatever your rules do not name falls through to this setting, and it is the single most
important choice on the page.

* **Allow unmatched tools.** Permissive. Only what you named is restricted, so day one is not
  spent clearing prompts.
* **Hold (ask) unmatched tools.** Everything you have not explicitly allowed asks first.
* **Deny unmatched tools.** Strictest. Only what you explicitly allowed can run.

Check which one your workspace currently has before you rely on either reading. Move to Hold or
Deny once you have watched a week of real sessions and know what your assistant reaches for. [How it works](/tools/how-it-works) shows what that week looks like.

chunks.heading: Publishing
chunks.text:
<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Save draft [#save-draft]

    Keeps your changes without affecting any running session. The page shows **Saved draft, not yet
    published** until you publish.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Activate for the plugin [#activate-for-the-plugin]

    Publishes a new version. The page confirms with the version number.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Restart your assistant session [#restart-your-assistant-session]

    A running session keeps the profile it started with. Start a new one to pick up the new version.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Verify a blocked call [#verify-a-blocked-call]

    Ask the assistant to do the thing you just restricted, and confirm it is stopped or held.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warn">
  Publishing confirms the rule reached the server. It does not by itself confirm your machine is
  enforcing it, which is why step four exists. ArmorCodex profile sync is not supported by its
  current policy format.
</Callout>

If your workspace restricts who may publish, activation returns a message asking you to have an
admin do it.

chunks.heading: Rules the simple editor does not show
chunks.text:
Policy Studio's editor covers the common shape: one rule, every agent, one tool, no conditions.
The underlying format is richer, supporting principals (agent, user, org, role), resource types
(workspace, file, directory, network, MCP server, secret), and conditions.

Anything more advanced than the editor understands is **preserved unchanged** and shown as a
count of scoped or advanced rules, with the raw definition available to expand. Editing simple
rules never rewrites or drops them.

chunks.heading: Server-side policies are separate
chunks.text:
The **Policies** screen lists policies that apply server-side to agents and MCP servers, with
their own statuses (active, draft, shadow, inactive, expired) and enforcement actions (block,
hold, allow and log, alert, quarantine).

Those are a different enforcement point from the plugin profile you publish here. A policy
listed there is not the same object as a tool rule in Policy Studio, and the two screens say so.

chunks.heading: Quickstart
chunks.text:
You need an account at [tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai) and either Claude Code or OpenAI
Codex already working on your machine.

Once you have an account, the console walks you through the last two steps below at
[tools.armoriq.ai/start](https://tools.armoriq.ai/start), and tracks your progress as you go.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Create your account [#create-your-account]

    Go to [tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai) and sign up with Google, GitHub, or an email
    address and password. Email sign-up sends a six-digit code, valid for five minutes.

    A workspace is created for you automatically on first sign-in. You do not have to name or
    configure anything.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Connect your terminal [#connect-your-terminal]

    Run one command. It installs the plugin into your assistant, plus the small `armoriq` CLI used
    for login and status.

    <Tabs items="['Claude Code', 'Codex']">
      <Tab value="Claude Code">
        ```bash
        curl -fsSL https://armoriq.ai/install_armorclaude.sh | bash
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab value="Codex">
        ```bash
        curl -fsSL https://armoriq.ai/install_armorcodex.sh | bash
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>

    The command first asks `Connect your ArmorIQ account now? (Y/n)`. Answer yes and it prints a
    **short code** and opens a browser tab asking you to approve this machine. Check the code in
    the browser matches the one in your terminal, then approve. If you decline, or if the terminal
    cannot prompt at all, the install still finishes and tells you to run `armoriq login` when you
    are ready.

    <Callout type="warn">
      Nothing is created until you approve. A code is valid for 15 minutes; if yours expires, run the
      command again for a fresh one.
    </Callout>

    On approval, one key is written to `~/.armoriq/credentials.json` with owner-only permissions.
    It reads nothing else on your machine and sends no source code.

    If you would rather not run shell commands yourself, the console offers a **Copy as a prompt**
    button that hands the whole install to your agent.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Run your first task [#run-your-first-task]

    Ask your assistant to do one small thing, so there is something to look at. The console
    suggests:

    ```text
    List the files in this directory and tell me what this project is.
    ```

    The prompt, the tools it used, the tokens, and the verdict arrive in the console within a few
    seconds. The setup page watches for it and marks itself complete the moment the first run
    lands.
  </Step>
</Steps>

chunks.heading: What you should see
chunks.text:
Open [tools.armoriq.ai](https://tools.armoriq.ai). The home page replaces the setup timeline with
your **Workspace overview**, and your run appears under **Recent runs**.

From there, three places are worth a look on day one:

* **[Sessions](/tools/console#sessions)** for the full list of calls in that run.
* **[Analytics](/tools/console#analytics)** for tokens and estimated cost.
* **[Policy Studio](/tools/policy-studio)** when you are ready to add your first rule.

chunks.heading: If nothing arrives
chunks.text:
Work down this list.

1. **Check the machine is connected.** In the console, open **Settings → API Keys**. An
   approved machine shows a key with a device name attached. No key means the approval did not
   complete, so run the install command again.
2. **Check the install actually reached the login step.** The installer asks
   `Connect your ArmorIQ account now? (Y/n)` before anything is created, and in a terminal it
   cannot prompt in (CI, and some IDE terminals) it skips login entirely and prints
   `Run armoriq login to connect later`. Running the install command again hits the same skip,
   so run `armoriq login` directly instead.
3. **Start a new assistant session.** The plugin attaches when a session starts. A session that
   was already running when you installed will not be recorded.
4. **Give it a moment.** The setup page polls every four seconds, then slows to every fifteen
   after two minutes. It never stops, and it re-checks whenever you return to the tab, so you
   do not need to reload.

A session that reports token usage but no tool traces is a known shape, not a bug: historical token
imports cannot reconstruct policy decisions, errors, or retries. The console labels it rather than
guessing.

chunks.heading: Next
chunks.text:
Rules are the other half of the product, and the part worth doing deliberately. Start with [how a
decision is made](/tools/how-it-works), then [write your first rule](/tools/policy-studio).

chunks.heading: Numbers are read, not estimated
chunks.text:
Token counts come from the assistant's own transcripts on your machine. The plugin reads what the
provider recorded and reports the aggregate. Nothing in that path tokenizes or estimates anything.

Cost is the exception, and it is labelled as one. It is computed from configured model rates, so it
is an estimate rather than a bill, and usage with no configured rate is left out of the total rather
than guessed at.

chunks.heading: "Unavailable" means unavailable
chunks.text:
This is the part worth understanding, because it changes how you read every screen.

* A failed request shows **unavailable**, never zero. An error is not turned into "0 runs, $0".
* A session with no recorded tool traces says so, rather than rendering an empty dashboard that
  looks like a quiet day.
* Evidence that cannot be classified is labelled **Unknown**, rather than counted as "no
  evaluation".
* A call with no linked policy decision says the link is missing, not that the call was
  unguarded.

A security tool that shows a reassuring blank screen when it is actually broken is worse than no
tool, because you stop looking. Every one of the behaviours above exists so that a problem with the
pipeline looks like a problem rather than like good news.

chunks.heading: What leaves your machine
chunks.text:
The plugin reports what your assistant did: tool names, timings, policy decisions, token counts, and
session and device identifiers. It does not send your source code. The key written at install is
scoped to run ingestion, and reads nothing else on the machine.

chunks.heading: Checking the pipeline itself
chunks.text:
The session detail screen carries an ingest health indicator, so you can tell a quiet week apart
from a broken reporting path. If spans are being rejected or duplicated, that shows up there rather
than as a plausible-looking number somewhere else.

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ SDK
chunks.text:
# ArmorIQ SDK [#armoriq-sdk]

**One API key. Email per request. Done.**

The ArmorIQ SDK lets you build AI agents whose every action is cryptographically
verified against an explicit plan - before it ever reaches an MCP tool.

chunks.heading: Why ArmorIQ
chunks.text:
* **Simple** - one API key, no cloud credentials, no user/agent IDs to manage
* **Secure** - every tool call is cryptographically verified against a signed plan
* **Auditable** - every decision (allow / hold / block) is attributed to an end-user email
* **Framework-native** - Google ADK, LangChain and Strands adapters in both
  Python and TypeScript; CrewAI in Python

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
1. You initialize the client once with your API key.
2. The agent produces a plan. The SDK canonicalizes it and mints an intent token
   (via CSRG-IAP).
3. Every `invoke()` call is checked against that plan at the proxy, and
   attributed to the end user you name.

Two ways to name the end user. Pass `user_email` per call, as below, or open a
per-user scope with `client.for_user(email)` and run a session from it. Sessions
add policy enforcement, holds, and approval waiting; see
[Client Initialization](/sdk/client-initialization).

**Traditional approach:**

<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    # Direct calls - no verification
    api.call("service1", "action1")
    api.call("service2", "action2")
    api.call("service3", "action3")  # Could be malicious!
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    // Direct calls - no verification
    api.call('service1', 'action1');
    api.call('service2', 'action2');
    api.call('service3', 'action3');  // Could be malicious!
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

**ArmorIQ approach:**

<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

    client = ArmorIQClient()  # reads ARMORIQ_API_KEY
    user   = "alice@example.com"

    plan = {
        "goal": "Fetch sales data and analyze Q4 performance",
        "steps": [
            {"action": "fetch_sales", "mcp": "data-mcp",      "params": {"quarter": "Q4"}},
            {"action": "analyze",     "mcp": "analytics-mcp", "params": {"metrics": ["revenue"]}},
        ],
    }

    captured = client.capture_plan(llm="gpt-4", prompt="...Q4 performance", plan=plan)
    token    = client.get_intent_token(captured)

    client.invoke("data-mcp", "fetch_sales", token, {"quarter": "Q4"}, user_email=user)         # OK
    client.invoke("analytics-mcp", "analyze", token, {"metrics": ["revenue"]}, user_email=user) # OK
    client.invoke("data-mcp", "delete_all", token, {}, user_email=user)                         # blocked
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import { ArmorIQClient } from '@armoriq/sdk';

    const client = new ArmorIQClient();              // reads ARMORIQ_API_KEY
    const user   = 'alice@example.com';

    const plan = {
      goal: 'Fetch sales data and analyze Q4 performance',
      steps: [
        { action: 'fetch_sales', mcp: 'data-mcp',      params: { quarter: 'Q4' } },
        { action: 'analyze',     mcp: 'analytics-mcp', params: { metrics: ['revenue'] } },
      ],
    };

    const captured = client.capturePlan('gpt-4', '...Q4 performance', plan);
    const token    = await client.getIntentToken(captured);

    // The 5th argument is merkleProof (optional); the 6th is the end-user email.
    await client.invoke('data-mcp', 'fetch_sales', token, { quarter: 'Q4' }, undefined, user);        // OK
    await client.invoke('analytics-mcp', 'analyze', token, { metrics: ['revenue'] }, undefined, user); // OK
    await client.invoke('data-mcp', 'delete_all', token, {}, undefined, user);                        // blocked
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The SDK validates your plan, CSRG-IAP creates the cryptographic proof
(`plan_hash`, `merkle_root`, `step_proofs`), and each `invoke()` is verified
against it at the Proxy. This prevents:

* Prompt-injection attacks that try to execute unplanned actions
* Unauthorized tool calls
* Plan tampering or modification

chunks.heading: SDK Observability
chunks.text:
# SDK Observability [#sdk-observability]

The ArmorIQ SDKs record one OpenTelemetry trace for each session. The trace holds spans for the plan, each policy decision, each model call, and each tool or command call. You add no span code, no trace ID code, and no flush code. This page is for developers who want the short version, with links to the full guides.

<Callout type="warn">
  This page describes the current releases: Python SDK `armoriq-sdk` **0.8.17** and TypeScript SDK `@armoriq/sdk` **0.8.23**. Older versions used a different recorder and a different route. See [Migrate from the legacy recorder](/platform/observability/migration).
</Callout>

```text
Session
└── Trace (one OpenTelemetry trace)
    ├── Plan
    ├── Policy decisions
    ├── Model calls
    └── Tool and command work
```

<Cards>
  <Card title="Set up tracing" href="/platform/observability/quickstart" description="Zero-touch setup for Python and TypeScript, and how to check the first trace" />

  <Card title="TypeScript SDK" href="/platform/observability/typescript-sdk" description="Options, environment variables, and session calls for @armoriq/sdk" />

  <Card title="Python SDK" href="/platform/observability/python-sdk" description="Options, environment variables, and session calls for armoriq-sdk" />

  <Card title="Framework support" href="/platform/observability/frameworks" description="Tested versions, lifecycle, native spans, and limits for LangChain, Strands, Google ADK, and direct model calls" />
</Cards>

chunks.heading: Shared Behavior
chunks.text:
* Tracing is on by default. You can turn it off for one session, for a process, or for the whole organization.
* The SDK builds a private tracer provider. A tracer provider is the OpenTelemetry object that creates spans and passes them to an exporter. The SDK does not use or change the provider that your application has.
* Spans go to ArmorIQ over OTLP (`POST /v1/traces`), by default. OTLP is the standard OpenTelemetry way to send trace data over HTTP. You can send them to your own OTLP endpoint or Collector, or to your own tracer provider. See [Choose who exports your traces](/platform/observability/provider-ownership).
* Your organization capture policy is the upper limit for the data that the SDK records. A local setting can only lower it. See [Organization controls](/platform/observability/organization-controls).
* Prompts, completions, and tool inputs and outputs are not recorded by default. Secrets and personal identifiers are removed in every mode. See [What data is captured](/platform/observability/data-capture).
* Telemetry errors are fail-open and do not change policy decisions.
* The SDK never falls back to another route, endpoint, or storage path. If an export destination is missing or not reachable, it exports nothing.
* Closing a session waits a short, fixed time to send the last spans. This is at most 3 seconds in Python and 1.5 seconds in TypeScript.

chunks.heading: What replaced the span primitives
chunks.text: Older SDKs exported low-level functions such as `startTrace`, `endTrace`, `openSpan`, `closeSpan`, `recordSpan`, `recordPolicyCall`, `recordEvent`, and `deriveTraceSummary`, and the classes `ObservabilityRecorder` and `ObservabilityShipper`. The current releases do not have them. The SDK now builds the span tree from the session API and the framework adapters. In Python, `session.record_generation(...)` and `session.flush_observability()` remain. See the [Python SDK](/platform/observability/python-sdk#optional-session-calls) and [TypeScript SDK](/platform/observability/typescript-sdk#optional-session-calls) pages for the calls that are optional, and the [migration guide](/platform/observability/migration) for the full list of removed names.

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ CLI
chunks.text:
# ArmorIQ CLI [#armoriq-cli]

The `armoriq` CLI ships with the Python SDK (`pip install armoriq-sdk`). It
handles auth, project setup, and control-plane registration so you don't have
to write any of that by hand.

chunks.heading: Commands
chunks.text:
| Command              | What it does                                           |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `armoriq init`       | Interactive setup - generates `armoriq.yaml`           |
| `armoriq login`      | Browser-based OAuth device-code login                  |
| `armoriq logout`     | Remove saved credentials                               |
| `armoriq whoami`     | Show current authentication status                     |
| `armoriq validate`   | Verify config, API key, and MCP connectivity           |
| `armoriq register`   | Push config to the ArmorIQ control plane               |
| `armoriq status`     | Show what's currently registered and active            |
| `armoriq logs`       | Stream activity logs in the terminal                   |
| `armoriq orgs`       | List organizations your account belongs to             |
| `armoriq switch-org` | Switch to a different org (mints a new scoped API key) |

chunks.heading: Typical first-time flow
chunks.text:
```bash
# 1. Install
pip install armoriq-sdk

# 2. Authenticate (opens a browser)
armoriq login

# 3. Scaffold a project
armoriq init

# 4. Verify config + API key + MCPs
armoriq validate

# 5. Push to ArmorIQ control plane
armoriq register
```

That leaves you with an `armoriq.yaml` in your project and credentials in
`~/.armoriq/`.

chunks.heading: State and logs
chunks.text:
The CLI keeps local state under `~/.armoriq/`:

* `state.json` - registered config, org context, login session
* `cli.log` - append-only audit log of CLI actions

chunks.text:
<Cards>
  <Card title="armoriq login" href="/sdk/cli/login" description="OAuth device-code login" />

  <Card title="armoriq init" href="/sdk/cli/init" description="Scaffold an armoriq.yaml" />

  <Card title="armoriq validate" href="/sdk/cli/validate" description="Check config, key, MCP connectivity" />

  <Card title="armoriq register" href="/sdk/cli/register" description="Push config to control plane" />

  <Card title="status + logs" href="/sdk/cli/status-and-logs" description="Inspect registered state and stream logs" />

  <Card title="orgs + switch" href="/sdk/cli/orgs" description="Multi-organization workflows" />
</Cards>

chunks.heading: armoriq init
chunks.text:
# `armoriq init` [#armoriq-init]

Interactive wizard that walks you through identity, proxy, MCP servers, and
policy defaults, and writes an `armoriq.yaml` you can check into your repo.

chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text:
```bash
armoriq init
armoriq init --output myproject.yaml    # custom path
```

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Flag       | Default        | Description                        |
| ---------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `--output` | `armoriq.yaml` | Path for the generated config file |

chunks.heading: What it prompts for
chunks.text:
* **Identity** - org, project name
* **Proxy** - the ArmorIQ proxy endpoint (defaults to production)
* **MCP servers** - one or more tool providers with URL + auth
* **Policy defaults** - allow / deny / hold rules

It will not overwrite an existing file without confirmation.

chunks.heading: Example output
chunks.text:
```yaml
# armoriq.yaml (generated)
identity:
  org: acme
  project: q4-sales-bot

proxy:
  url: https://proxy.armoriq.ai

mcp_servers:
  - id: data-mcp
    url: https://data.internal/mcp
    auth:
      type: bearer
      token_env: DATA_MCP_TOKEN

policy:
  default: allow
  rules:
    - match: { mcp: data-mcp, action: delete_all }
      decision: block
```

chunks.heading: Next steps
chunks.text:
```bash
armoriq validate    # check it works
armoriq register    # push to control plane
```

Or load the config directly from Python:

```python
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient
client = ArmorIQClient.from_config("armoriq.yaml")
```

chunks.heading: armoriq login
chunks.text:
# `armoriq login` [#armoriq-login]

Browser-based OAuth device-code flow. Saves credentials under `~/.armoriq/` so
subsequent CLI and SDK calls pick them up automatically.

chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text:
```bash
armoriq login
```

With flags:

```bash
armoriq login --backend https://api.armoriq.ai
armoriq login --org "Acme Inc"          # pre-select an org
armoriq login --org 5e1c...              # or by org id
```

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Flag        | Description                                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--backend` | Override the backend URL (useful for staging / local dev)                               |
| `--org`     | Pre-select an organization by id or exact name. You can still change it in the browser. |

chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
1. Prints a short device code and a URL.
2. Opens the URL in your browser for you to confirm.
3. On success, stores credentials locally.

chunks.heading: Related
chunks.text:
* [`armoriq whoami`](/sdk/cli) - see who's currently logged in
* [`armoriq logout`](/sdk/cli) - clear saved credentials
* [`armoriq orgs`](/sdk/cli/orgs) - list or switch orgs

chunks.heading: armoriq orgs & switch-org
chunks.text:
# `armoriq orgs` and `armoriq switch-org` [#armoriq-orgs-and-armoriq-switch-org]

Every API key is scoped to a single organization. If your account belongs to
more than one org, use these commands to list them and mint a new key for a
different one.

chunks.heading: `armoriq orgs`
chunks.text:
Lists every organization your logged-in account belongs to.

```bash
armoriq orgs
```

Output shows org id, name, and whether it's the currently active one.

Requires you to be logged in - run [`armoriq login`](/sdk/cli/login) first.

chunks.heading: `armoriq switch-org`
chunks.text:
Switches to a different organization. This mints a **new API key scoped to the
target org** and updates your local credentials to use it.

```bash
armoriq switch-org "Acme Inc"
armoriq switch-org 5e1c1234-....                    # by org id
armoriq switch-org "Acme Inc" --key-name prod-2026  # name the new key
```

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Flag         | Description                                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `org`        | Target org - either the UUID or the exact organization name   |
| `--key-name` | Optional name for the new API key (default: `cli-YYYY-MM-DD`) |

chunks.heading: Related
chunks.text:
* [`armoriq login --org <id-or-name>`](/sdk/cli/login) - pre-select an org at login time
* [`armoriq whoami`](/sdk/cli) - show current org context

chunks.heading: armoriq register
chunks.text:
# `armoriq register` [#armoriq-register]

Uploads your `armoriq.yaml` to the ArmorIQ control plane so the proxy and IAP
know about your MCP servers, policies, and agent identity.

Usually run after `armoriq validate` passes.

chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text:
```bash
armoriq register
armoriq register --config path/to/config.yaml
armoriq register --dry-run
```

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Flag        | Default        | Description                                                 |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--config`  | `armoriq.yaml` | Config file to register                                     |
| `--dry-run` | off            | Skip the network call - just write local registration state |

chunks.heading: What it does
chunks.text:
1. Loads and re-validates the config.
2. Calls `POST /iap/sdk/register` on the control plane with your API key.
3. Persists the returned registration state to `~/.armoriq/state.json`.

After a successful registration, your agents can run against this config:

```python
from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient
client = ArmorIQClient.from_config("armoriq.yaml")
```

chunks.heading: Re-registering
chunks.text:
Safe to run repeatedly - re-registration is how you ship config changes
(new MCPs, updated policies). Run `armoriq validate` first.

chunks.heading: armoriq status & logs
chunks.text: # `armoriq status` and `armoriq logs` [#armoriq-status-and-armoriq-logs]

chunks.heading: `armoriq status`
chunks.text:
Shows what's currently registered with the control plane - org, project, MCPs,
policy summary, and the last successful registration timestamp.

```bash
armoriq status
```

Reads from `~/.armoriq/state.json`. If nothing has been registered yet, it
will tell you to run [`armoriq register`](/sdk/cli/register).

chunks.heading: `armoriq logs`
chunks.text:
Streams the CLI activity log from `~/.armoriq/cli.log`.

```bash
armoriq logs                 # default: follow if stdout is a TTY
armoriq logs --follow        # force-follow
armoriq logs --no-follow     # print once and exit
```

Each line is a JSON record with a timestamp, event type, and details (login,
register, validation failures, etc.). Useful for debugging flaky setup or
auditing who-registered-what on a shared machine.

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Command        | Flag          | Description                        |
| -------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `armoriq logs` | `--follow`    | Keep streaming new log lines       |
| `armoriq logs` | `--no-follow` | Print current log content and exit |

chunks.heading: armoriq validate
chunks.text:
# `armoriq validate` [#armoriq-validate]

Checks that your `armoriq.yaml` is well-formed, your API key is accepted by the
proxy, and every MCP server in the config is reachable and reports its tools.

Run this before `armoriq register`.

chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.text:
```bash
armoriq validate
armoriq validate --config path/to/config.yaml
```

chunks.heading: Flags
chunks.text:
| Flag       | Default        | Description             |
| ---------- | -------------- | ----------------------- |
| `--config` | `armoriq.yaml` | Config file to validate |

chunks.heading: What it checks
chunks.text:
1. **Schema** - the YAML parses and matches the expected shape.
2. **API key** - hits the proxy's `/health` endpoint with your key.
3. **MCP discovery** - for each MCP server, lists tools to confirm it's reachable.
4. **Policy** - checks that every tool referenced in policy rules exists in the MCPs.

chunks.heading: Exit codes
chunks.text:
* `0` - all checks passed
* `1` - one or more checks failed; details printed to stdout

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
```bash
$ armoriq validate
✓ armoriq.yaml schema
✓ API key validated at https://proxy.armoriq.ai
✓ data-mcp - 12 tools
✓ analytics-mcp - 4 tools
✓ policy rules reference only known tools
```

chunks.heading: Client Initialization
chunks.text:
# Client Initialization [#client-initialization]

The ArmorIQ SDK follows a **one-key, per-request-email** model.

You initialize the client once per process with your API key. For every
end-user interaction, you derive a per-user scope with
`client.for_user(email)` - that is how the SDK tags policies, audit trails,
and intent tokens with the caller's identity. There is no `user_id` or
`agent_id` to manage in your code; the backend resolves them from the API
key + email.

chunks.heading: ArmorIQClient
chunks.text:
<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

    client = ArmorIQClient(
        api_key="ak_live_..."   # or read ARMORIQ_API_KEY from env
    )
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    import { ArmorIQClient } from '@armoriq/sdk';

    const client = new ArmorIQClient({
      apiKey: 'ak_live_...'   // or read ARMORIQ_API_KEY from env
    });
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

chunks.heading: Parameters
chunks.text:
<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    | Parameter         | Type  | Required | Default                   | Description                                                          |
    | ----------------- | ----- | -------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    | api\_key          | str   | Yes      | `ARMORIQ_API_KEY` env var | Your API key - must start with `ak_live_`, `ak_test_`, or `ak_claw_` |
    | iap\_endpoint     | str   | No       | resolved from env         | CSRG/IAP service URL                                                 |
    | proxy\_endpoint   | str   | No       | resolved from env         | ArmorIQ Proxy URL                                                    |
    | backend\_endpoint | str   | No       | resolved from env         | Control-plane backend URL                                            |
    | use\_production   | bool  | No       | `True`                    | Set `False` for local development endpoints                          |
    | timeout           | float | No       | `30.0`                    | HTTP timeout in seconds                                              |
    | max\_retries      | int   | No       | `3`                       | Max retry attempts for failed requests                               |
    | verify\_ssl       | bool  | No       | `True`                    | Verify SSL certificates                                              |
    | mcp\_credentials  | dict  | No       | `None`                    | Per-MCP auth overrides (also read from env)                          |
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    | Parameter       | Type    | Required | Default                   | Description                                                          |
    | --------------- | ------- | -------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    | apiKey          | string  | Yes      | `ARMORIQ_API_KEY` env var | Your API key - must start with `ak_live_`, `ak_test_`, or `ak_claw_` |
    | iapEndpoint     | string  | No       | resolved from env         | CSRG/IAP service URL                                                 |
    | proxyEndpoint   | string  | No       | resolved from env         | ArmorIQ Proxy URL                                                    |
    | backendEndpoint | string  | No       | resolved from env         | Control-plane backend URL                                            |
    | useProduction   | boolean | No       | `true`                    | Set `false` for local development endpoints                          |
    | timeout         | number  | No       | `30000`                   | HTTP timeout in milliseconds                                         |
    | maxRetries      | number  | No       | `3`                       | Max retry attempts for failed requests                               |
    | verifySsl       | boolean | No       | `true`                    | Verify SSL certificates                                              |
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

chunks.heading: Returns
chunks.text: An `ArmorIQClient` instance.

chunks.heading: Raises
chunks.text: * `ConfigurationException` - missing or malformed API key

chunks.heading: Per-user scopes
chunks.text:
All enforcement, token minting, and audit is scoped by user email. Open a
scope with `for_user()`:

<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    scope = client.for_user("alice@example.com")
    session = scope.start_session()
    session.start_plan([
        {"action": "fetch_sales", "mcp": "data-mcp"},
        {"action": "analyze",      "mcp": "analytics-mcp"},
    ])
    decision = session.check("fetch_sales", {"quarter": "Q4"})
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    const scope = client.forUser('alice@example.com');
    const session = scope.startSession();
    session.startPlan([
      { action: 'fetch_sales', mcp: 'data-mcp' },
      { action: 'analyze',     mcp: 'analytics-mcp' },
    ]);
    const decision = session.check('fetch_sales', { quarter: 'Q4' });
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

`for_user(email)` is cheap to call - the user context (org membership,
applicable policies, approver chain) is cached per email for 5 minutes.

chunks.heading: Loading from armoriq.yaml
chunks.text:
If you set up the project with the `armoriq` CLI (`armoriq init`), you get
an `armoriq.yaml` file you can load directly from Python. The CLI itself is
Python-only today; TypeScript config-file loading is on the roadmap.

<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    from armoriq_sdk import ArmorIQClient

    client = ArmorIQClient.from_config("armoriq.yaml")
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    // Coming soon - use environment variables or explicit args for now.
    const client = new ArmorIQClient({
      apiKey: process.env.ARMORIQ_API_KEY!,
    });
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

See [Configuration](/sdk/configuration) for the full YAML schema.

chunks.heading: Environment variables

chunks.heading: Migrating from an older SDK
chunks.text:
If you have existing code passing `user_id` / `agent_id` (or `userId` /
`agentId`), remove them. The SDK no longer requires these - they are
resolved per-request from the API key and the email you pass to
`for_user()`.

<Tabs groupId="language" items="['Python', 'TypeScript']">
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```python
    # before
    client = ArmorIQClient(
        api_key=...,
        user_id="user_12345",
        agent_id="analytics_bot_v1",
    )

    # after
    client = ArmorIQClient(api_key=...)
    scope = client.for_user("alice@example.com")
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    // before
    const client = new ArmorIQClient({
      apiKey: '...',
      userId: 'user_12345',
      agentId: 'analytics_bot_v1',
    });

    // after
    const client = new ArmorIQClient({ apiKey: '...' });
    const scope = client.forUser('alice@example.com');
    ```

chunks.heading: Architecture Overview
chunks.text:
# Architecture Overview [#architecture-overview]

ArmorIQ uses a **proxy-based architecture** where all agent requests flow through a secure verification layer before reaching MCP servers.

chunks.heading: System Components
chunks.text:
| Component         | Purpose                                                                           |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **ArmorIQ SDK**   | Client library that enables agents to securely connect and interact with services |
| **ArmorIQ API**   | Token generation and plan validation service                                      |
| **ArmorIQ Proxy** | Security gateway that verifies and routes requests                                |
| **MCP Servers**   | Service providers that execute specific actions (data, analytics, etc.)           |
| **MCP Registry**  | Catalog of available services and their supported actions                         |

chunks.heading: 1. Plan Capture
chunks.text:
```python
captured_plan = client.capture_plan(
    llm="gpt-4",
    prompt="Fetch sales data and analyze"
)
```

**Flow:**

* SDK sends plan to ArmorIQ API
* API validates plan structure against registry
* Canonical representation created
* Plan stored with unique ID
* Plan details returned to agent

chunks.heading: 2. Token Generation
chunks.text:
```python
token = client.get_intent_token(
    plan_capture=captured_plan,
    policy={"allow": ["*"], "deny": []}
)
```

**Flow:**

* SDK sends plan + policy to ArmorIQ API
* API verifies plan structure
* Canonical plan hash generated
* Token cryptographically signed with:
  * Plan hash
  * Policy constraints
  * Expiration time
  * User/agent identity
* Signed token returned to agent

chunks.heading: 3. Action Execution
chunks.text:
```python
result = client.invoke(
    mcp="data-mcp",
    action="fetch_data",
    intent_token=token,
    params={"query": "sales"}
)
```

**Flow:**

* SDK sends request to ArmorIQ Proxy with token and Merkle proof
* Proxy verifies:
  * Ed25519 signature validity
  * Merkle proof of action in plan
  * Policy constraints
  * Token expiration
  * Rate limits
* If verified, request forwarded to MCP
* MCP response returned to agent with signature
* Audit log created

chunks.heading: Layer 1: Authentication
chunks.text:
* API key validation
* User identity verification
* Agent identification

chunks.heading: Layer 2: Authorization (Policy)
chunks.text:
* Action allowlist/denylist
* Time-based restrictions
* IP whitelisting
* Rate limiting

chunks.heading: Layer 3: Intent Verification
chunks.text:
* Token signature validation
* Plan hash verification
* Merkle proof validation
* Action-plan matching
* Token expiration check

chunks.heading: Layer 4: Audit Trail
chunks.text:
* Complete request logging
* Plan history tracking
* Token usage monitoring
* Anomaly detection

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ API
chunks.text:
**Responsibilities:**

* Token generation and signing
* Plan canonicalization
* Plan validation
* Cryptographic operations

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ Proxy
chunks.text:
**Responsibilities:**

* Request gateway and routing
* Token signature verification
* Merkle proof verification
* Policy enforcement
* Rate limiting
* Audit logging

chunks.heading: MCP Servers
chunks.text:
**Responsibilities:**

* Execute specific business logic
* Return structured results
* Follow MCP protocol standards

chunks.heading: MCP Registry
chunks.text:
**Responsibilities:**

* Service discovery
* Action catalog
* Schema validation
* Version management

chunks.heading: Complete Agent Flow
chunks.text: Here's how a complete agent interaction works from user input to result:

chunks.heading: Flow Explanation
chunks.text:
**Planning Phase:**

1. User sends message to agent backend
2. Backend streams request to LLM provider
3. LLM determines required tool calls (e.g., "loan\_calculator")
4. Backend calls `capture_plan()` with tool calls
5. SDK sends plan to ArmorIQ API for token generation
6. API validates plan and returns signed IntentToken
7. Backend receives token for execution

**Execution Phase:**

1. Backend calls `invoke()` with action and token
2. SDK sends request to Proxy with token and Merkle proof
3. Proxy performs three-step verification:
   * Verifies Ed25519 signature
   * Validates Merkle proof (action in plan)
   * Enforces policy constraints
4. Proxy forwards request to appropriate MCP server
5. MCP executes action and returns result
6. Proxy signs result and returns to SDK
7. SDK returns result to backend
8. Backend streams result to user

chunks.heading: Cloud Deployment
chunks.text:
```
Load Balancer
   │
   ├──▶ API Instance (Token Generation)
   │
   ├──▶ Proxy Instances (Request Verification)
   │     └── Connects to MCP Servers
   │
   └──▶ Database (Plans, Tokens, Audit Logs)
```

chunks.heading: Scalability
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ is designed for horizontal scaling:

* **Stateless Services**: Add more instances as needed
* **Token Caching**: Reduce token generation load
* **Distributed Verification**: Multiple proxy instances
* **Load Balancing**: Distribute requests evenly

chunks.heading: What is ArmorIQ?
chunks.text:
# What is ArmorIQ? [#what-is-armoriq]

ArmorIQ is a **security platform for AI agents** that enables cryptographically verified action execution across multiple services. Think of it as a **zero-trust security layer** specifically designed for LLM-powered agents.

chunks.heading: The Problem We Solve
chunks.text:
Traditional AI agents face critical security challenges:

* **Prompt Injection Attacks**: Malicious prompts can trick agents into executing unauthorized actions
* **Agent Drift**: Agents can deviate from intended behavior during execution
* **Lack of Auditability**: No clear trail of what the agent planned vs. what it executed
* **Unauthorized Escalation**: Compromised agents can access services beyond their scope

chunks.heading: The ArmorIQ Solution
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ bridges two worlds:

1. **AI Agents** that use LLMs to reason and plan dynamically
2. **Zero-Trust Security** that cryptographically verifies every action

chunks.heading: Traditional Approach
chunks.text:
```python
# Direct calls - no verification
api.call("service1", "action1")
api.call("service2", "action2")
api.call("service3", "action3")  # Could be malicious!
```

chunks.heading: ArmorIQ Approach
chunks.text:
```python
# Step 1: Agent captures intent (LLM generates plan)
captured_plan = client.capture_plan(
    llm="gpt-4",
    prompt="Fetch sales data and analyze Q4 performance"
)
# LLM decides: data-mcp/fetch_sales → analytics-mcp/analyze

# Step 2: Get cryptographic proof for the LLM-generated plan
token = client.get_intent_token(captured_plan)

# Step 3: Only declared actions can execute
client.invoke(
    mcp="data-mcp",
    action="fetch_sales",
    intent_token=token,
    params={...}
)   # ✓ Verified (in plan)

client.invoke(
    mcp="analytics-mcp",
    action="analyze",
    intent_token=token,
    params={...}
)  # ✓ Verified (in plan)

client.invoke(
    mcp="data-mcp",
    action="delete_all",
    intent_token=token,
    params={...}
)    # ✗ Fails - LLM didn't plan this!
```

chunks.heading: Key Insights
chunks.text:
**Even though the LLM generated the plan dynamically, every action is cryptographically verified.** This prevents:

* **Prompt injection attacks**: Malicious prompts can't execute unplanned actions
* **Agent drift**: Agent can't deviate from captured intent
* **Unauthorized escalation**: Even if compromised, agent is bound to the plan

chunks.heading: 1. Intent-Based Execution
chunks.text: Instead of directly calling services, you declare your **intent** (what you want to do) upfront. This intent becomes a cryptographically verified contract.

chunks.heading: 2. Zero Trust Security
chunks.text:
ArmorIQ follows zero trust principles:

* Every action is verified cryptographically
* Tokens are short-lived and scoped to a specific plan (see [Security Model](/sdk/concepts/security-model) for current replay-protection limits)
* Plans are immutable once signed
* All requests are authenticated
* Complete audit trail maintained

chunks.heading: 3. LLM-Generated Plans
chunks.text:
Plans are **declarative** and **LLM-generated**, not manually coded:

```python
# ✓ Agent captures intent from natural language
captured_plan = client.capture_plan(
    llm="gpt-4",
    prompt="Fetch user data and calculate credit score"
)
# LLM generates declarative plan:
# [
#   {"action": "fetch_data", "mcp": "data-mcp"},
#   {"action": "calculate_score", "mcp": "analytics-mcp"}
# ]
```

**Why This Matters:**

* **LLM Autonomy**: Agent decides the best approach based on prompt
* **Cryptographic Binding**: Even dynamic plans are immutably verified
* **Declarative Security**: You secure what the agent wants, not how it does it
* **No Implementation Details**: MCPs handle the how, plans declare the what
